threads.author: threeway_02
threads.title: 36 and switching to electrical: union apprenticeship, trade school, or just find a shop?
threads.body:
I'm 36, been in insurance claims for 11 years and I'm done with it. I want to get into electrical. I've read a lot and I keep going in circles on the three options:

1. Apply to the IBEW apprenticeship (I'm in Irvington, so I think that's 102?)
2. Do a night program somewhere first
3. Just call shops and try to get hired as a helper

I have some savings but not a ton. Which of these actually gets me working and learning soonest? I'd appreciate honest answers, including "you're too late for X" if that's the case.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Not too late for any of them. We've had first-years in their late 30s and they tend to be the ones who show up.

On the union side: I can't give you dates, the application window and the aptitude test schedule are posted by the apprenticeship itself, so go to their site or call and ask. When I applied it was an aptitude test (math and reading), then an interview, then a ranked list. Could be different now. Irvington, I'd check whether you fall under 102 or another local before you apply; jurisdiction lines are not always where you'd guess.

While you wait, get hired by a shop. Hours on a job never hurt an application. Stay safe.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body:
Honestly I'd do 2 and 3 at the same time. Night school while you work as a helper. The list can take a while and you're 36, you want to be earning something now.

I went the trade school route and got hired faster than any of my buddies on the list. That was me though, and it was a long time ago. Your mileage may vary.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: 4th year in 164. applied at 24, got in the second time I took the test. worth it for me... but go work somewhere while you wait, the guys who come in with some hours are way ahead day one

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Different trade but same question I get from every kid who walks in my shop. I was in the union a few years before I came back to my father's business. The school and the benefits were the best part and I won't pretend otherwise. My father used to say the union teaches you the trade and a good shop teaches you the customer. You want both eventually.

replies.author: threeway_02
replies.body:
This is really helpful, thank you. Sounds like the answer is "apply, and get a helper job now regardless."

edit: thanks everyone. Called two shops today, one wants me to come in Monday.

threads.author: Edison.volts
threads.title: Ranked way down the list after the interview. Is it over?
threads.body: Did the aptitude test and the interview this summer. Got my ranking and I'm way down, like 180-something. Vo-tech grad, no family in the trade. Is it basically over for this year? Should I just retest? Working nights at a warehouse right now so I can pay for my car.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Not over. Lists move: people take other jobs, move, don't show up. How far a list moves in a year depends on how much work there is, and I can't speak for how your local runs theirs.

Call the apprenticeship office and ask, politely, how retesting works and whether a retest replaces your score. Then go get a job in the meantime.

replies.author: ThreeWayConfusion
replies.body: I was ranked bad my first time too. Kept working at a shop in Lakewood, retook it, did way better on the interview because I could actually talk about work I'd done. 2nd year now.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Plenty of non-union shops in Middlesex would hire a vo-tech grad tomorrow. Your hours count for something either way.

replies.author: Edison.volts
replies.body: update: got hired as a helper at a shop out of New Brunswick, started last week. still going to retest. thanks

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: 40 and haven't even picked a trade yet. Am I kidding myself?
threads.body:
So I'm 40, Piscataway, been managing a call center for a long time. I like working with my hands, I fix everything at home, and I'm tired of spreadsheets about other people's work.

Problem is I can't decide between electrical, HVAC, and plumbing, and every week I change my mind. Also the money: I make decent now and I know the first year or two is a big cut. And my knees aren't 20 anymore.

For anyone who switched later in life, how did you decide, and how bad was the first year really?

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body:
What's your actual question? Because I see three: which trade, can I afford it, will my body hold up.

Which trade: go ride along for a day in each if you can. You'll know within an hour which one you hate.
Afford it: only you know. Write down your real monthly number before you quit anything.
Body: plumbing is hard on knees and backs, I won't lie to you.

I came in at 26 from restaurant management. Different age, same fear. It was the right call for me.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Pay-cut math I'd do before deciding:
- Your take-home now vs a helper's hourly rate times realistic hours (not 60/week, assume 45)
- Months of savings that covers the gap for 2 years, not 1
- Whether the shop pays for school, tools, a van, overtime
- Health insurance: who covers it and what it costs you

If the numbers work for 2 years, the age part is the easy part.

replies.author: big_zach_hvac
replies.body: did it at 40 last year, hvac. first winter was rough, knees are fine so far. pick one and go, you'll never feel ready

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire, for what it's worth: shows up on time, listens, doesn't need to be told twice. Age isn't on that list. Some of my best guys started in their 30s and 40s.

replies.author: QuickChekCrew
replies.body: I'd look at the night program at the county vo-tech before anything... I'm 33 and doing the HVAC one twice a week. Cheap compared to the private schools... not sure about electrical though

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body: Appreciate all of this. The ride-along idea is the one I didn't think of. Going to ask around and try to do one in each before the end of the year.

Brother, the only answer that matters is the one on the official apprenticeship site, because it's changed more than once since I got in 21 years ago. When I applied there was a test and an interview. Don't trust anybody's uncle on this, including mine.

replies.body: Apex grad here. I applied last year. I'm not going to say how the process works because I'm honestly not sure what's the same this year. Follow the official site and don't miss the window. I'm working non-union in the Bronx while I wait.

replies.body: In the city it's different from Jersey in a lot of ways, but one thing is the same: plenty of people build good careers non-union too. Apply, and don't put your life on hold waiting.

threads.author: BergenPlumber
threads.title: What license do I actually have when I top out?
threads.body: 3rd year apprentice. guys on the job say different things. when I finish, what am I? journeyman? do I need a license to work? when can I go for master? NJ. trying to plan ahead instead of finding out at the end.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Kid, this confuses everybody. NJ is built around the master license: that's the one that lets you pull permits and run work. There's a journeyman license too, and last I checked whether you need it depends on who you work for and what you're doing.

Don't take my word or anybody's on the job. Go to the state board of master plumbers' page and read the requirements, or call them. It's changed since I took mine.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: From what I remember you need five years as a journeyman before you can sit for the master. Took me forever.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: I don't think that's right anymore, and I'm not sure it was right when we did it either. Rules have moved around. That's exactly why he should call the board instead of listening to two old guys.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Fair. He's right, call the board. Ignore me on the number.

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: call the board. keep a log of your hours from day one, dates and who you worked under. you will need it.

threads.author: ms_almonte
threads.title: EPA 608: what my students get wrong every year
threads.body:
Every fall somebody in my class assumes the 608 is a formality. Here's what actually trips people up, in order.

First, they skip the Core section because it "isn't technical." Core is where people fail. It's rules, dates, recovery requirements, and it's all memorization.

Second, they cram the night before. You need to know the rules, not just recognize answers.

Third, they don't ask how their specific test is given. The format depends on which type and who's proctoring it, so ask the testing organization before you show up.

Go for Universal if you can. Ask me how I know you'll want it later.

replies.author: ExRetail_NowHVAC
replies.body: Starting my first HVAC job next month (came from retail, 35). Boss said get the 608 before I start. Is Universal realistic for someone with zero background or should I do Type II first?

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Realistic if you study. Plenty of my 17-year-olds pass it. Do the practice tests until Core is boring.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... I had a guy on my crew who failed Core three times because he kept saying it was common sense lol. It isn't. Study the dates.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: universal. dont overthink it, just dont skip core

replies.author: dahvacnj
replies.body: Type 1 I did open book online back in school, the rest was proctored. At least that's how mine was, ask whoever's giving yours

threads.author: LiveFrontLessons
threads.title: failed rough-in, boss says the inspector is wrong. who do i believe
threads.body:
1st year out of vo-tech, working for a small shop near asbury. we failed a rough in on a bathroom remodel today. inspector wrote up "physical protection" on a couple runs where the cable goes through studs, and something about the box by the vanity being too full.

boss says the inspector is being picky and he's done it this way for years. i don't want to say anything dumb but i also want to understand it. who's right

edit: it was nail plates on two studs where the holes were close to the edge. boss fixed it, passed on reinspection. thanks for explaining instead of just dunking on me

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it. When cable runs through a hole close to the edge of a stud, it needs protection so a drywall screw doesn't find it. That's what a nail plate is for, and it's one of the most common write-ups I see. Box fill is counting conductors, devices and clamps against the box's volume; a small box with a GFCI and a couple of cables fills up fast.

The inspector is enforcing whatever code edition is in effect for that permit. Next time, ask politely for the section number. Most inspectors will give it to you and respect you more for asking.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly nail plates are the number one thing I see guys skip on remodels down here. Your boss knows better, he just didn't want to hear it in front of you.

replies.author: Passaic_Sparky
replies.body: your boss is wrong lol. 9 times out of 10 when somebody says the inspector is picky, it's nail plates

replies.author: LiveFrontLessons
replies.body: thanks both. going to buy my own box of nail plates so it's never my fault again

threads.author: LateStartPlumber
threads.title: starting plumbing at 42 on staten island. is a master license even realistic?
threads.body: career change at 42, about to start as a helper. long term i'd want my own small business. how does the master plumber license work in the city vs nj? my brother in law in toms river says it's easier over there. is it even realistic to get there starting this late

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body:
In the city it's different. Last I checked the master plumber license wants years of documented experience working under a licensed master (I remember it as seven, but read the DOB's licensing page for the current rules), and the documentation is a real thing: affidavits from the masters you worked for. So start keeping records now. Every employer, dates, what you did.

Realistic at 42? If you stay with it, yes. You'd be in your 50s with a license, and plenty of guys run shops into their 60s.

replies.author: plumbguy917
replies.body: do the work first, worry about the license in 5 years. half the guys i know who talk about their own shop at year 1 are gone by year 3

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Jersey side isn't 'easier,' kid, it's just a different board with different rules. Pick where you want to work for the next 10 years and follow that one.

threads.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
threads.title: 6 months of demo and carrying water heaters. am I being used as a laborer?
threads.body:
Six months in at a small shop out of Bayonne. 90% of my day is demo, carrying material, cleaning up, and running to the supply house. I've sweated maybe 10 fittings total. The other helper has been there a year and says it was the same for him.

Is this normal or am I being used as cheap labor? Don't want to quit too early and look like a flake.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Six months of demo and material is normal, kid. Everybody carries water heaters. That's the job.

Red flags are different: no one explaining anything when you ask, still nothing but demo at a year, no talk about school, getting paid cash with no paperwork. If none of those are true, keep your head down a little longer and start asking for one new thing a week.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question: is it normal, or how do you get more? It's normal. To get more, ask your lead the night before: 'Can I do the fittings on tomorrow's job while you watch?' Specific asks get yeses.

replies.author: big_paulie_plumb
replies.body: i carried water heaters up 3rd floor walkups in north bergen for a year. hated it. it's also why i know how every tank in that town is piped lol

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire, and it applies to the helper who wants more: the guy who's already standing next to the work, watching, when the demo's done. Make it easy for them to teach you.

replies.body: same boat here... 4 months, mostly cleanup. this thread makes me feel better

threads.body: Three years at the same shop in Deptford. Paid cash every Friday. He won't send me to school, says I'll learn more on the job. I mostly get PEX on new construction, boilers in the winter if they're short a guy. Good guy, but I'm not going anywhere. How do I leave without burning it?

My father used to say never quit angry and never quit without the next job lined up. Small state. Everybody knows everybody. Line up the next shop, give him notice, thank him for the three years. That's it.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, but on the licensing side: start writing down every job, date, and who supervised you, now. If you ever go for a license you'll need to show experience, and cash with no records makes that hard.

threads.author: DinerCoffeeHVAC
threads.title: On call this winter for the first time. Lots of old steam in Bayonne. Tips?
threads.body: Shop is putting me on the on-call rotation this winter. Two years in, mostly forced air so far. Half our customers in Bayonne and JC have old one-pipe steam and I've only been on maybe five steam calls with my lead. What should I check first on a no-heat steam call so I don't look lost at 2am?

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Steam's simpler than people make it, kid, but it'll punish you for rushing.

Look at the sight glass first. Low water is the most common no-heat I see on old steam. If the glass is empty and the boiler's been firing, do NOT feed cold water into it hot. Shut it down, let it cool, then figure out why it's low. Then check the low-water cutoff, the pressuretrol, and whether the burner's even trying.

And call your lead. Nobody expects a 2-year guy to know everything on steam at 2am. That's the job.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Second thing my students forget: the house usually has a story. Ask the homeowner when it stopped, whether anyone added water, whether it's been banging. Two questions save you an hour.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... ok not AC, Pennsauken, first no-heat call on my own I spent 40 minutes on the burner and the switch at the top of the basement stairs was off lol. Check the switch.

replies.body: saving this thread. i'm on call for the first time this winter too, clifton

threads.author: benplumb79
threads.title: What should a 2nd-year non-union plumber make in Central Jersey?
threads.body:
Two years in at a non-union shop near Manville. Service and some remodel work. I'm at $21/hr, no overtime most weeks, I drive my own car to jobs. A guy I went to school with says I'm getting robbed, another says that's normal.

Not trying to start a fight, just want to know if I should ask for a raise and what's reasonable to ask for.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Rates swing a lot by shop and trade, so look at the whole package, not just the hourly:
- Do they pay for school or your license prep?
- Overtime: how often, and is it paid at time and a half?
- Mileage or a van: you driving your own car is a real cost
- Health insurance, PTO, tools

$21 with your own car and no benefits is on the low side for 2 years in, from what I see around here. Ask for a review, come with what you've learned to do on your own.

replies.author: Woodbridge.ducts
replies.body: my buddy is 2nd year and makes $40/hr. you're getting robbed

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Careful with numbers like that. A 2nd-year non-union helper at $40 an hour in Central Jersey isn't typical. Either your buddy's in the union and you're hearing the total package, or he's on a prevailing-wage job, or it's a story. Comparing a cash rate to a union package isn't apples to apples.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: He's right. The locals usually publish their wage and benefit package, so look that up on the local's site if you want a real comparison, and remember the benefits are a big piece of the number.

replies.author: CondensateOverflow
replies.body: 3rd year hvac non-union in bound brook, i make a little more than you but i have a van. the van matters more than people think

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Thanks. Going to ask for a review next month and bring up mileage. Will report back.

threads.author: WawaRunWired
threads.title: neighbors keep asking me to do outlets and ceiling fans. worth it?
threads.body: 1 yr in, non union shop in bergen. word got around the block that i do electrical and now 3 neighbors want outlets swapped and fans hung. cash. easy money right? or bad idea

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: in NJ, electrical work for pay is supposed to be done by or under a licensed electrical contractor, with a permit where one's required. If you do it on your own and something goes wrong (a fire, a shock), you have no insurance and no license behind you, and the homeowner's insurance company is going to ask who did the work.

Easy money until it isn't.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I did side work at your age. Got lucky. One of my buddies didn't, and a small job turned into a very expensive year for him. Also your boss will fire you if he hears about it, and he will hear about it.

replies.body: charge like $75 a fan and $25 an outlet. more if it's a high ceiling

replies.author: thiago_sparks

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: You're not licensed, kid. Tell them to call your boss. If your boss gets the job, you look good. That's the job.

threads.author: Kash_sing
threads.title: Before you go out on your own: what nobody tells you about year one
threads.body:
I get asked about this every week, so here's my list from 25 years, the last 14 running my own company:
- Get your license first. As I understand NJ's rules, registering as a home improvement contractor is not the same as holding a trade license, and it doesn't let you do licensed work. Check with Consumer Affairs.
- Insurance will cost more than you think, and you need it before your first job, not after.
- Price for callbacks. If you don't, every callback comes out of your pocket.
- Your first truck doesn't need to be new. It needs to start every morning in January.
- Keep your books from day one, or pay someone who will.
- Most new owners undercharge for the first two years. I did.

Ask questions below, I'll answer what I can.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: I'd add: decide early whether you want public work. Prevailing-wage jobs mean certified payroll and a lot of paperwork, at least on every one we've done. Good money, different business.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: And if you're taking over a family shop instead of starting one, it's all the same plus your father second-guessing every price you quote. Ask me how that's going.

replies.author: CondensateOverflow
replies.body: question on the first one, so if i register as a home improvement contractor i still can't do hvac work on my own? thought that was the whole point

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Short answer as I understand it:
- Home improvement registration is for general home improvement work
- HVACR work needs the HVACR license (or working under someone who has it)
- Check with Consumer Affairs for your situation; don't take a contractor's word for legal stuff, including mine

replies.body: saving this. 'start every morning in January' is going on the wall

threads.author: Exit117Plumber
threads.title: Why did my sweat joint leak? Should I just learn press?
threads.body: Vo-tech senior, helping my uncle on weekends. Sweated a 3/4 tee on Saturday, cleaned it, fluxed it, looked perfect. Turned the water on and it dripped. Redid it and it dripped again. Uncle says just buy a press tool and stop wasting solder lol. Is sweating even worth learning anymore?

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Learn to sweat, kid. Press is great and I own the tools, but you'll be on jobs where you can't press, and you need to know why joints fail.

Nine out of ten times a joint that looks perfect and drips has water in the line. Water in the pipe pulls the heat away and the solder never flows all the way in. Was there a valve or a low spot near that tee?

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Agree with Ziggy. And heat the fitting, not the solder. When the solder gets pulled in on its own, you're there.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What size torch tip and how long were you heating it? 3/4 takes more than people think, especially next to a valve body.

replies.author: FluxOnMyBoots
replies.body: guy in my night class showed us the white bread trick for water in the line. felt dumb, works

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: There was a valve about a foot away that was weeping a little. So yeah, probably water.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: There's your water. Fix the valve or get the water out first, then sweat it. You'll never forget this one.

threads.author: epa60812_2
threads.title: superheat vs subcool, when do i use which
threads.body: helper at a residential hvac shop in paterson, started this summer. my lead checks superheat on some systems and subcool on others and when i ask why he says 'it depends.' depends on what?? trying to actually understand it not just memorize

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Depends on the metering device... fixed orifice/piston, you're looking at superheat. TXV or EEV, you're looking at subcool. Your lead isn't being difficult, it really does depend lol. Look at what's on the indoor coil.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: and before any of that check airflow. dirty filter, dirty coil, blower speed. charge it with bad airflow and youre chasing ghosts

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Both right. Two things I'd add:
- Use the manufacturer's charging chart or label when there is one; it beats rules of thumb
- Write down what you measured every time, so you learn what normal looks like

replies.author: epa60812_2
replies.body: ok that actually makes sense. going to look at the coil on every job now

threads.author: RainDayRestock
threads.title: 3-way switches are breaking my brain
threads.body: First month as a helper in Brick. Boss had me watch him wire a pair of 3-ways in a hallway and I nodded like I got it. I didn't. Which wire goes on the dark screw and why are there two travelers? Is there a simple way to think about it?

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body:
Honestly everybody's brain breaks on 3-ways once. Think of it like this: the common (dark screw) on one switch is where power comes in, the common on the other switch is where it goes out to the light. The two travelers just run between the two switches, and flipping either switch picks which traveler is live.

Draw it on a piece of cardboard on the job. Seriously.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: And test, don't guess. Turn the breaker off, verify it's dead with a tester before you touch anything, then check your work with the power back on.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: drew it on a 2x4 my first year... still have the 2x4

threads.author: benplumb79
threads.title: Two years non-union in Somerset. Too late to try for the UA apprenticeship?
threads.body:
Sorry if this has been asked a hundred times. I posted a while back about making $21 an hour near Manville. I did ask for the review. I got fifty cents and a "we'll see in the spring."

I like the work and the guys, but I keep thinking about the union apprenticeship. I'm two years in. Would I be starting over at zero? Is there any credit for time already worked, or do they not care? I'd also be risking a paycheck I count on for something I might not get.

Not trying to trash my shop, they've been fair in other ways. I just want to know if this is a smart move or a step backward.
fact_risk: whether UA programs credit prior non-union experience
UA Local 9 covers the Manville area
application periods

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: call local 9 and ask how they treat prior experience. nobody on here can tell you that for sure.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Not a step backward. Different trade from mine, so take this as general.

Time you've already worked counts for something in the interview, because you can talk about real jobs. Whether it shortens the apprenticeship itself is a question for that program, not for me. Some programs have a way to evaluate prior experience and some don't, and those rules change.

What I'd do: apply while you keep the paycheck. Filling out an application doesn't require quitting anything. If you get called, then you decide. Stay safe.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body:
I'll give you the other side. I went union for a few years and then came back to my father's shop. The benefits were real and the school was better than anything I got on the job. What I didn't like was having no say in where I went.

My father used to say a man who takes the first offer never learns what he's worth. Ask the union your questions, ask your shop what their plan for you is, then compare.

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
replies.body: brother you're 2 years in and they gave you 50 cents. apply. worst case they say no and you still have the job

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly 50 cents after two years would bug me too. But don't hear 'we'll see' as a no, small shops get squeezed in the fall. Ask him straight what you'd need to show by spring to get a real bump. If he can't answer, that's your answer.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire, from the other side of the table: someone two years in who can explain what they did on a job, start to finish. That's worth more than a certificate. Union or not, keep a record of your work with dates and who supervised you. Whoever you talk to next will ask.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Kid, the guys who regret it are the ones who never applied. A form costs you nothing. Keep showing up to the shop until somebody hands you something better. That's the job.

replies.author: breakerbox_884
replies.body: Local 456, 3rd year, different trade, but I did a year non-union in Linden first. My interview went way better because I actually knew what a box was. Grabbed a Wawa coffee on the way and almost spilled it on my paperwork lol.

Thank you all, this is more than I expected. I'm going to call Local 9 this week and ask how prior experience works before I do anything else.

edit: called and left a message, waiting on a callback. Started writing down my last two years of jobs from my phone calendar in the meantime.

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: My shop teacher won't stop pushing the union application. Why is he so sure?
threads.body:
Some context first because it matters. I'm in the electrical program at the Mercer County vo-tech, I've been doing weekend helper stuff for a guy in Hamilton since June (mostly carrying, some pulling wire), and my shop teacher brings up the IBEW application basically every class. Like every single class. He hands out the flyer, he talks about the pension, he tells us non-union is a dead end.

The guy I work weekends for is non-union and he's doing fine. Owns two vans, takes his family to Wildwood every August.

So who's right? I'm not against the union. I just don't like being told there's one answer when I can see with my own eyes there's at least two.
fact_risk: union apprenticeship features (wage scale, benefits, school)
IBEW Local 400 jurisdiction for Manahawkin

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Your teacher has probably watched what the apprenticeship did for students before you, and that's a fair reason to push it. Structured school, a wage scale that steps up on a schedule, benefits, safety training built in. Those are real.

"Dead end" is too strong, though. Plenty of non-union electricians do well, and your weekend guy is proof. The honest version: the union path is a known path, and a good non-union shop can also be a good path. Apply, keep working weekends, and decide with real offers in front of you. Stay safe.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I'm the non-union guy your teacher is warning you about. Own my shop in Long Branch, went to trade school, did fine. But I'll admit the union guys my age have a pension I don't. Both things are true. Don't let either side tell you the other one's a scam.

replies.author: peteq75
replies.body: Former teacher here (middle school, not shop). Teachers push the thing they've watched work for their students. Doesn't make it the only thing, but he's not trying to scam you. Sorry, I know that's not a real answer.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body:
> he's not trying to scam you

Fair. I didn't mean he's scamming anybody. It's the "dead end" thing that gets me, because my weekend guy clearly isn't one.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: I left the union and I half regret it, so take that for what it is. What I miss most is the training. What I don't miss is sitting by the phone between jobs some years. My father used to say every road has tolls, you just have to know which ones you're paying.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire a kid out of vo-tech: shows up, has some hours, can pass a background check. Whether he applied to the union doesn't come into it. If you end up non-union, ask about school and how raises work before you take the job.

replies.author: Flushing.sparks
replies.body: Same thing at my school in Queens, except it's Local 3 every class. The foreman at my weekend job says the same thing yours does.

replies.author: HelperForNow
replies.body: non-union in manahawkin, 1 year. i put in for 400 anyway just to see what happens. no harm in having options

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: 4th year in 164... your teacher isn't wrong and neither is your weekend guy. my foreman says some of the best apprentices he gets came from shops like that... apply and keep the weekend job

background check requirements on public school jobs
OSHA 10 cost and availability

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
Here's what I'd tell him, from Burlington County. There's a UA local that covers South Jersey. I believe it's 322, but have him look it up and confirm; don't go off a contractor's memory.

Separately, plenty of shops down here hire helpers straight out of high school, especially commercial and service. Tell him to have a driver's license and be ready for a background check. Those two things get kids hired more than anything on paper.

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: Deptford here, 15 minutes away. Plenty of shops. Does he want benefits from day one, or is he okay with cash to start? I did three years of cash and wouldn't do it again. Appreciate you looking out for him.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Kid, the best thing you can tell him is to stop working at Wawa and start carrying pipe for somebody, anybody, while he figures out the rest. He'll know in a month whether he even likes it.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: Camden County vo-tech grad here... I think the county schools down here have some adult night programs but I don't know Gloucester's specifically. worth a phone call. edit: my old teacher says call the adult ed office directly, not the main number

replies.author: plumbguy917
replies.body: Appreciate it. 322 sounds right, I'll have him check. What's the deal with the background check thing though, is that a union thing or a shop thing

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Both, depending. A lot of our public work is in schools, so anyone on those sites has to clear whatever the district requires. Shops that don't do schools may not care. Tell him to keep his record clean and he'll never have to think about it.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: One thing nobody's said: tell him to keep a notebook from the first day. Every job, every date, every boss. My father kept one his whole career, and when I took over the shop it was the most useful thing he left me besides the trucks.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I'd put trade school on the list too, even though I'm biased. I think there's a private technical school or two around Blackwood. Costs real money though, so he should get a helper job first and find out if he likes it before signing anything.

replies.author: big_nicole_plumb
replies.body: Burlington County, 3 yrs non-union. Agree on the license and background check. Also tell him to buy a decent pair of boots before day one, my first shop sent a kid home for wearing sneakers.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Good on you for asking instead of guessing. One practical thing: whichever way he goes, he should get his OSHA 10 if he can find a class. It's cheap or even free in some places, it shows initiative, and it teaches him what not to do on a site. Stay safe.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Ha... I had a helper from Williamstown once, best kid I ever trained lol. Came from a pizza place. Tell your cousin attitude beats everything down here, and there are shops all along the Black Horse Pike that need helpers.

replies.author: plumbguy917
replies.body: update: he called two shops near Glassboro and one wants him to come in Thursday. Also told him about the notebook. Thanks everybody, this was way more than I would've known to tell him.

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: Do any non-union shops actually pay for night school?
threads.body:
Follow-up to my shop teacher thread. Assume I go non-union. Everyone keeps saying "find a shop that pays for school." Okay, but do those actually exist around Mercer, or is that just something people say?

The guy I work weekends for told me he'd "think about it" when I asked. I'm not expecting a free ride. I'd just like to know what's normal to ask for before I graduate and start applying for real jobs, so I don't ask for something crazy or settle for nothing.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly they exist, I'm one of them. I pay for night classes for my helpers once they've been with me a while, because I'd rather pay for school than keep training new guys. Not every shop does it. Ask in the interview: 'Do you help with school, and when does that start?' A shop that gets weird about the question just told you something.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Mine doesn't, for what it's worth, and I didn't ask before I took the job. I wish I had. Sorry, that's more of a warning than an answer.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Not dumb and not weird. People apply to more than one program all the time. In the interview, be honest: say you went to school for HVAC, say what draws you to electrical, and show you've thought about it. What hurts people is looking like they'd take anything. HVAC is a good background anyway; you've already been around controls and disconnects. Stay safe.

replies.author: ThreeWayConfusion
replies.body: Local 400 2nd year here, Jackson. A guy in my class did HVAC at a vo-tech before this and he's honestly the best at controls in the room. Nobody held it against him.

replies.author: groundrod_05
replies.body: Both matter. When I applied they asked about school and about work, so I would not let either one go. Drop Sundays and keep Saturdays. You still get the experience and your mother calms down. Appreciate you asking before it got worse.

replies.author: auelecny

threads.author: blowerwheel_91
threads.title: Two HVAC offers: big company with a sales quota or a 3-truck shop. Which one?
threads.body:
Apologies if this is not the right place. Morris County vo-tech, HVAC, class of '24. I have been doing boilers and furnaces at a small place, but they are slowing down and I'm looking.

Two offers. One is a big residential company with a lot of trucks and ads everywhere. The pay is a little higher, but the techs I talked to said they are expected to sell maintenance plans and equipment, and there is a number every month. It's also down 287 every morning. The other is a small shop in Dover, three trucks, the owner still goes on calls, a bit less money, fifteen minutes from me.

I want to learn the trade properly. Which one would you take at my stage? Thanks in advance.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Speaking as someone who runs a company and has no patience for quota culture:
- At two years in, who teaches you matters more than the extra dollar
- Ask the big company how much of the pay is commission or spiffs; the base is what you can count on
- Ask the small shop if the owner will put you on installs and service, not just maintenance
- Either way, ask what happens to you in January when the phones are busy and you're the junior guy

If the small shop answers those well, I'd take it.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: I worked for a big outfit for a year early on, out of Cherry Hill. Learned a lot about talking to customers, not a lot about troubleshooting lol. Small shop if you want to fix things.

replies.author: DinerCoffeeHVAC
replies.body: Sorry if this is obvious, but my buddy works for one of those big outfits and he's stressed every month about his number. He does make good money though. Depends what you want.

replies.author: TaylorHamHVAC
replies.body: came from a call center with quotas. would not do quotas again for an extra dollar. is the small shop offering any school or 608 help? that would decide it for me

replies.author: blowerwheel_91
replies.body: Thank you, this is helpful. I asked the small shop about installs and January, and the owner said I would be on installs with him through the winter. I'm going to take it.

residency vs workplace rules

Whether you can apply to more than one program in the same cycle, and whether it's where you live or where you work that counts, can differ from program to program. Ask each one. Write down who you talked to and when. Stay safe.

replies.author: threeway_02

threads.author: epa60812_2
threads.title: does my non-union time count for anything when i apply to the union?
threads.body: started at a non-union hvac shop in paterson in june, paid hourly, no benefits yet. been thinking about applying to a union apprenticeship next time one opens, maybe even electrical, i haven't decided. question for anyone who's been through it, brother: does the time i've already put in count for anything? like does it get you ranked higher, or skip a year, or nothing? i keep hearing alot of totally different answers. one guy at the supply house said it hurts you because you picked up bad habits lol

threads.author: oldsteam_zig
threads.title: To the kids who ranked low this summer
threads.body:
Saw a few of you beating yourselves up over a number. Here's what I tell my own helpers.

A ranking is one morning of your life. It doesn't know whether you show up, whether you listen, or whether you can carry a 50-gallon heater up a split-level's stairs without banging the drywall.

Go get a job with somebody who'll teach you. Learn to solder, learn to read a boiler, learn to talk to a homeowner without making her nervous. Then apply again with something to say. I've hired plenty of kids who never got into anything, and they're running service calls on their own now.

Don't quit on it. That's the job.

threads.author: peteplumb80
threads.title: Buddy from my vo-tech class ranked low and says he's done trying. What do I tell him?
threads.body:
Kind of a different one. I'm a 1st year in Local 24, got in my first try, and I know that's partly luck. My best friend from school applied the same time, ranked way down, and now he's saying he's done. He's going to keep working at the Wawa in Montclair and "figure it out."

He's better with his hands than me, honestly. I don't want to be the guy who got in lecturing him, but I also don't want him to waste a year. What would you have wanted someone to say to you? Or is it better to just leave him alone for a while?

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: I was your buddy... took me two tries. what helped was a guy at my shop saying 'you're working here anyway, apply again, what's it cost you.' no speech, just that

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Don't lecture him, brother. Get him a job carrying something. Ask your foreman if anybody's looking for a helper. That does more than any pep talk.

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: That's a good idea. My foreman knows half the shops in Essex County.

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: Did he say why he's done, or is he just embarrassed? Those are different. I'd let him be embarrassed for a week, then ask him to come help on something.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: The useful thing you can do is make the next step small. Not 'reapply,' just 'come with me Saturday, a buddy's shop needs a hand.' Once he's working near the trade again, the application stops feeling like a verdict on him. Stay safe.

replies.author: BergenPlumber
replies.body: Took me two tries at the test too. The second time is easier because you know what's coming. Tell him that.

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: tell him once, plainly. then leave it alone and let him decide.

replies.author: NorthJerseyCopper
replies.body: Ranked low twice before I got in. Tell him it's not the end of anything.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question: what to say, or whether to say anything? Say one thing, once, and make it an offer instead of advice. Then go back to being his friend.

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: update: brought him to a Saturday side thing with my foreman's buddy, a basement bathroom in Bloomfield. He was better at it than me lol. Says he'll 'think about' reapplying. I'll take it.

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: Apply right out of high school, or wait a year so I don't tank the ranking?
threads.body:
Third time posting about this stuff, sorry, the shop teacher thread got me thinking. If I apply to the IBEW the first chance I get after I graduate, I'll walk into the interview with one summer job, weekend helper hours and nothing else. If I wait a year and work full time at a shop, I'd have a full year of real work to talk about.

Logic says wait. My teacher says apply right away, every time, because "you can't get picked if you're not in the pile." I see his point, but I also don't want my first impression to be a weak one if it follows me. Does a bad first interview stick with you, or is every year a fresh start?
fact_risk: application fees
whether programs keep notes from prior interviews
eligibility age

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Your teacher has the stronger argument. I can't tell you whether any program keeps notes from a previous interview; ask them. But I've never heard anyone say they regret applying early. Apply when you're eligible, work full time while the process runs, and if you need a second try you'll have the year of experience anyway. You get both. Stay safe.

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body: From the other end of the age range: I wish I'd applied to anything at 18. Two questions back at you though. What's the actual downside of applying? And would you take it if they called?

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Different trade, but here's how I'd weigh it:
- Applying costs you a morning and maybe an application fee
- Waiting costs you a year of possible apprenticeship time
- A weak interview at 18 is expected; nobody expects an 18-year-old to sound like a foreman
Apply.

replies.author: auelecny
replies.body: Brother, I waited eleven years to start because I thought I wasn't ready. Idk your situation, but don't wait for ready.

replies.author: threeway_91
replies.body: same advice my boss gave me in tottenville, he said apply every year until theyre sick of you. i'm non-union for now and that's fine, but i applied anyway brother

threads.author: Exit117Plumber
threads.title: Do my vo-tech shop hours count toward anything after I graduate?
threads.body: In the plumbing program at the Middlesex County vo-tech. We do a lot of shop time, plus I help my uncle on weekends (he jokes I'm basically his foreman now lol, I'm not). Ziggy's been answering my questions on here and he said to ask the people who actually run the programs, which I will, but I want to know what others found. Do the hours in a vo-tech program count toward an apprenticeship or a license later? Or is it just a diploma and a head start?
fact_risk: whether vo-tech hours count toward a UA apprenticeship
whether schooling counts toward NJ plumbing license experience

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Speaking as someone who teaches in one: first, ask your program's coordinator directly, because whatever arrangements exist are specific to your school and to the apprenticeship you apply to. Second, assume nothing transfers automatically. Some apprenticeships may look favorably on a program, and some licensing paths may count certain schooling, but you'll want it in writing either way. Third, keep every certificate and transcript. Ask me how I know you'll need them years later.

replies.author: BergenPlumber
replies.body: My vo-tech didn't count as hours in 24 as far as I know, but it helped a lot in the interview. Thanks in advance if anyone knows different.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: It counts in the way that matters most: you'll know which end of a torch is hot on your first day. My father used to hire the vo-tech kids over everyone else for exactly that reason. I still do.

threads.author: Woodbridge.ducts
threads.title: Private HVAC night program while I'm already working. Worth the money?
threads.body: Less than a year in at a non-union HVAC shop in Woodbridge. Hourly, no benefits yet. A buddy is doing the evening HVAC program at one of the private tech schools and says I should too. He told me they quoted him something like the price of a used car. My boss says I'll learn more on the truck. Is a private program worth that kind of money if I already have the job? Or should I look at the county school's adult classes first. Honest answers, brother.
fact_risk: private trade school evening program cost
county adult HVAC classes in Middlesex

threads.author: Kash_sing
threads.title: Before you sign a private trade school loan, ask these questions
threads.body:
Every few weeks a new hire tells me what they owe on a private trade school program, and some of them didn't need to owe it. I'm not against private schools. Some are good. But ask these before you sign anything:
- What's the total cost, including tools, books and fees, not the monthly payment
- How many hours are hands-on shop time versus classroom
- What share of graduates are working in the trade a year later, and how do they count that
- Does the county vo-tech or community college near you have an adult program for less
- Would an employer pay for it if you got hired first

If the admissions person gets pushy when you ask, that's an answer too.
fact_risk: private school vs county adult program cost difference

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: All good questions. I'd add one from my side: ask to sit in on a shop class before you enroll, on a normal night. You'll see in ten minutes whether students are working or watching. Ask me how I know some programs don't love that request.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire, since it's related: I don't check where someone went to school. I check whether they can do the work and whether they show up. A certificate helps you get the interview, not the job.

replies.author: QuickChekCrew
replies.body: I'm doing the county night HVAC program twice a week... it was a fraction of what the private school quoted me... thanks in advance to anyone who knows if the county ones are any good for electrical too

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I'm the guy who went to a private trade school and it worked for me. But I was 19, lived with my parents and had no bills. It's different math if you're 35 with rent. I'd push back a little on making it sound like a trap.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Fair point, Thiago, and I'm not saying skip them:
- If the cost works and you learn better in a classroom, it can be worth it
- If you can get hired as a helper first, try that before you borrow

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: My father used to say never borrow for something you can get paid to learn. He wasn't always right, but he was right about that one.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: refrigeration side, nobody ever asked where i went to school. they asked if i could find a leak on a walk-in in july. winter is when you learn, and you can learn it for free if you're on somebody's truck

replies.author: WhichTradeTho
replies.body: I'm taking one night class at the community college to test the waters before I commit to anything. Cheaper than any program and I'll know by December if I hate it.

threads.author: big_ben_tools
threads.title: My dad is 45 and wants to do the HVAC night program. Too old?
threads.body:
Kind of a weird one. I'm in the HVAC program at the Gloucester County vo-tech, and my dad has been helping me study for the 608 at the kitchen table. Now he's into it. He's 45, works in a warehouse in Swedesboro, back's okay, and he's asking if he's too old to do the adult night program and switch.

I told him I'd ask people who actually do this. Is 45 too late to start in HVAC? Would anyone hire him as a helper at that age?

edit: he says thanks in advance and that he's "not that old" lol
fact_risk: county vo-tech adult night HVAC program

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Tell your father this, from someone who hires every year: here's what I look for when I hire, and age isn't on the list. Reliability, listening, and a clean driving record. Warehouse guys usually have the first two down. The real question is his body in an attic in July, so have him ride along on a hot day before he quits anything.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
From my side:
- 45 is not too late; he'd have 20 working years in the trade
- The pay cut is the real issue, so he should know his monthly number first
- The adult night program lets him keep the warehouse job while he finds out
Good on him for studying with you.

threads.author: OpenNeutralBlues
threads.title: 17 and every shop says come back when I'm 18. Is that a real rule?
threads.body: Electrical program at the Essex County vo-tech. Trying to get a weekend helper job. Called five shops around Nutley and Belleville. Three said call back when I'm 18. One said insurance. One hung up. I turn 18 in March. Is that an actual law, or just shops not wanting to deal with a kid? Right now I work Sundays at a Wawa on Franklin Ave. Would rather be on a job.
fact_risk: NJ restrictions on minors on construction sites
co-op / work-based learning programs at county vo-techs
insurance age requirements

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: there are labor rules about what minors can do on certain kinds of sites and with certain equipment, and insurance carriers can add their own requirements on top. Ask your school whether it runs a co-op or work-based placement; that's often how students get onto a site properly before 18.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: Same spot here but plumbing. I only get work because it's my uncle's shop lol. My shop teacher says the co-op thing is how most of the seniors get placed.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
A few things that may help:
- Ask your program about co-op or work-based learning placements
- Supply houses sometimes hire 17-year-olds for the counter or the warehouse; you'll learn every part by name
- In March, call the same five shops back. They'll remember you called

replies.author: blowerwheel_91
replies.body: Apologies if this is off topic, but I worked the counter at a supply house in Morristown at 17 before my first shop job. It helped more than I expected. I knew what everything was called on day one.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Call those three back the week of your birthday. I mean it. Persistence is half of why my father let me on the trucks young. The one that hung up, forget them.

threads.author: OpenNeutralBlues
threads.title: Is it dumb to pick electrical just because it's supposed to pay the most?
threads.body: Everybody at my school says electrical pays the best, so that's why I signed up for it. Honestly I like the plumbing kids' projects better. Is the pay difference between the trades actually big in North Jersey? Or is that just something people say at the Wawa? Don't want to pick the wrong one for the wrong reason and be stuck.
fact_risk: union wage scales roughly similar across trades in North NJ
locals publish wage and benefit packages

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: Plumber obviously, so I'm biased lol. From what I see on the union side the scales are pretty close between the trades, at least up here. Pick the one where you don't watch the clock. And the Wawa guys don't know anything, I say that as a Wawa guy.

replies.author: NorthJerseyCopper
replies.body: Same as him. Pick what you like doing. Idk anyone who stayed in a trade they hated just for the money.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
How I'd compare them:
- Look up the wage and benefit packages for the locals near you; most post them
- Non-union pay varies more by shop than by trade
- Long term, the money follows whoever gets good and runs work, in any trade
- You'll get good faster at the one you like

threads.author: EssexPipes
threads.title: Career switchers keep getting hired over us vo-tech kids. What gives?
threads.body: Not trying to start a war. Two years out of the Essex County vo-tech, plumbing, still mostly doing demo at a shop near Bloomfield. My shop just hired a 35-year-old guy who used to sell cars, and he's already on fittings while I'm still breaking up cast iron. Second time I've seen this. Is it because they think older guys are more reliable? Or am I doing something wrong? Kind of burns, I went to school for this for four years.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: I'll be straight with you: a car salesman knows how to talk to a homeowner, and he usually knows how to ask for what he wants. That's often why he moves up faster. It isn't age, it's that he probably asked. Go to your lead tomorrow and say, 'I'd like to do the fittings on the next job.' Your four years of school will show the minute they let you.

replies.author: DinerCoffeeHVAC
replies.body: Sorry, maybe a dumb take, but the same thing happened at my shop in Bayonne and it turned out the new guy just kept asking. I never asked. Started asking, it got better.

replies.author: plumbguy917
replies.body: the car salesman guy probably talks to the boss at lunch lol. your gonna have to do that too, it's half the job

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
From the owner side:
- Older hires often come in asking about the path, so owners see them as long-term
- Younger hires sometimes look like they're passing through, even when they aren't
- Tell your boss your plan; owners invest in people who say they're staying

replies.author: leadfree98
replies.body: wait so is it a good idea to just tell your boss you want more? I've been scared to, idk if it makes you look pushy, or is that only at some shops

replies.author: EssexPipes
replies.body: Fair, I never actually asked. Asked today if I could do the fittings on a vanity swap Monday. He said yes. Kind of annoyed it was that easy honestly. Is that how it works everywhere?

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: Update: did a ride-along in all three trades. Here's what happened
threads.body:
A while back I posted about being 40 and unable to pick a trade. Joy suggested ride-alongs, and she's been mentoring me since, so here's the report.

Plumbing: a day on a repipe in an old Colonial in Metuchen. Loved the problem-solving, hated my knees by 2pm.
HVAC: a changeout in a split-level in Edison in August. The attic was brutal, but the diagnosis part was interesting.
Electrical: a service upgrade in Highland Park, panel swap, PSE&G had to come out to pull the meter. That was the one where I lost track of time.

So I'm leaning electrical, and maybe the low-voltage side later because of my knees. Two questions: did anyone else pick partly because of their body? And is it crazy to plan around knees at 40?

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Proud of you for doing all three. What's your actual question, though? You already picked. You lost track of time on the panel job. That's the answer.

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body: Ha. Fair. I think I wanted someone to tell me it's okay that it's not plumbing, after you set the whole thing up.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: It's more than okay. I'd rather you pick the right one than mine.

replies.author: wchen_controls
replies.body: fwiw low voltage is a real trade and your knees will thank you. i've been doing bms and fire alarm for 14 years, most of my day is a laptop, a ladder and a ceiling tile. don't let anyone tell you it isn't real electrical work

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Planning around your body at 40 isn't crazy, it's smart. When I hire someone in their 40s, the ones I keep know their limits and tell me up front. That's worth more to me than someone who says yes to every attic and gets hurt in a month.

replies.author: GSP_Exit82
replies.body: this is really cool to read. im in the trades program at the ocean county vo-tech and my foreman at my summer job said the same thing, you know which one when you lose track of time. appreciate it

replies.author: big_zach_hvac
replies.body: did hvac at 40 too. attics in august are no joke. knees ok, back less ok. electrical makes sense, good luck

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: As a vo-tech kid who thinks about this way too much: a panel swap was the best day of my whole summer too, and the meter pull part is wild the first time you see it.

replies.author: QuickChekCrew
replies.body: Congrats... I'm still doing the HVAC night classes, I'm 33 and my knees already complain... thanks in advance for posting the follow-up when you start

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Good process. If you go electrical and later want low voltage:
- Get your OSHA 10 early
- Ask every shop you interview with whether they do any controls or fire alarm work
- Keep notes on every panel and service you touch

replies.author: WhichTradeTho
replies.body: 40 here too, bartending, same three-way choice. This is the most useful thing I've read on here. Doing my own ride-along next month because of it.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Love this. One thing my older students tell me: the first year is harder on the body than any year after, because you're doing everything the slow way. It gets easier as you get efficient. So don't judge your knees by one day on a repipe.

replies.author: peteq75
replies.body: Career switcher too (36, used to teach middle school). Did basically the same thing and electrical won. Sorry for the dumb question, but did they let you actually do anything on the ride-alongs or just watch?

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body: Mostly watching. On the electrical one he had me land a couple of breakers with the power off, after he tested it, him standing right there. Probably why I liked it lol.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Ha, 'the attic was brutal' is every HVAC guy's August... respect for trying all three, most people never do lol

replies.author: middlesex_coils
replies.body: 35, woodbridge, ex-bartender, hvac helper now. reading this made me feel better about how i picked. the attic part is very real

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body:
Appreciate everyone. Not deciding yet: the HVAC startup day last Saturday threw me, more on that in its own post, and I'll look at the low-voltage side once I know what I'm doing.

edit: two interviews set up already.

threads.author: joyd_plumbing
threads.title: Came in at 26 from restaurant management. Career switchers, ask me.
threads.body: I get the same five questions from switchers, so I'll take them here. Background: ran a restaurant for a few years, quit at 26, got hired as a helper by a plumber in Jersey City who needed someone who could handle customers. 17 years later I'm a master plumber with a three-person crew doing multifamily and co-ops in Hudson County. I'm not going to tell you it was easy or that it'll work for you. I'll tell you what happened to me. Ask.

replies.author: plumbnj88
replies.body: 36, bartending, woodbridge. how did you handle the pay cut the first year? that's the whole thing for me

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Badly at first. I'd saved about six months of rent and burned through it in four. What saved me was picking up two shifts a week at a restaurant that first year. Know your number before you quit. Not after.

replies.author: LateStartPlumber
replies.body: sorry if this is a dumb question but did anyone treat you differently for starting late? i'm 42 on staten island and i worry about that more than the work

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Some did. Mostly younger guys who felt competition. The masters who hired me cared that I could talk to a building super without starting a fight. Your age is a skill there. Use it.

replies.author: FluxOnMyBoots
replies.body: how long before you stopped feeling like the dumbest person on the job lol

threads.author: WhichTradeTho
threads.title: How do I put together a resume for a helper job when it's all bartending?
threads.body:
40, Perth Amboy, bartending most of my adult life, managed a bar in South Amboy for six years. Taking a night class to test the waters before I quit.

When I start applying for helper jobs, what do I even put on a resume? I've got nothing trade-related except fixing stuff at the bar: replaced a few faucets, cleared the floor drains more times than I want to remember, helped the beer guy run new lines to the taps. Do shops even want a resume? Or do you just show up?

edit: thanks everyone, printing one page tonight.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for when I hire a switcher, and a resume is a small part of it. One page. Put the bar management job first and say what you were responsible for: opening and closing, staff, cash, handling problems. That tells me you're reliable and can deal with people. Then one short line about the hands-on work. Bring it in person if you can, early morning, and ask for the owner. A lot of small shops don't read email.

replies.author: plumbnj88
replies.body: ex bartender too. i just walked in with a printed page at 7am. got hired at the second place. dont overthink it

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Bartenders make good helpers, I've had two. You already know how to keep a crowd calm and stay on your feet for ten hours. Say that. My father used to say the trade can be taught and the attitude can't.

replies.author: carlosu88
replies.body: call center to trades here. had the same question last month. one page, in person, worked for me.

threads.author: jess2093
threads.title: 28, woman, calling plumbing shops in Gloucester County. Two hung up on me.
threads.body: Left insurance claims a few weeks ago. Want to do plumbing. Have been calling shops around Glassboro and Pitman for a helper job. Two hung up after I said my name. One said they don't really have a bathroom on the jobs, hon. One was nice and said call back in October. I know some of this is just shops being shops, but it's hard not to take it personally. Any women here who got in this way? What worked? Should I just show up in person instead? Appreciate it.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Show up in person. Early, in work clothes, with a one-page sheet. It's harder to hang up on someone standing at your counter. I got the same comments at 26. The ones who said dumb things weren't shops I wanted to work for anyway. The one who hired me cared that I came back twice. Call the nice one back in October like they said, and mention that you called before.

replies.author: big_nicole_plumb
replies.body:
Burlington County, 3 years. The bathroom thing is so dumb, every job has a porta john or a Wawa down the road. Keep calling. There are good shops down here that hire women, mine's one of them, they just don't advertise it.

edit: also ask at the supply house counter. They know which shops are decent.

replies.author: ginaj75
replies.body: plumbing, pleasantville, vo-tech grad. only girl in my class. got hired by the 4th shop i walked into. the first 3 were weird about it. keep going

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: Deptford here. Appreciate you posting this. Were the ones that hung up small one-man outfits or bigger shops? Not asking for names. The bigger ones around here are usually better about it.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: When you walk in, ask for the owner by name if it's on the truck or the sign. My father hired two of his best people because they came in and asked for him, not for 'whoever's hiring.'

threads.author: Turnpike_Tech
threads.title: can i try a trade part time on weekends before i quit my day job?
threads.body: 34, voorhees, wife is supportive but honestly nervous about me taking a pay cut with a kid on the way. i work a desk job monday to friday that pays the bills. is there any way to do helper work on saturdays for a couple months to see if i even like it before i quit? or do shops not want part time guys? i'd do anything, carry stuff, clean up, whatever. not really looking for money, more like a test drive. thanks in advance

threads.author: peteplumb80
threads.title: First real paycheck in the apprenticeship. What tools are actually worth buying now?
threads.body: 1st year in Local 24, mostly commercial bathrooms so far. Got the tool list at the start and bought the basics. Now I've got a couple real paychecks and I'm tempted to go nuts at the big box store. What did you actually end up using every day in your first year that wasn't on the list? And what's a waste of money until later? I spend enough at Wawa already, trying to be smart about this.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Kid, buy what you reach for, and borrow twice before you buy anything else. First year, you want good channel locks in two sizes, a decent tubing cutter, a level that isn't junk, and a headlamp. Anything with a battery can wait until you know what your shop doesn't supply. And put your initials on all of it. Things walk on commercial jobs. That's the job.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First, a good headlamp. Second, knee pads you'll actually wear. Third, a tape measure you like holding. Students always skip the knee pads and regret it by 30. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Different trade, same rule: buy safety glasses you'll actually keep on your face. If they fog or pinch, you'll take them off, and that's when something finds your eye. Spend money there first. Stay safe.

replies.author: big_paulie_plumb
replies.body: 4 yrs in, my biggest waste was a fancy cordless set i bought my first year when the shop already had everything on the trucks. dont do that lol

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
replies.body: brother get a decent bucket organizer and stop carrying stuff in your pockets. took me 6 months to learn that one

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: Okay so headlamp, knee pads, glasses, initials on everything, and no battery stuff yet. My wallet thanks you guys.

threads.author: Bergen_Ducts
threads.title: New kid at my shop showed up in running sneakers. What boots do I tell him to get?
threads.body: So we hired a new helper last week... nice kid, 18, straight out of school... and he shows up to a basement in Hackensack in white running sneakers. Boss sent him to buy boots on his lunch and he came back with the cheapest pair in the store, which I get, he doesn't have money yet. I'm two years in so the boss told me to 'help him out.' What do you all tell a brand new guy about boots? Steel toe vs composite, waterproof, do they need to be 8 inch... and is there a budget pair that won't wreck his feet by October? I already bought him a Wawa coffee, I'm not buying him boots lol
fact_risk: EH (electrical hazard) boot rating
safety-toe requirements on commercial sites

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Waterproof, safety toe, good sole, and comfortable enough that he doesn't take them off at lunch. The cheap ones are fine for a month while he figures out what his feet hate. Then he buys a real pair. Tell him to try them on at the end of the day when his feet are swollen.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: If he'll be anywhere near electrical work, look for the EH (electrical hazard) rating on the label, and check whether your shop or the GC has a site rule on safety toes; commercial sites usually do. Composite toe is lighter and doesn't get as cold in winter. Beyond that, fit matters more than brand. A boot that's half a size wrong ruins a ten-hour day. Stay safe.

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: I'm still in school so I can't speak to brands, but our shop teacher made everybody buy boots the first week and said the same thing about trying them on at the end of the day. I got mine at a store on Route 23 in Wayne. Sorry, I'm over-explaining again, it's a habit.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First, safety toe. Second, a sole that grips a wet basement floor, because that's where he'll live all winter. Third, wool-blend socks, two pairs. Students blame the boot when it's really the cotton socks. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: waterproof. he will stand in a walk-in drain pan at some point. july or january, doesn't matter, wet feet all day is the worst

replies.author: dahvacnj

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: 8 inch if he's on ladders or uneven ground a lot. 6 is fine for bathrooms. That's just what my journeyman told me.

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: clifton, under a year in. i got the cheap ones at first like your kid and my feet were destroyed by the end of august. switched to a better pair and it was definately like a different job. tell him to save up for it, it's the first thing worth spending on

replies.author: Passaic_Sparky
replies.body: idk why everyone sleeps on insoles. cheap boots plus a good insole gets you through till payday

threads.author: Dev_H
threads.title: Starting at a new shop Monday after 3 years at the cash place. What should I bring?
threads.body: Took Rui's advice from my cash-pay thread. Lined up a new shop in Pitman before I gave notice, left on good terms, start Monday. Real payroll, they do service and boilers, five minutes off 55. Three years in, but I've never started somewhere new as anything but a kid. What do I bring day one? My own tools or wait and see? And how do I handle it if they treat me like a first-year when I'm not?

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Congratulations on doing it the right way. Bring your hand tools, clean and organized, and your PPE. Leave the big stuff home until you see what's on the trucks. On the first-year thing: expect it for a week or two. They need to see how you work before they hand you anything. Show them, don't tell them. Ask on day one who you report to and what they expect by the end of the first month. Stay safe.

replies.author: FluxOnMyBoots
replies.body: congrats. also pack a lunch the first week, you never know where you'll end up lol

replies.author: QuickChekCrew

threads.author: JerseyTomatoWires

replies.author: codebook_dale

replies.author: epa60812_2

threads.author: groundrod_05
threads.title: Got called for the Local 3 interview after a year of waiting. What do they look for?
threads.body:
Apex grad, working non-union in the Bronx for two years while I waited. I got the letter this week: I have an interview. I have been preparing with my mentor here, but I want to hear from more people.

What did your interview look like? What do they want to hear from someone who already has some field experience? I do not want to sound like I know everything, but I also do not want to undersell the two years I put in. Appreciate any advice.

how applicants are notified

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body:
Brother, you already know what I think, but for everyone else reading: the format changes, so I'm talking about what matters, not what the room looks like.

Be on time. Dress clean and simple. Answer the question they asked. When they ask about your year, give one real job start to finish and one mistake you made and what you learned. Don't trash your current shop. And leave an hour early, the trains have been a disaster.

replies.author: Flushing.sparks

replies.author: wchen_controls

replies.author: groundrod_05

replies.author: bklyn_arkady

replies.author: auelecny

replies.author: groundrod_05

threads.author: wchen_controls
threads.title: low voltage is a way in, and nobody at the vo-tech ever mentions it
threads.body:
small rant, then useful info. every year i meet vo-tech kids who've only heard about two options: line-voltage electrician, union or non-union. nobody tells them about building automation, fire alarm, security, data.

i've been in bms and fire alarm 14 years, somerset and middlesex mostly. it's a real trade. you still need to understand electricity, you still work under codes and permits, and in nj fire alarm work has its own licensing as far as i know, so check what applies to the work you'd be doing.

the pay is fine, a lot of the work is indoors, and your knees last longer. fwiw if you like troubleshooting more than pulling wire, look at it. ask me anything.

threads.author: mbell_wireman
threads.title: Before application season: get your paperwork together now, not the week it opens
threads.body:
Every year I watch people scramble for documents the week an application opens. Don't be that person.

I can't tell you what any specific program requires; each apprenticeship posts its own list, and you should go by that. But in my experience the usual suspects are proof of age, your high school diploma or equivalent, sometimes a transcript, a driver's license, and for veterans, discharge paperwork. Some of those take weeks to get.

Request your transcript now. Find your birth certificate now. If your license is suspended, deal with it now. None of this is exciting. All of it has cost people a year. Stay safe.
fact_risk: typical apprenticeship application documents
transcript turnaround times

replies.author: mbell_wireman

Fair question, no lecture. I can't speak to any program's current policy; ask them directly or read their application materials.

From the job side: a lot of the sites we work on, especially big commercial and data centers, have their own testing rules regardless of state law, and contractors follow the site's rules. Legal at home doesn't mean allowed on a site. If you want the job, plan as if you'll be tested. You're working around energized equipment. Stay safe.

threads.author: neutral_bar_99
threads.title: How do I explain to my parents that the trades aren't a step down?
threads.body:
This needs some background. I'm in the electrical program at the Passaic County vo-tech, and I'm good at it. My parents are both accountants in Wayne and they want me to go to a four-year college. They're not mean about it, they just think trades are what you do if college doesn't work out.

I want to apply to an apprenticeship and work. I've tried explaining, but I end up sounding like a kid who doesn't want to study. How did any of you have this conversation with your parents? What actually convinced them, if anything did?

I'm writing this from the Wawa parking lot on Hamburg Turnpike because I didn't want to have this argument again tonight.
fact_risk: college credit arrangements for apprenticeship coursework
apprentices paid while training

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: I have this conversation with parents every semester at open house. First, show them a plan, not a feeling: the apprenticeship, the school hours, the pay scale, the license at the end. Accountants love a plan. Second, point out that apprentices are generally paid while they train, which a lot of parents don't realize. Third, invite them to talk to someone in the trade.
