threads.author: codebook_dale
threads.title: From the inspection side: whose license belongs on a heat pump swap
threads.body:
I get some version of this question every week this time of year, so I'll put it in one place. Not legal advice; your local construction office has the final word.

As I understand the current rules, a condenser or heat pump replacement in NJ usually touches more than one subcode. The mechanical work goes on a permit from a contractor holding the HVACR license. The new disconnect, the whip and any circuit changes are electrical work, which means an Electrical Contractor pulls that permit or the work is done under one. Some companies have both licenses in-house. Plenty don't, and that's where I see trouble: the HVAC crew runs a new circuit because the panel was right there, and nobody pulled the electrical.

The HVACR license is also newer than a lot of people assume. If I remember right it became required around 2014, so you'll still meet techs who talk like it doesn't exist.

If you're a helper and you don't know whose license a job is under, it's a fair thing to ask. And find out which edition of the code the permit falls under; it changes what I look for.

threads.author: mbell_wireman
threads.title: Don't cut a line set on demo until someone certified has recovered it
threads.body:
Saw this twice this summer on fit-outs, so I'm posting it for the electrical apprentices.

You're demoing a space, there's an old split system or a rooftop unit coming out, and someone hands a first-year a pair of cutters and points at the copper. Don't. Unless someone with a 608 has recovered the refrigerant and told you it's done, that line set may still be charged. Cutting it vents refrigerant, which as I understand it is illegal, and at close range it can freeze-burn your hands and face.

Ask the GC or the HVAC sub, "has this been recovered?" and get a name. It's the same as LOTO: you don't assume it's dead because somebody said it probably is. Glasses and gloves either way. Stay safe.

replies.author: Kash_sing

fact_risk: the NJ UCC adopts one set of subcodes statewide; enforcement is local

threads.author: JerseyTomatoWires

threads.body:

isn't the code supposed to be the same everywhere in NJ? how does that even happen

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
The code is statewide; the UCC adopts one set of subcodes for everybody. The people enforcing it are local, and some sections leave room for judgment, so two good inspectors can read the same sentence differently.

What I'd do: ask the one who wrote it up for the code section, politely, and bring it to your foreman. If it's a real disagreement, the construction official in that town can sort it out. Also look at the permit dates. Permits filed at different times may not be under the same code edition.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Not legal advice, and plumbing isn't my subcode, but I can tell you how the UCC generally works. Many construction offices treat a water heater swap as permit work, sometimes under a quicker category where you can start right away and the inspection follows. The gas connection and the venting are part of what gets looked at.

Call the town's construction office for how they handle it. And your boss is right.

First year non-union, Denville. Failed the rough on a basement finish today. Inspector circled a bunch of runs and wrote "cable not secured within required distance of box," plus something about stacking cables under one staple. My lead was out sick so I did most of those runs myself, which is great.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
For NM cable, the editions I've enforced want it secured within 12 inches of a box and at intervals of no more than 4 1/2 feet after that, with exceptions for things like fishing through finished walls. Check which code edition is in effect for your permit, but that part hasn't changed in a long time.

On two cables under one staple: it depends on the staple. Some are listed for two cables stacked flat and some aren't. Look at the box they came in. If the listing doesn't allow it, it's a fair write-up.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Agree with Dale. And since your lead was out: next time, it's fine to ask the shop for someone to look over your runs before the inspector does. A second set of eyes beats a red tag. Stay safe.

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body:
In the city it's different from anything I knew growing up in Jersey. As I understand the current rules, gas work has to be done by a licensed master plumber or by someone working for one who holds a DOB gas work qualification. Getting the qualification means an approved training course, and there's more than one level of it. I won't quote you hours or prerequisites; they've been adjusted since it started, and the DOB's page has the current list.

It's separate from the master license. The master is years down the road and needs documented experience with affidavits. The gas qualification is what lets you actually work on gas for a licensed master in the meantime. Ask your foreman which course the shop uses.

Today a homeowner in Washington Township told my boss he'd already pulled the plumbing permit himself to "save money" and just wanted us to do the work. Boss said no and walked away from a decent job.

Is that a real rule or is my boss being stubborn? Can a homeowner even pull a plumbing permit in NJ? And if he can, why can't a licensed shop just work under it?

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Your boss isn't being stubborn. My father used to say the permit is your name on the job. As I understand it, a homeowner can pull a permit for work on his own single-family house that he lives in, when he's doing the work himself. Once he hires a contractor, the contractor is supposed to pull it under his own license. Working under the homeowner's permit doesn't take your boss's license off the line if something goes wrong.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice. That matches how I've seen it handled across the subcodes: the homeowner permit is for a homeowner doing his own work. Call the local construction office if you want it from them; most will explain it in two minutes.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question, whether to be mad at your boss? Don't be. He just kept his license clean.

replies.author: plumbnj77
replies.body: brother my old cash shop used to do exactly this lol. one of the reasons i left. good on your boss

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: Appreciate it. Told my boss what you all said and he laughed and said now you know why I walked.

threads.author: JerseyTomatoWires
threads.title: My first-year thinks he's just a laborer. How do I tell him what's normal?
threads.body:
4th year in 164. foreman paired me with a first-year on a warehouse fit-out in secaucus about 2 months ago... good kid, shows up, doesn't complain on the job. but at lunch he told me he thinks he's being used as a laborer. material, gang box, sweeping, fire watch. he's thinking about quiting.

problem is i half agree with him. i don't want to lie and say it's all fine. i also don't want to go over the foreman's head for him.

what do i actually tell him... what's normal at 2 months and what isn't? and is it my place to say something to the foreman? appreciate it

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Tell him the truth, kid. The first months are carrying stuff, and the way out is being good at carrying stuff. He knows where everything is, has the next thing in his hand before the journeyman asks.

Then tell him the other truth: if it's still only material at a year, he should say something. Different trade, same job.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
Here's what I look for when I hire, and what I'd want a 4th year doing for my first-years: give him one real task a day that you can check. Pull a run, terminate a row of devices, label a panel schedule. Then tell the foreman what he did right, by name.

You're not going over anyone's head. You're vouching for him. Foremen move the first-years somebody vouches for.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body:
> give him one real task a day that you can check

that part i can actually do... foreman lets me run my own little area so i can hand him stuff

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question? How to talk to him, or whether to talk to the foreman? Talk to him first. When you go to the foreman, go to say he's ready for more, not to complain for him.

replies.author: big_paulie_plumb
replies.body: my first year i would've killed for a 4th year who even noticed me lol. sorry, not super helpful, but the fact you're asking means he's lucky

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Brother, half my first-years think they're laborers because the job is a tower and they're on the material hoist all week. Tell him a building gets built in order. Right now the order is material. In two months it's pipe and wire. That's how big jobs go.

replies.author: TwistAndTape
replies.body: 2nd year in 164 and i was the gang box guy for like 5 months on my first job lol. then one day the journeyman handed me the bender and never took it back

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly the union side and the small-shop side look different here. In a shop like mine a first-year is doing real work by week three because there's nobody else. On a big job you can sit in material for months. Neither one is wrong, but he should know that's the trade-off he picked.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: My father used to say the apprentice who complains at the lunch table is still learning, the one who complains to the foreman is gone. Tell him to bring it to you, not the table. Lunch table talk travels.

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
replies.body: I was that guy a few weeks ago, plumbing side. What helped was someone telling me the actual red flags instead of just 'it's normal.' Then I asked for something specific and got it.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: ok so what are the red flags, straight up? so i can tell him something real and not just 'hang in there'

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Nobody explains anything even when he asks. Still nothing but material at a year. Paid off the books. No talk about school. He's in the Local, so school and paper are handled. That leaves the first two. At two months, neither one is true yet from what you're saying.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: From the inspection side: have him walk with you when the inspector comes through. A first-year who hears why something passes or fails learns more in twenty minutes than in a week of material runs.

replies.author: hudson_conduit
replies.body: lol at 'used as a laborer.' we're all laborers until someone trusts us with something. the trick is not acting like it's beneath you

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Mostly agree with hudson. But if he's asking, he cares. Don't make him feel dumb for asking. That's how you lose the good ones.

replies.author: Exit145Electric
replies.body: sounds like your foreman is the problem tbh. i'd tell him to find a different shop that actually lets him work

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: he's not at a shop... we're both in the local, he can't just switch shops lol. but i get what you mean

replies.author: sweatjoint200amp
replies.body: first-year here (plumbing, 5 months)... honestly just hearing a 4th year say 'this is normal and here's when it isn't' would help me more than anything. tell him what you'd want to hear

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: One more, since you'll top out soon: this is part of the job now. Teaching the first-year is what makes a good journeyman. Foremen notice who the first-years want to work with.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: update: told him basically what Haddad and Ziggy said, the red flags and the one-task thing. had him terminate a whole row of receptacles yesterday and i checked every one with him. foreman walked by and saw. kid was smiling at lunch for once... appreciate everybody

threads.author: OpenNeutralBlues
threads.title: Senior-year co-op has me sweeping and doing the Wawa run. Ask the school to move me?
threads.body:
Vo-tech senior in Essex County, electrical. Our co-op started in September, I'm placed with a small contractor in Nutley three afternoons a week. So far it's been sweeping, carrying boxes of fittings up from the van and going to Wawa for the guys. Two weeks of that.

My shop teacher said if the placement is bad we can ask to switch. I don't want to look like I'm complaining. Is two weeks too early to say something?

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: I've taken co-op students. Here's what I look for: does the kid ask what we're doing tomorrow. Before you go to the school, ask your lead that, and ask to carry the tools for that task, not just the material. If it's still only sweeping in a month, then talk to your co-op coordinator. They'd rather move you than lose you.

replies.author: groundrod_05
replies.body: Apex grad. Did basically the same thing in the Bronx for my first few months. Two weeks is early. Give it a few more before you burn the placement.

replies.author: auelecny
replies.body: brother i'm 35 and i swept for 3 months when i switched. idk if that makes you feel better or worse

replies.author: threeway_02
replies.body: Career switcher, about six weeks into my first helper job. My lead told me the sweeping is where you learn where everything goes in a house. He wasn't wrong. I can find a panel in a split-level in about ten seconds now.

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: wawa runs and sweeping are how everybody starts. ask one question a day. two weeks is too early to call it

threads.author: BergenPlumber
threads.title: 3rd year and still running material while the 1st years hang pipe
threads.body: 3rd year in 24. on a big commercial job in hackensack, and the foreman has me on material and fire watch while two first years are cutting in hangers and risers. is it because he thinks i'm good at material? do i ask him or go to the steward? don't want to make it a thing. thanks in advance

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Ask the foreman first, kid, not the steward. The steward is for when it's a problem, and this isn't a problem yet. Some foremen keep the reliable guy on material because he's reliable. Tell him you want time on the pipe before you top out. That's the job, but you can still say something.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: From the contractor side: the foreman may not even have noticed. Big jobs have a lot going on. Ask for something specific, like 'can I get on the risers next week,' and he'll probably say yes.

threads.author: neutral_bar_99
threads.title: Saturday helper job is all carrying, and my parents want me doing SAT prep instead
threads.body:
I'll try to give the full picture. I'm in the electrical program at the Passaic County vo-tech, senior year. All summer and now on Saturdays I've been helping a residential electrician out of Wayne. It's mostly carrying, sweeping, holding the ladder, and the occasional Wawa run. I like it anyway, and he's a good guy.

My parents want college. They say if I'm "just carrying boxes" I should quit and spend Saturdays on SAT prep instead. Part of me thinks they have a point, because I'm honestly not learning a lot of electrical yet.

Is carrying boxes at 16 worth anything? Or am I wasting time I could use on school?
fact_risk: rules on what minors may do on job sites
apprenticeship diploma/algebra requirements

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Kid, your parents aren't wrong that school matters, and you're not wrong that the job matters. Every one of us started carrying. Don't quit because it's carrying. Quit if he's not teaching you anything when you ask.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: carrying is how they find out if you show up... you showing up on saturdays at 16 is already more than most people do

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body: In the city it's different with summer helpers, and I'd guess Jersey has its own rules too: there are limits on what a minor is allowed to do on a job, and insurance has opinions. So it may not be him holding you back. Ask him what he's allowed to let you do at your age.

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: That's a good point I hadn't considered. He did say something about insurance once and I thought he was just saying it. I'll ask him next Saturday.

replies.author: LiveFrontLessons
replies.body: vo-tech grad here. the summer job i had before senior year is honestly why i got hired out of school, the boss called my summer guy. so it counts even if its sweeping

replies.author: plumbguy917
replies.body: my parents wanted college too lol. now i'm in Local 1 and my mom tells everyone at church about it. they come around

replies.author: WiremanFromPiscataway
replies.body: for what it's worth i did college and then switched at 33. not saying don't go, just saying the trade will still be here. appreciate you asking this, wish i had at your age

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Talk to your parents with facts. Most apprenticeship programs I know of want a high school diploma and solid algebra, and they look at your grades, so school is part of this plan, not against it. Show them you know that. Then keep the Saturday job if you can keep your grades up.

And whatever you're doing on site, glasses and boots every time, even for sweeping. Stay safe.

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: Thank you. I'm going to show my parents this thread, which may or may not help my case.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Show them the part about keeping your grades up, kid. That's the part parents read.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: same situation in hamilton except my dad's a plumber and STILL wants me to go to college lol. you're not alone

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: update: kept the job. Parents agreed as long as my grades stay where they are. He let me make up whips for two condenser disconnects last Saturday (nothing live, and he checked every one). Small thing but it felt huge.

threads.author: ThreeWayConfusion
threads.title: Eight months pulling wire in the same warehouse. Do I ask to be moved?
threads.body:
2nd year in 400. Since February I've been on one warehouse job off Route 537 near Jackson. It's huge, so it's been pulling wire, more pulling wire, some terminations, a lot of lift time. I'm not complaining about the work exactly, I'm getting good at it and the crew is fine.

But my buddy from the same class has been on three different jobs, a school, a strip mall and some service work, and he talks about stuff I've never touched. Am I falling behind by staying on one job? Is it normal to ask to be moved, or does that look like I'm not a team player?

replies.author: JughandleJourneyman
replies.body: same thing happened to me in 164... 9 months on one job in secaucus. our training people told us you can ask about seeing different work, some locals care about rotation more than others... ask yours, at least that's how they explained it to us

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Not bad for you. Long jobs teach things short ones don't, like how a big job is sequenced. Ask anyway, politely, when the job's winding down.

replies.author: peteq75
replies.body: sorry if this is dumb, but isn't a long job a good thing? steady checks? i'm brand new, non-union and i'd definately take 8 months in one building over driving to 4 towns a day

threads.author: HelperForNow
threads.title: the GC keeps borrowing me for drywall cleanup on our remodel jobs
threads.body:
helper at a small electrical shop, residential remodels around manahawkin and the island. on the last two jobs the gc has been grabbing me when my boss isn't there. "hey can you help carry this drywall out," "can you sweep the kitchen for the tile guy." i say yes because i don't want to be rude, and then i'm behind on my own stuff.

is this normal? how do i say no to a gc without it getting back to my boss wrong

edit: told my boss. he was not happy with the gc. pretty sure that's handled now.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question? Whether it's okay, or how to say no? It's not okay if your boss doesn't know about it. Tell your boss and let him tell the GC. Not your fight.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Your boss is paying you, kid. The GC isn't. If the GC wants a laborer he can hire one. Tell your boss tonight, not the GC tomorrow.

threads.author: codebook_dale
threads.title: Inspectors notice which helpers are paying attention
threads.body:
Something I've noticed from the inspection side, for anyone stuck in the material-and-cleanup months.

The helpers who come along on inspections and actually listen are the ones I later see running jobs. Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: if your boss lets you, be there when the inspector walks the rough. Ask what he's looking at. Ask which code edition is in effect for that permit, and then go read the section he wrote up. Bring the permit card and the plans without being asked.

You'll carry material for months no matter what. Spend twenty minutes of it learning what passes and why. It's the cheapest education on the job.

threads.author: NorthJerseyCopper
threads.title: Old cash boss won't write a letter confirming my two years
threads.body:
Before I got into the Local I worked two years for a plumber in Garfield. All cash, every Friday. Now people keep telling me prior experience can matter later, either for credit somewhere or for a license someday. I asked him for a short letter saying what I did and when.

He won't do it. Says he "doesn't do paperwork." Not angry about it, just no.

idk what to do. Is it even worth chasing? Or do those two years just not exist now?
fact_risk: documenting hours for licensing
credit for prior experience in an apprenticeship

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body:
This is the trouble with cash. He won't sign because a letter is paper showing he had an employee. My father put everybody on the books and used to say that's what lets you sleep at night.

What you can do: write your own record now while you still remember it. Jobs, towns, rough dates, what you did. Keep texts, photos of you on jobs, anything with a date on it. Whether any of it counts for anything, ask your apprenticeship now and the board later. Don't assume either way.

replies.author: NorthJerseyCopper
replies.body: I have a lot of texts from him with job addresses and times. idk if that counts for anything.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Keep them, kid. Screenshots, backed up somewhere that isn't your phone. Whether they count is for somebody else to decide, but you can't use what you deleted.

replies.author: ParkwayPipes
replies.body: my old boss did the exact same thing. i stopped asking. been fine so far, 3 years in now. does it actually matter for union guys though?

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly don't burn him over it either. He'll say no to a letter, but he might pick up the phone if somebody calls him someday to ask about you. Small state.

replies.author: epa60812_2
replies.body: brother just go work for a shop that pays on the books, problem solved

replies.author: NorthJerseyCopper
replies.body: I am in the Local now. This is about the two years before that.

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: Is this why my shop teacher keeps telling us to keep a log from day one? I genuinely thought it was just a school assignment.

threads.author: plumbnj88
threads.title: saturdays with a plumber for cash while i still bartend. dumb idea?
threads.body:
36, woodbridge. still bartending nights, doing the night class. a plumber i know from the bar offered me saturdays, cash, carrying and helping on repipes. my mentor on here said keep a log of everything i do from day one so i started one.

question is whether cash saturdays are worth anything or if i'm just wearing myself out. not trying to quit the bar until i know.

replies.author: Edison.volts
replies.body: Did basically that before I got hired, brother. It helped because I could say I'd actually been on jobs. Thiago told me to get on with a real shop as soon as I could, though, and he was right about that.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Not dumb, kid. It's a smart way to test it before you quit the bar. Just know cash Saturdays don't cover you if you get hurt, and they probably won't count for much on paper. Treat it like a tryout.

threads.author: Flushing.sparks
threads.title: Weekend boss pays cash and says Local 3 is a waste of five years
threads.body:
I asked about the Local 3 application here a while back. Update and a new question. I've been working weekends for an electrician in Ridgewood, cash. He found out I'm planning to apply and now he's offering me full time when I graduate, more cash than I'd make as a first-year apprentice he says, and he keeps telling me the union is a waste of five years.

Money's good for my age. But is cash going to hurt me later? He says "nobody checks."
fact_risk: documenting experience for NYC DOB licensing
workers comp coverage for off-the-books work

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body:
In the city it's different from Jersey on the license side, but this part is the same: if you ever want a license, the DOB wants experience you can document, and in my experience "cash, nobody checks" doesn't document anything. Also ask him what happens if you get hurt. Off the books, that's on you.

Apply to the Local anyway. You can always say no to them later. You can't always get back in line.

replies.author: groundrod_05
replies.body: I'm non-union (Bronx shop, the Queens one starts next week) while I wait on 3, but I'm on the books. Big difference. If he really wants you full time, he can put you on payroll.

replies.author: wchen_controls
replies.body: fwiw 'nobody checks' is what people say right up until somebody checks. take the money for now if you need it, but keep the application in

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: Similar age and situation here in Jersey. My teacher says anything off the books is basically invisible later. Not sure that's literally true, but he says it a lot.

replies.author: OpenNeutralBlues
replies.body: keep applying. you can't get the time back later. nobody i know who applied regrets it, even the ones still waiting

threads.author: haddad_mech
threads.title: From the hiring side: why a paper trail matters more than you think
threads.body:
Here's what I look for when I hire, and it's not what most young guys expect.

When someone tells me they have three years of experience and all of it was cash, I usually believe them. But I can't verify it, and on our public jobs everybody goes on certified payroll from day one, so I'm starting them at zero on paper whether I like it or not.

The applicants who stand out walk in with something I can check: pay stubs or W-2s, a 608 card, a letter from a past employer, a log of jobs with dates and who they worked under. It doesn't have to be fancy. It has to exist.

If you're getting paid cash right now, start that log tonight. Nobody's coming to build it for you later.
fact_risk: certified payroll on public (prevailing-wage) jobs

replies.author: blowerwheel_91
replies.body: Sorry if this is a basic question, but does a log I keep myself count for anything with you, or does it need to be signed by someone? Thanks in advance.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: a log you keep yourself helps you remember. A supervisor's signature or a pay stub is something someone else can check. For a license, read what the board actually asks for before you assume either one is enough.

replies.author: dahvacnj
replies.body: kept every pay stub since school in a folder in the truck. guess i'm doing one thing right

threads.author: BergenPlumber
threads.title: foreman wants me on his weekend side jobs for cash. allowed if I'm in the Local?
threads.body: foreman on my job does bathrooms on weekends and asked if i want to make extra cash saturdays. good guy, taught me a lot this year. two questions. is that even allowed being in the local? and if something goes wrong, whose license is it on? he says he has his master's so it's fine. he also says he pulls permits "when it needs one." thanks in advance
fact_risk: permit requirements for bathroom work in NJ
union rules on members doing side work
unlicensed work exposure

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly that's two questions. Whether the Local cares, ask your business agent or read your agreement. I'm non-union and won't guess at that one. Whose license: if he's a master running it as a real business, with permits and insurance, that's one thing. If it's cash and no permits, it's on him and on you.

replies.author: BergenPlumber
replies.body: the 'when it needs one' part is what's bugging me. idk what that means honestly

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: It means sometimes he doesn't pull one, kid. Think about what that means for the helper who was there.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: whether a job needs a permit is decided by the code and the town, not by the plumber's opinion of the job. Bathroom work that moves or adds fixtures typically needs one where I've worked. If an inspector never sees it and something fails, the homeowner's insurer will ask who did the work, and your name comes up as the guy who was there.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: guys in 164 talk about this all the time... ask the steward quietly. some locals are a lot stricter about side work than people think. don't find out the hard way

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: I was in the union a few years and I'll admit I did some Saturdays back then. Not proud of all of it. The money's good until you're the one on the job that floods the downstairs neighbor.

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: not plumbing but my boss in clifton offered the same kind of thing for weekend ac installs. i asked kash about it (he's my mentor on here) and he basically said if it's not on the company's books and insurance, don't. so i didn't. not sure if it's the same for union guys tho, or if it's worse

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: 1st year in 24 here. Our instructor brought this up in class, actually. Said read the bylaws and ask. Didn't say yes or no, just said ask.

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: ask the hall. then do what they say. never needed the saturday money that bad in thirty years

replies.author: BergenPlumber
replies.body:
> never needed the saturday money that bad

fair. i'm not desperate, just tempted. he's a good guy, that's the hard part

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question: is it legal, or how do you say no to a guy you like? The second one's easier than you think. 'Can't, I've got stuff Saturdays.' He'll ask somebody else.

replies.author: Exit145Electric
replies.body: i do side work for cash all the time, nobody cares. just dont tell anyone lol

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Respectfully, 'nobody cares' is what everyone says until something goes wrong. I'd rather he hear it here than from an insurance adjuster.

replies.author: PlumbFromMorris
replies.body: 4th year in 24. sorry, not trying to pile on, but a guy a couple years ahead of me did weekends with a foreman and when one of those jobs leaked, guess who got blamed. not the foreman.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: That's the part people miss. When something goes wrong, the helper is the easiest one to point at.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: And a foreman who's good to you on the job doesn't stop being your foreman on Saturday. Say no nicely and he'll respect it. That's the job.

replies.author: BergenPlumber
replies.body: update: asked the steward, quietly. he pointed me to the part of the agreement that covers it and told me to read it myself. read it. not doing it. told my foreman i'm busy saturdays, he said no problem and moved on. thanks everyone

threads.author: Woodbridge.ducts
threads.title: Thirty hours on the check, the rest cash. Normal?
threads.body:
Started at a residential HVAC shop in Woodbridge in the spring. Boss puts 30 hours a week on my paycheck and pays the rest in cash on Fridays. Says it's "better for both of us." Some weeks that's 15 hours cash.

Is it better for me, brother? I'd like to know before tax time, not after.
fact_risk: legality of splitting pay between payroll and cash
workers comp coverage for unreported hours

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
Not normal at any shop I'd want to work for, and as I understand it, not legal either. Here's what I'd think about. The cash hours probably aren't covered if you get hurt on them. Your W-2 will show less than you earned, which matters for a car loan, an apartment, unemployment. Only the paper hours are easy to prove later. And taxes on the cash are still your problem.

Talk to a tax preparer before April. Not a contractor, including me.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I see this a lot down the shore. 'Better for both of us' usually means better for him. Doesn't make him a bad guy, but you should know what you're giving up.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Sorry to jump in, I'm in a similar spot (not the cash part, just no benefits yet). Is there a polite way to ask a boss to put everything on the check without it turning into a whole thing?

threads.author: Exit145Electric
threads.title: gave my two weeks and now my boss barely talks to me
threads.body:
3 years at a small shop in garfield. boss is decent but wouldn't pay for school and i got tired of waiting. got an offer from a bigger shop in paramus that does. gave my two weeks monday.

since then he barely talks to me and i'm getting every crawlspace job on the board lol. the new shop's owner knows him from the supply house on 46 so i'm worried about what he says.

did i mess up? how do i get through the two weeks without burning it. small state, everyone knows everyone. thanks in advance

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body:
You didn't mess up. My father used to say a boss who's hurt that you're leaving is a boss who thought you were worth keeping.

Finish the two weeks better than you started. Clean van, labeled panels, notes on every job you're leaving open so the next guy isn't lost. On your last day, shake his hand and thank him for three years. He'll be talking about you at the supply house either way. Give him something good to say. I left the union badly once and I still hear about it.

replies.author: Exit145Electric
replies.body:
> Your work will talk louder

appreciate it. yeah i think i'm mostly worried the new guy hears something before i even start

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly in a small state the new owner already called somebody about you before he made the offer. If he'd heard anything bad, you wouldn't have the offer.

replies.author: WawaRunWired
replies.body: also bergen, also a small shop. how did you even bring up leaving? asking for a friend (me). sorry if thats off topic

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: That's how it should be done. In person, early, short. The 'ok' and walking out is his problem, not yours. I've had people leave my company exactly that way, and I've hired two of them back since.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Something nobody's mentioned: crawlspaces are a safety job, and a bad two weeks is when people rush. GFCI on your cords, check what's live before you go in, lock out what you're working on, and don't let being angry make you careless. Stay safe.

replies.author: Exit145Electric

threads.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
threads.title: Boss calls late September 'boiler cleaning month.' What am I actually doing?
threads.body:
About 7 months in at the shop out of Bayonne. Boss says starting next week it's boiler cleanings and fall service every day until it gets cold, mostly old one-pipe steam in Bayonne and JC, some hot water. Joy told me to ask for one new thing a week so this is me asking ahead of time.

What actually happens on a fall service for an old steam boiler? What should I be watching so I'm not just the guy holding the light? brother I've seen maybe three steam boilers up close.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Fall service on steam is about making sure January is boring, kid.

Your lead will look at the water line in the gauge glass, check the low-water cutoff and flush it if it's the kind you flush, look at the pressure control and the pigtail under it, check the burner and the flue, and look for leaks on the near-boiler piping. You'll be holding the bucket and the light. Watch the order he does it in and ask why after, not during.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First, bring a notebook. Second, write down the make and model of every boiler and what the water looked like in the glass. Third, ask your lead what "normal" is for that one, because every old steam system has its own normal. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
replies.body: what's a pigtail? sorry. is that the loop thing under the gauge?

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: That's the one. It protects the control from live steam. Old ones clog up with crud, which is why we look at them every fall. You'll see.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: we barely see steam down here in cherry hill... mostly hot water and forced air. honestly jealous, sounds like you learn more up there

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Two years in and I've done maybe four steam boilers around Manville. What surprised me was how much the homeowner knows about their own system. Ask them what it does when it's acting up.

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: Is it true you're never supposed to add water to a steam boiler while it's hot? My teacher said that once and I wasn't sure if it was a rule or a saying.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: It's a real rule. Feeding cold water into a hot boiler that's run low can crack it, or worse. That's why we teach people to stop and find out why it's low before anything else. On a fall service your lead handles that, not the helper.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: electrical guy here... the amount of boiler room wiring in bayonne that's older than me is scary. watch where your hands go near the burner controls

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
replies.body: update: 6 cleanings this week with my lead. held a lot of buckets. he let me do the gauge glass on the last one while he watched. the pigtails were exactly as gross as Ziggy said

threads.author: NorthJerseyCopper
threads.title: What was your first no-heat call like?
threads.body: Shop just put the winter emergency list on the board and my name is on it with a journeyman starting in November. Mostly service and drain work up to now, Fair Lawn and around. Not scared exactly. idk. Curious what your first one was like, the real version. Was it the boiler, the customer, or just being tired?

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... ok it was Haddonfield, not AC lol. 3am, lady swearing the heat was broken. house had two thermostats and she was turning up the one for the AC. check what's actually calling for heat before you open anything

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Cold, tired, and somebody's grandmother watching you work. You'll be fine, kid. Take the customer seriously, take the call seriously, and call your lead before you guess. That's the job.

threads.author: chris.plumb
threads.title: first cold night and the phones blew up. what do you check on a boiler that sat all summer
threads.body: first night in the 40s and our board went crazy, 11 no-heat calls before noon. foreman sent me out with a journeyman on 4 of them. two were the thermostat. what else is usually wrong on startup week? and is there a order you guys go in or is it just experience. bound brook, mostly hot water boilers and some steam

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Fall startup calls we see every year around now:
- Thermostat batteries died over the summer, or it's still set to cool
- Service switch got turned off for the summer
- Pilot out on older standing-pilot boilers
- Low pressure on hot water systems nobody looked at since spring
- Circulator stuck after sitting all summer
Check the simple things first, in that order, and do a combustion and CO check before you leave. A callback on startup week costs more than the call.

replies.author: chris.plumb
replies.body: the thermostat one got us twice today lol. foreman said the same, check the stat before you open anything

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: Ziggy told me basically the same thing in another thread, simple stuff first. My uncle's phone hasn't stopped ringing all week either.

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: Circulators. Two stuck ones this week, one in Deptford and one in Woodbury. Appreciate the list.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: electrical side but over-explaining as usual: my teacher says half the no-heat calls his old shop in hamilton ran were a tripped breaker or a service switch somebody flipped thinking it was a light. so check that too before anyone opens the boiler

threads.author: big_ben_tools
threads.title: First furnace we fired this fall filled the house with burning smell. When is that normal?
threads.body:
Doing a co-op this fall with a residential shop in Glassboro, mostly furnace and boiler tune-ups. First furnace we fired today, the house filled up with that burning dust smell and the homeowner freaked out, thought it was a gas leak. My lead stayed calm and talked to her, and it went away after a few minutes.

How do you tell the difference between the normal first-fire smell and something actually wrong? I don't want to be the guy who says "that's normal" and it isn't.

edit: asked my lead about the readings. CO in the flue was where he wanted it and zero in the house. makes a lot more sense now.
fact_risk: NJ CO alarm requirements

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Good instinct. First, dust burning off a heat exchanger smells like hot dust and fades in minutes. Second, gas has that rotten-egg smell and that is never normal: you stop, get everyone out, and call the gas utility or 911 from outside. Third, a combustion analyzer and a CO meter answer the question your nose can't. Your lead should be testing every tune-up. Ask him to walk you through the numbers.

replies.author: big_ben_tools
replies.body: he did test it, i just didn't know what the numbers meant. going to ask him tomorrow

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... ok Sewell lol, same thing, lady called the fire department on the first fire of the year. they came, smelled dust, left. better she calls than doesn't

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
What I tell my techs on fall tune-ups:
- Tell the homeowner before you fire it that there may be a dust smell for a few minutes
- Change the filter first so you're not burning off a summer of dust
- Test CO in the flue and in the living space, and write the numbers on the ticket

replies.author: epa60812_2
replies.body: brother we had the same thing in paterson last week. my lead opened a window and just talked to her the whole time. that's half the job i think

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: One more: ask whether the house has working CO alarms. Not legal advice, but NJ has CO alarm requirements for many homes, and a startup call is a good time to make sure theirs actually work.

replies.author: ExRetail_NowHVAC
replies.body: First week at my new job and we did tune-ups every day. Telling them about the smell before you fire it saved me from this exact situation twice already.

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: your nose is a tool. the meter is the answer. trust the meter and you sleep fine

threads.author: threeway_02
threads.title: Electrical helper here. Boss says we get no-heat calls in winter too?
threads.body:
About a month into my first helper job (residential electrical, Irvington and around). My lead mentioned that once it gets cold we'll get calls from people whose boiler or furnace "has no power," and that half the time it's something electrical.

I assumed no-heat was an HVAC or plumbing call. What are electricians usually finding on these? And where's the line between our job and the heating guy's? I don't want to be the new guy poking at a burner.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly most of them are simple: a service switch somebody turned off, a tripped breaker, a thermostat wire that got chewed or cut during a remodel, a bad transformer feeding the controls. The electrician's job is to prove power is getting where it's supposed to, and stop there if it's the heating side. Test, don't guess, and don't start replacing HVAC parts you weren't called for.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: From the HVAC side, first: tell the homeowner you're there for the electrical, not the boiler. Second, if your side checks out, say so and let them call the heating company. Electricians who start adjusting burner controls make my life harder.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: got called in once behind an electrician who swapped a whole thermostat when the problem was a blown fuse on the control board lol. know what you're looking at or don't touch it

replies.author: threeway_02
replies.body: That helps. So the line is: confirm power to the equipment and the controls, then hand it off. Marcus already has me testing everything before I touch it, so at least that part's a habit.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: That's the line. And when you find the switch at the top of the basement stairs turned off, don't laugh in front of the customer. Laugh in the truck.

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: Ride-along update from the 40-and-undecided guy: leaning HVAC after startup day
threads.body:
Update from the 40-and-undecided guy. After my first round of ride-alongs I leaned electrical, but Joy said to do a second day in whatever I was least sure about, so last Saturday I went out with an HVAC shop doing boiler and furnace startups.

The HVAC day was the one where I didn't check my phone once. Ten houses, every one different, and the tech explained everything while he worked. My knees were fine in the basements. An attic in August would probably be another story.

For people who picked HVAC: what made you sure? And is the heat-season-then-AC-season thing as brutal as it sounds?

replies.author: big_zach_hvac
replies.body: did it at 40 too. the not checking your phone thing is how i knew. summers are brutal, winters are long, spring and fall you catch your breath. worth it for me so far

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
From the owner side, what HVAC looks like across a year around here:
- Spring and fall: maintenance, installs, the steady money
- Summer: no-cool calls, long days, attics
- Winter: no-heat calls, on-call rotations
- Heat pumps are blurring that, more year-round install work than when I started
If startup day felt right, most of the year feels like that, just louder.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First, the phone thing is real, I've watched students light up the same way. Second, ask that shop what their July looks like and believe them. Third, look at the night program at your county vo-tech so you're not walking in cold. Ask me how I know that matters.

> ask that shop what their July looks like

The owner said almost the same thing. His words were "come back in July if you still want it." I'd rather not wait that long, honestly.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Not unfair. A day of drains would scare off plenty of people who'd make good plumbers. But you picked the day that felt right, and that counts for something. You can fake liking a job for a week, not for a whole career.

replies.author: wchen_controls
replies.body: fwiw if the troubleshooting is the part you liked, keep controls in the back of your mind too. thermostats, zoning, boiler controls, bms on the commercial side. low voltage is a real trade and it's easier on the knees

replies.author: WhichTradeTho
replies.body: Also 40, also undecided, also Middlesex. Bartending nights and testing the waters with a night class. This thread is basically my life. If you pick HVAC, please post how the first month goes.

threads.author: blowerwheel_91
threads.title: Oil-to-gas conversion in Rockaway and the customer keeps asking me about her buried tank
threads.body:
Sorry if this is basic. I'm on my first oil-to-gas conversion with my lead, an old split-level in Rockaway. The homeowner keeps asking me, not my lead, what happens to the buried oil tank in the side yard and whether we take it out. I told her I'd find out.

I honestly don't know whose job that is or what the rules are, and I don't want to tell her something wrong. My lead says there are a lot of these up here in Morris County. Thanks in advance.
fact_risk: residential oil tank removal/abandonment rules and permits
who is certified to do tank work in NJ

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Good call not answering. How I'd handle it:
- Tank removal or abandonment is its own specialty, not the HVAC contractor's, at least at my company
- From what I understand, the town will want a permit for it and some situations involve soil testing; that's not something to guess at in a driveway
- Tell her to call a tank company and her town's construction office, and that her insurance company and any future buyer will care about the paperwork
- Your job is the new equipment, the gas piping, and disconnecting the oil supply to the old burner properly
Point her to the right people. Don't become the tank expert.

replies.author: PlumbFromMorris
replies.body: rockaway is full of these. half the houses on my street had tanks pulled before they sold. sorry not that helpful, just confirming your lead is right lol

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Up in Morris and Sussex you'll see more buried tanks than you ever wanted to, kid. A leaker can turn into real money for a homeowner. Never guess on that question.

replies.author: blowerwheel_91
replies.body: Thank you, this helps a lot. I told her to call the town and a tank company and wrote it on the ticket. My lead said that's what he would've told her.

threads.author: oldsteam_zig
threads.title: Last week of September: what I want my helpers doing before the phones start
threads.body:
Every year the last week of September is the calm before the phones. Here's what I tell my helpers.

Stock your truck like it's January. Fittings for the old stuff, not just the new stuff. Nipples, unions, gauge glasses, pigtails, a couple of the controls we always end up needing.

Know where every shutoff is on your regular customers' boilers before it's dark at five.

Test your flashlight, your CO meter, your combustion analyzer. Get your boots resoled now, not the first wet week.

And sleep. On-call season is long, kid. The guy who's rested at 2am does better work than the guy who's been up since Tuesday. That's the job.

replies.author: sweatjoint200amp
replies.body: the boots one... mine already have a hole in them. ordering new ones tonight. thanks zig

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: I'd add one, Ziggy, and push back on one. Add: update your customers' contact info now, half my building supers changed this year. Push back: don't stock every control on every truck. Two on the lead truck is plenty. The rest is money sitting on a shelf.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Fair. My trucks, my bad habit. Two on the lead truck it is. Don't tell my guys I said that.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: My uncle's truck is a disaster right now. Sending him this. He's going to pretend he didn't read it.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: My father used to say the truck tells the customer who you are before you open your mouth. He was right, and mine still doesn't look like his did.

replies.author: FluxOnMyBoots
replies.body: night class guy, not on a truck yet. writing all this down for when i am lol

threads.author: WawaRunWired
threads.title: panel was labeled wrong and the outlet was still hot after i flipped the breaker
threads.body:
1 yr in, non union shop in bergen. changing a kitchen receptacle in fair lawn today. boss said kill the kitchen circuit so i flipped the one labeled kitchen. went to pull the device and my tester lit up. still hot. turns out the kitchen counter was on the one labeled "dining" and nobody ever fixed the panel schedule.

i didn't touch anything but i'm pretty shook. i did test thank god, that's the only reason i'm posting this and not in the er. what should i have done different? sorry if dumb

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
You did the most important thing right: you tested. Never trust a panel label. What I'd add: check your tester on a known live source before and after, so you know it actually works. Lock out and tag the breaker you turned off, even in a house. And tell your boss about the labeling so the customer gets it fixed.

This isn't a dumb question. This is the question. Stay safe.

replies.author: emt_bender_200amp
replies.body: our teacher in queens literally says 'the label is a suggestion.' glad you tested. did your tester go off right away or only when you got close to the device?

replies.author: threeway_02
replies.body: New helper here, a few weeks in. Marcus told me the same thing about checking the tester on something live first. I didn't really understand why until I read this.

threads.author: BackflowBlues
threads.title: got dizzy pulling galvanized out of an attic in the heat. foreman was mad i didn't say something
threads.body:
demo day on an old cape in hamilton, like 97 out. foreman had me pulling old galvanized out of the attic for a bathroom reno. after maybe an hour i got dizzy and noticed i'd stopped sweating, which i thought was a good thing lol. foreman made me sit in the truck with the ac on and drink water. felt fine after a while.

he was mad i didn't say something sooner. was it actually a big deal or is he overreacting

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Your foreman is right, and he may have done you a real favor. Dizziness and stopping sweating in that kind of heat are warning signs of heat illness, and it can get serious fast. Next time: water before you're thirsty, breaks out of the attic, and tell someone the moment you feel off. If someone gets confused or stops sweating, that's a call for medical help, not a break.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: stopping sweating is not good lol. it's bad. watched a guy go down in a condenser room on the boardwalk one july. your foreman did the right thing. listen to him

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
What we do on summer attic days:
- Attic work first thing in the morning, done before 11 if possible
- Two people, one stays where he can see the other
- Water and electrolytes in the truck, not "I'll grab something later"
- Anyone can stop the job if they feel off, no questions asked

replies.author: big_nicole_plumb
replies.body: not to scare you but this happened to me my first july in burlington. went home thinking i was fine and felt terrible for two days. say something early. edit: early, not after

replies.author: ThirdYearTinknocker
replies.body: 3rd summer in attics. the thing nobody tells you is drink water the night before too. appreciate this thread, sending it to our new guy

threads.author: big_hector_plumb
threads.title: CO meter went off before I hit the bottom of the basement stairs
threads.body:
service call in a 4-family in union city, water heater "making a smell." basement door was shut. my CO meter started going off before i got to the bottom of the stairs. flue pipe had come apart at the chimney.

got out, got the tenants out of the first floor, called the gas company from the sidewalk. they shut it down. the super was mad at ME lol.

4 years in and never had my meter go off like that. how many of you actually carry one, and actually turn it on?

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: You did it right. Got out, got people out, called it in. The super being mad is the super's problem. I'm in those buildings every week. Every one of my guys carries a meter, clipped on and turned on, before they open the basement door.

replies.author: big_hector_plumb
replies.body: turned on before the door is the part. i usually forget to turn mine on till i'm already down there lol. not anymore

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Glad you're okay. What you did is the right order: get out, get others out, call the utility or 911 from outside, and don't go back in until it's been cleared. A personal CO meter is PPE, same as your glasses. Bump test or check it the way the manufacturer says, so you know it works when you need it. Different trade, same rule. Stay safe.

replies.author: Elizabeth.traps
replies.body: how often are you supposed to calibrate them? mine came with the job and idk if anyone has ever done it. foreman probably doesn't know either

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First, follow the manufacturer's calibration and bump-test schedule. It's in the manual and it's not optional. Second, a cheap meter that works beats an expensive one sitting in the truck. Third, if nobody knows when yours was last checked, assume it hasn't been. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: we got ours from the shop this summer... nobody told us anything about bump testing. going to ask monday

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Scary one. My father had a call like that in Harrison years ago. What I'd tell a young guy: if the meter goes off, open it up, let it air out, and once the meter clears, fix the flue and get on with it.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Respectfully, Rui, I wouldn't tell a young guy that. Get out first. Let the gas company or the fire department clear the building and find the source. Then you come back. Airing it out and going back to work is how good mechanics end up in the hospital.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: You're right, Ziggy. I said that wrong. Out first, utility or fire department, then the work. Thanks for catching it.

replies.author: ginaj75
replies.body: pleasantville. had my meter go off in a crawlspace last winter with no gas appliance anywhere near me. turned out to be the neighbor's generator. you never know

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: once you're allowed back in, make sure the building's CO alarms are there and working. A flue that came apart at the chimney may also mean somebody did work without an inspection. Worth noting on your ticket.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
What every one of my techs carries on every call:
- Personal CO meter, on, before entering the basement
- Combustion analyzer on any fuel-burning work
- The gas utility's emergency number saved in the phone
And they're trained to leave first and diagnose second.

replies.author: big_paulie_plumb
replies.body: north bergen, same kind of buildings. sorry, dumb question, but how did the super blame you? you're the one who found it

replies.author: big_hector_plumb
replies.body: he said i 'broke it' when i was looking at it lol. the gas company guy told him it had been off the chimney a while. he shut up after that

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... hotel kitchen, the exhaust fan was dead and everyone had headaches and blamed the heat lol. my meter was the only reason we figured it out. carry it everywhere

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter
replies.body: bayonne helper here, about 7 months in. i don't have a meter, my lead does. should i buy my own or is that overkill?

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Not overkill. Buy your own. Your lead won't always be standing next to you.

replies.author: DinerCoffeeHVAC
replies.body: Sorry if this is off topic, but this is why I hate those basements with the door shut. Bayonne and JC are full of them. Glad you're okay.

replies.author: hudson_conduit
replies.body: electrical guy, also union city. didn't know we should carry these too. we're in those basements for panels all the time. ordering one

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Yes, you should. Electricians spend plenty of time in rooms with fuel-burning equipment, and the meter doesn't care what trade you're in.

replies.author: PlumberFromRahway
replies.body: our instructor made all of us buy one first year and honestly i thought it was a racket. not anymore after reading this one

replies.author: Elizabeth.traps
replies.body: update on mine: asked the foreman, he had no idea when it was last checked. shop is getting new ones this week

replies.author: big_hector_plumb
replies.body: appreciate everybody. went back to that building today. new flue, CO alarms in the basement now. super even said thanks. kind of

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: follow up: asked about bump testing like ms almonte said. nobody at my shop knew either lol. we're doing it now

threads.author: plumbnj77
threads.title: slid down a hot roof to the gutter on a one-story. you guys tying off for that?
threads.body: on a roof in toms river tuesday putting a boot on a vent stack for an addition on a split level. low pitch, one story side, figured no big deal. shingles were so hot my boot just let go and i slid on my butt to the gutter. gutter held. didn't go off the edge. boss laughed. i didn't. are you guys tying off on a one story roof? is that overkill brother
fact_risk: fall protection requirements on residential roofs

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: fall protection requirements depend on the height and the work, not on how easy the roof looks, and residential roofs are where a lot of serious falls happen. Ask your boss what the shop's fall protection plan is. If there isn't one, that's your answer.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Not overkill, kid. A one-story fall puts guys out for a year. Hot shingles in summer are like ice. Proper fall protection, a ladder that's set right, and somebody on the ground. Your boss laughing is the part that worries me.

threads.author: benplumb79
threads.title: Felt a tingle in a wet crawlspace in Manville. What do you check before going under a house?
threads.body:
Crawlspace job in Manville last week, replacing a section of drain under an old ranch. There was an inch of water down there from the storms. The work light was on an extension cord plugged into a garage outlet, no GFCI. Halfway through, the light flickered and I felt a tingle in my hand where I was holding the light and kneeling in the water. I got out right away.

The cord had a nick in it. I'm fine. My boss said I should have checked the cord, and he's right, but I also had no idea the garage outlet wasn't GFCI protected.

What do you all do before going into a wet crawlspace? I'd like a routine instead of luck.
fact_risk: GFCI requirements for temporary power
permit-required confined space determination

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
First: you got out. That was the right call. A tingle in a wet space is a warning, not a nuisance.

Before any wet crawlspace: GFCI protection at the source, or a portable GFCI at the plug, and test it every time. Inspect the whole cord, end to end. Use lights rated for damp locations. And if there's standing water and anything electrical involved, the job can wait until it's dry. Stay safe.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: I didn't know portable GFCIs were a thing. Ordering one tonight.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Ground-fault protection for temporary power on a job is a standard requirement, and a garage outlet in an older house may well predate GFCI. Don't assume any outlet in an older house is protected. Test it.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly after Sandy we did hundreds of crawlspaces down here, and that's the one thing I drilled into every helper. Portable GFCI on every cord, every time. Water under a house is a different job.

replies.author: condensate_3way
replies.body: sorry dumb q but does a gfci actually stop you from getting shocked, or does it just stop it from killing you lol

replies.author: wchen_controls
replies.body: fwiw it doesn't stop the first bit of current. it trips fast enough that it usually isn't dangerous, so you might still feel something. that's why you also fix the cord and stay out of the water

replies.author: CondensateOverflow
replies.body: bound brook here, everything flooded that same week. idk how many crawlspaces we've been in since. glad you're ok

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Crawlspace routine at my company:
- Look before you crawl: water, wiring, animals, smell
- Portable GFCI and a cord you've inspected
- Someone outside who knows you're in there
- Phone or radio on you
- If it smells like sewage or gas, nobody goes in yet

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: 1st year here. Our instructor calls crawlspaces confined spaces 'in spirit.' Not sure that's the official definition, but it stuck with me.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Careful with that one. Whether a space counts as a permit-required confined space is a specific determination, and some crawlspaces could qualify depending on the hazards. On our jobs the competent person makes that call. Your instructor's instinct is right, though: treat it with that respect.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: vo-tech electrical guy here, over-explaining: a nicked cord plus wet ground means you were the path. that's literally what our teacher draws on the board every year. glad you're not the example now

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body:
> you were the path

That's a sentence I won't forget anytime soon.

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: your boss is right about the cord. you're right nobody told you about the outlet. both true. now you know

replies.author: SumpPumpSeason
replies.body: Every sump call in a finished basement after a storm, I think about this. Appreciate you posting it. Buying a second portable GFCI for the van.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: You asked what we do. Look first, test the GFCI, tell someone. You know all that now. The thing I'd add: say no when it's not safe yet, even to your boss.

replies.author: chris.plumb
replies.body: bound brook. foreman made us start carrying portable gfcis after one of our guys got bit last year. didnt think about why until now

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: Did a flooded crawlspace in Deptford after the August storms. Didn't think twice about the cord. I will now. Appreciate it.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: One more: if you ever take a real shock, even if you feel fine afterward, tell someone and consider getting checked out. Some injuries don't show up right away.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Thank you. I hadn't thought about getting checked. I felt fine, but I'll mention it to my doctor anyway.

replies.author: matt_the_hvac
replies.body: bound brook too, hvac. we had a whole unit on this in school and i still almost did the same thing last month lol. saved this

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: update: the shop bought portable GFCIs for every truck after I showed my boss this thread. Small win.

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: Rung cracked on the homeowner's old wooden ladder during my ride-along
threads.body: Quick one from the electrician ride-along. Our ladder was on the other truck and the homeowner insisted we use her old wooden extension ladder from the garage. I went up first to look at a soffit light and a rung cracked under my foot. I caught myself, nothing happened. The electrician just said "that's why we don't use customer ladders" and moved on. Is that an actual rule people follow, or did he just say it because I almost fell?

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: It's a real rule at every good shop I've known. You don't know how a customer's ladder was stored, what it's rated for, or what's cracked. Your own ladder, inspected, set at the right angle, on stable ground. He was teaching you something. Take it.

replies.author: plumbnj88
replies.body: almost the same thing happened to me on a step stool at the bar lol. not the same at all but i get it. glad you're ok, keep posting these ride along stories

threads.author: hec_does_ac
threads.title: Heat wave week: 14 no-cool calls in two days and what I keep telling new techs
threads.body:
So this one time in AC... ok it's this week, not one time lol. 14 no-cool calls Monday and Tuesday between Cherry Hill and Washington Township. Half were dirty filters and clogged condensate lines, a couple capacitors, one frozen coil the homeowner "fixed" by turning the thermostat down to 60.

What I keep telling my new guys on ride-alongs... check airflow before you even think about the charge. Check the condensate before you blame the unit. Drink water in the truck between every call, not when you're already dizzy. And if the attic is an oven, do the attic part first thing in the morning and come down for air often. Nobody gets a medal for passing out over an air handler.

What are you guys seeing this week?

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: walk-ins down here. every restaurant on the boardwalk calls at 4pm on a saturday when the box hits 50. dirty condensers, every one. winter is when you learn, summer is when you survive

replies.author: epa60812_2
replies.body: first summer brother... 3 frozen coils this week in paterson, all filters. my lead makes me check airflow first every single time now

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Same here in Middlesex. What I'd add for the new techs:
- Write down what you found, even on the easy calls; patterns show up
- Don't promise same-day on a part you don't have on the truck
- Heat-wave callbacks cost more than the calls did

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Kash with the callbacks lol. he's right though... the heat wave callback is the one that eats your saturday

replies.author: dahvacnj
replies.body: toms river. capacitors and clogged drains all week. drank like 6 waters yesterday and still got a headache. thanks for the reminder

replies.author: Dev.R

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: Route 1 at 6am in my mom's car for a $17/hr summer job. Ask about travel or suck it up?
threads.body:
Over-explaining as usual. Got a summer job with an electrical contractor whose shop is in North Brunswick, and the jobs are all over Middlesex and Mercer. I live in Hamilton and I don't have my own car, so I'm borrowing my mom's. Route 1 at 6am is a parking lot from the Quaker Bridge area up, and when I take the Turnpike instead the tolls add up fast. Gas is killing me too. I make $17 an hour.

Is it normal for a shop to pay nothing for travel for a summer kid? Should I ask, or just suck it up until school starts?
fact_risk: toll amounts

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Normal for a summer kid, unfortunately. My father never paid travel for helpers, and I swore I'd change that when I took over. I only half did. What you can ask: can you meet at the job instead of the shop, or ride in with a guy who lives near you. Owners say yes to that a lot more often than to money.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Small thing, but your toll cost depends a lot on E-ZPass and the time of day. Run your real route through the toll calculator instead of guessing. And ask about meeting at the job. Commute time is easier to fix than pay.

threads.author: WawaRunWired
threads.title: boss offered me the van home but it's GPS tracked with no personal stops
threads.body: boss offered to let me take the van home starting next month. catch is gps tracking, no personal stops, not even wawa on the way in lol, and i'd be on the emergency list some weekends. saves my car and gas money. but it kind of feels like a leash. do you guys take the van home? worth it? thanks in advance

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: GPS is normal now, most shops have it. Whether it's worth it depends on how often they'll call you out. Ask how weekend calls get paid before you say yes.

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: i take my shop's van home in clifton. honestly the gas savings alone is like a raise. they don't care about a coffee stop on the way in though, ask if wawa counts lol

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: My guys take the trucks home. From the owner side, kid: a truck at your house means I can send you straight to a job at 7, or to a no-heat call at night. The no-stops rule is about insurance and about customers seeing my truck parked outside a bar. A coffee on the way in I don't care about, but ask yours. Get the rules in writing so nobody argues later.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: One thing to ask while you're at it: who's insured if you're in an accident on the way home. Not legal advice, but that's a question for your boss and his insurance agent, not something to guess at.

threads.author: threeway_91

threads.body:
tottenville, staten island. working for a small shop on the island, boss is decent but won't pay for school. got an offer from a shop in woodbridge that does pay for school. it's like 15 min over the outerbridge without traffic. the bridge going into jersey is free i think, it's coming back into the city that costs money and it's not cheap. so every day i'd pay to come home lol.

also if i ever want a nyc license someday, does jersey work even count? sorry for over explaining brother
fact_risk: Outerbridge Crossing toll direction and cost
whether out-of-state experience counts toward NYC DOB licensing

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body: In the city it's different, and you're asking the right question early. Last I checked, the DOB wants documented experience, and whether out-of-state work counts depends on the license and how it's documented. Read the DOB's own requirements for your trade before deciding based on that. School paid for and a shorter commute than most guys on Brooklyn jobs? Woodbridge sounds good to me.

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Brother, guys on my crew pay way more in tunnel tolls every day. One bridge toll home to get your school paid for? Take it. Just don't count on the Outerbridge being 15 minutes. It isn't.

replies.author: threeway_02
replies.body: Career switcher in Irvington, different situation, but my commute's 35 minutes each way on a good day. School being paid for is worth a lot of tolls from what everyone told me here.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Two different questions. Tolls: ask the new shop whether they reimburse, some do. License: think about where you want to be working in ten years and follow that board.

replies.author: HelperForNow
replies.body: manahawkin here. some weeks i drive the parkway an hour each way to jobs. a 15 minute bridge sounds like a vacation honestly

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Another angle: a shop that pays for school is investing in you, and that usually shows up in how they train you on the job too. I'd weigh that more than the toll. And give yourself extra time on that bridge in the winter.

threads.author: EssexPipes
threads.title: three Hoboken parking tickets in four days and my boss won't cover them
threads.body: Shop sent me to a brownstone job in Hoboken for two weeks. No driveway, no permit, and the parking enforcement is out at 8am sharp. Three tickets in four days. Boss says parking is part of the job and he won't pay them. Is that normal or is he full of it? And how are you guys parking in Hoboken and JC with a van full of material?
fact_risk: Hoboken/Jersey City contractor parking permits

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question: who pays, or how to park? Who pays: at my shop, if I sent you there, the parking is on me. Not every shop does that. How to park: before the job, have the GC or homeowner ask the city about contractor permits or temporary no-parking signs, unload and move the van, and walk from a lot. Hoboken doesn't care that you have a van.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: cherry hill guy so idk hoboken at all... but 3 tickets in 4 days would be my whole week's lunch money lol. at least ask him to split them

threads.author: LateStartPlumber
threads.title: starting next week in brooklyn and they want me driving my own car to jobs
threads.body: starting as a helper next week, 42, career change. the shop is in brooklyn and they want me to drive my own car to jobs around brooklyn and the island. verrazzano toll every time i cross (the resident discount helps i think), plus parking in bay ridge and park slope. about gas they said "we'll see." sorry if this is a dumb question but is it normal to ask about mileage before you even start? i don't want to seem difficult before day one
