mileage reimbursement norms

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Not dumb. Ask before you start, it's easier now than six months from now. Keep it simple: "How do you handle tolls and mileage when I use my car for jobs?" A good shop has an answer. "We'll see" isn't an answer yet, so ask again before your first day.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: I drive my own car to jobs around Somerset County and didn't ask when I started. Two years later I'm only now getting ready to bring up mileage. Ask now. I wish I had.

replies.author: plumbnj88
replies.body: 36 here, also switching. had the same worry about seeming difficult. everyone told me asking isn't difficult, it's normal. good luck next week

threads.author: groundrod_05
threads.title: Bronx shop landed a Midtown high-rise. Driving in, or the 6 train with my tools?
threads.body:
My non-union shop in the Bronx got a three-month job on a high-rise in Midtown. First time I'll be working in Manhattan. Driving in means the congestion charge plus parking, and the foreman says garages near the job cost about as much as a car payment. Taking the subway means carrying my tools on the 6 at 5:30am.

How do you guys do it? Does anyone's shop actually pay for parking in the city? Appreciate it.

edit: shop says they'll cover parking for the lead only. subway it is.
fact_risk: Manhattan congestion pricing charge
Midtown garage costs

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Brother, I've been doing this 21 years. Nobody drives to Midtown unless the company pays. Your gang box stays on the job and you carry a small bag. Get there early, because the freight elevator line is the real commute. Find out day one where the shanty is and who runs the hoist. And for what it's worth, the 7 is worse than the 6.

replies.author: groundrod_05
replies.body: Gang box stays on the job, that makes sense. I've been carrying my whole bag home every night like an idiot. Appreciate it.

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body: In the city it's different from Jersey shops: plenty of NYC shops don't pay parking at all, and some pay a garage for the lead only, like yours. Ask before every new job. Don't assume either way.

replies.author: BayRidge.traps
replies.body: Apex grad, plumbing. My foreman takes the R in with a small bag too. Once you do it a week it's fine. The 5am train is basically all trades anyway.

replies.author: hudson_conduit
replies.body: jersey guy here, union city. how do they even get material up a high-rise if nobody drives in? do trucks just block the whole street?

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Deliveries are scheduled, usually early, with a loading area and a time slot for the hoist. On the city jobs I did back in my union days, miss your slot and you wait half a day. The city teaches you patience whether you want it or not.

threads.author: dreb_jman
threads.title: For the Jersey guys walking onto my Midtown job late: tunnels, PATH, and DOB inspection days
threads.body:
Brother, this is for the Jersey guys I keep watching walk in at 6:58 with a coffee from the tunnel line.

One: leave earlier than you think. The Lincoln on a random Tuesday will eat 40 minutes for no reason.

Two: the PATH or the bus plus a walk beats driving unless the company pays the garage, and most don't.

Three: on inspection days, the inspector sees your area before he sees your work. Clean, covers on, panels labeled, no open boxes you can't explain. In my experience an inspector who walks into a mess starts looking harder. I've watched good work get picked apart because the floor looked like a dumpster.

Get in early on inspection day. That's all I've got.
fact_risk: NYC DOB electrical inspection practices on high-rise jobs

replies.author: hudson_conduit
replies.body: union city, i can see the helix from my window and on days the shop sends me into the city i still leave at 5. the lincoln is a coin flip every morning lol

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body: In the city it's different from Jersey on inspection day too: more people walking the job, more paperwork on the wall. Same rule as yours though. A clean area buys you patience.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Same on the Jersey side. Inspection day is also a safety day: covers on, nothing energized left open, everyone in their PPE. An inspector notices a crew that works safe.

replies.author: groundrod_05
replies.body: Took your gang box advice from my Midtown thread over the summer. Now it's the inspection day advice. Appreciate it.

replies.author: JughandleJourneyman
replies.body: 164 guy, not in the city... but my cousin's in 3 and commutes from teaneck. he says the same thing, the bus beats driving most days... and a wawa stop is not an option lol

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Your cousin's right. The bus and a walk beat sitting in the helix with your engine running, every time.

replies.author: Flushing.sparks
replies.body: Queens trade program, applying to 3 this round. Writing all of this down for when I'm on a job like that someday.

threads.author: tnguyen_refrig
threads.title: Boardwalk's slow after Labor Day. That's when I take a helper.
threads.body:
boardwalk's quiet now. july was brutal, walk-ins dying every afternoon, ice machines, a whole freezer of shrimp at a place i won't name. now it's slow and that's when i take a helper along.

people think summer is when you learn. summer is when you run. winter is when you learn. you've got time to open things up, explain them, let you braze something without a restaurant owner standing over you yelling about his fish.

if you're down here, atlantic or cape may, and curious about refrigeration, ask around the shops in october. we're all slower and nicer. a little.

replies.body: egg harbor brother, residential hvac 1 yr. never touched refrigeration. is it worth asking even with zero commercial experience?

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: tnguyen's right... I did casino chillers in AC for years and the winters were where I actually learned the big stuff. summers you just survive lol

threads.author: ThirdYearTinknocker
threads.title: crane day at a middle school, finished the rooftop swaps the night before teachers came back
threads.body:
long one sorry. our shop had rooftop unit swaps at a middle school near asbury, 4 units, and they had to be done before teachers came back. crane day was a 5am start, roof was already hot by 9. i was on tag lines and the curb adapters. foreman was strict about the swing zone, nobody under the pick, nobody on the edge without being tied off, and honestly after hearing stories in here i didn't mind.

3rd year and it's the first job where i felt like i actually built something. appreciate the crew i'm on.

threads.author: JughandleJourneyman
threads.title: journeyman has me on the morning wawa run and 'forgets' to pay me back
threads.body: so this is a dumb one... 2nd year in 164, my journeyman has me do the wawa run every morning before we start. coffee, his hoagie for lunch, sometimes for 3 guys. he always says he'll get me back friday... friday never comes lol. it's like $20-30 a week. i like him, he teaches me a lot. do i say something or is this just part of being the apprentice? thanks in advance

replies.author: Bergen_Ducts

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: lol my first lead owed me like $200 in coffee by christmas lol. finally said something and he paid me in one lump and bought me a pork roll egg and cheese every day for a week. say something

replies.author: mbell_wireman

replies.author: JughandleJourneyman

threads.author: CentralJersey_Coils
threads.title: Weekend helper offer at $17/hr while I finish vo-tech. Fair or lowball?
threads.body:
I'm in the HVAC program at the county vo-tech, graduating next year. A residential shop near Neptune offered me Saturdays plus some days over winter break at $17 an hour, mostly carrying equipment and cleaning up after installs. My cousin says that's a lowball. My teacher says take anything that gets me hours.

I care more about the experience than the money, but I also don't want to get taken advantage of. Is $17 reasonable for a student with zero hours?

edit: I first wrote that it was cash. It's on the books, I misread the text.

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: the rate matters less than whether anyone teaches you. on the books is the right answer.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
From what I hear around here, that's within the normal range for a student doing weekend helper work. I'd care more about three other things: that it's on the books (it is), that someone gives you a real safety talk before they put you in an attic, and that someone explains what you're carrying and why. If you get those, you're being paid twice.

Attics on a Saturday in summer are no joke. Stay safe.

replies.author: chris.plumb
replies.body: i started at about that out of school, got bumped after 3 months when my foreman told the boss i was worth it. did they say anything about a raise once you graduate? and do they do service or only installs

replies.author: CentralJersey_Coils
replies.body: Installs mostly, some maintenance in the fall. Didn't ask about a raise yet, I'll ask when I go in Saturday. Thanks brother.

fact_risk: specific wage numbers ($21 -> $23/hr) are one person's; hedged
threads.author: benplumb79
threads.title: Update on my $21/hr question: had the review
threads.body:
Sorry, this is long. A while back I asked whether $21/hr was low for a 2nd-year non-union plumber near Manville. I had my review on Friday.

I brought a written list of what I can do alone now: water heaters, toilets, most drain calls, two small repipes. I asked for $24 plus mileage. I got $23 and mileage at a set rate per mile, which is less than I asked for but more than I had. My boss said we'd "talk again in the spring."

Is it normal to land in the middle like that, or did I leave money on the table?

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
Here's what I look for when I give a raise, and you did most of it: you came in with what you can do on your own, not what you think you deserve. Landing in the middle is normal; most owners expect to.

The part I'd lock down is "talk again in the spring." Ask him what specifically he wants to see by then, and write it down while you're still in the room.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Good outcome. Two things to check now that it's settled:
- Is the mileage on your pay stub, or cash in an envelope? It should be on paper
- Get the new rate in writing, even a text
The $2 matters, but the mileage is the part most guys forget to ask for.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly that's a solid review. I've had guys walk in asking for five dollars more with nothing to show me. You showed up with a list. Keep adding to it every month and spring takes care of itself.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: nice... i asked for a raise in june with no list and got 'we'll see'. doing the list thing next time

replies.author: Woodbridge.ducts
replies.body: fair brother. the $40 number I threw out in your other thread was my buddy counting his whole union package, found out after. $23 and mileage sounds right from what I've heard since

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: edit: thanks all. I texted him asking for the spring goals like haddad_mech said and he actually sent them back. Two items. Writing them on the inside of my truck visor.

threads.author: Exit145Electric
threads.title: 3 years non-union. would applying to 164 mean taking a pay cut?
threads.body: so i'm 3 years in at a small non-union shop near garfield. decent boss, no school though. been thinking about applying to the IBEW apprenticeship but from what i can tell a first year apprentice makes less per hour than i do now. i'm at $25 on the books, no benefits, no retirement. is the cut worth it? do they give you credit for the years you already have or do i start at zero? not trying to start a union vs non-union fight, just trying to do the math. thanks in advance

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Fair question, and you're doing the math the right way. Compare the whole package, not the hourly. Apprentice wages usually step up each year as a percentage of the journeyman rate, and on top of the check there's health coverage, pension and annuity contributions, and the schooling, none of which you have now.

Whether they credit prior experience is a question for the apprenticeship office directly. I won't guess for 164. Some programs have ways to place experienced applicants, but don't count on it. Stay safe.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
If you want the math to be honest, price out what you have now:
- Health insurance you'd buy on your own: get a real quote
- Retirement: $0 now, so that's a real gap
- School: what night classes would cost you out of pocket
Add those to your $25 and then compare. Sometimes the cut is smaller than it looks. Sometimes it isn't.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly, three years in a good non-union shop isn't nothing. If your boss will sign off on your experience toward a license someday, that's a path too. I went that way and it worked for me. But no school and no retirement at year 3 is the part I'd want fixed one way or the other.

replies.body: don't quit before you get in, the list can take forever... wait you didn't say you were quitting lol. ignore me. but still, don't quit early

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: One thing from the hiring side: three years with nothing on paper is the weak spot either way. Start keeping a log of your work now and ask your boss to put your hours in writing. If you stay non-union and want a license someday, you'll need it. If you apply, it helps at the interview.

replies.author: JughandleJourneyman

replies.author: Exit145Electric
replies.body: appreciate it. the health insurance quote is a good point, never priced it. would a 1st year rate be like half of what a journeyman makes?

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Roughly in that neighborhood for a first-year, from what I've seen, but each program sets its own percentages and steps. The local publishes its wage sheet. Look at the actual numbers instead of guessing, and ask the apprenticeship office.

Code is my area, not wage law, so check the NJ Department of Labor's wage and hour pages or call them before you take my word for it.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
Here's how it works at my shop, and at every shop I'd put my name on: hourly helpers get time and a half after 40, period. Our payroll company wouldn't let us do it any other way.

The state labor department is the place to check, like he said. Before you go there, ask the owner directly and calmly, in person, with your hours written down. Sometimes it's an office mistake. Sometimes it isn't, and then you know what kind of shop it is.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Agree with both. Keep your own record from now on:
- Start and end times every day, written down that day
- Which calls, which truck
- Screenshots of any texts about hours
If it ever turns into a dispute, notes you made at the time carry weight.

threads.author: Kash_sing
threads.title: Side jobs, from the owner's side: what happens when yours calls my office
threads.body:
Happened again this month, so I'll write it down. A homeowner called us for a no-cool on a mini-split installed last year. Not our install. A helper from another shop put it in on weekends, cash. No permit, no proper evacuation, flare connections leaking. The homeowner wanted to know who to call about it, and the answer was nobody.

What it looks like from my side:
- The homeowner pays twice, once to him and once to us
- If your own boss gets that call, you're probably done there
- Handling refrigerant without your 608 is its own problem, and having the card doesn't make an unpermitted install legal
- You have no insurance, so whatever goes wrong is on you

I'm not telling anyone what to do on their own time. I'm telling you what it costs when it goes wrong.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it. On the electrical side of these, I see the disconnect and the circuit done wrong more than anything else. When unpermitted work turns up later, at a sale or after a problem, the homeowner is usually the one left holding the bill. Check which code edition is in effect and what the town requires before anyone touches a line set.

replies.author: dahvacnj
replies.body: sorry if this is dumb but what about stuff with no refrigerant, like cleaning coils and changing filters for neighbors? my neighbor keeps asking. thanks in advance

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Smaller exposure, same basic problem:
- You're still uninsured if you fall off a ladder or break something
- "Just cleaning coils" turns into "while you're here, can you look at this" fast
- Your boss may see it as taking his customers
Ask your boss if the shop wants the maintenance work. Usually they do, and you get the hours.

threads.author: LiveFrontLessons
threads.title: me and a buddy want to start an LLC doing handyman + small electrical. is HIC enough?
threads.body: ok so hear me out. my buddy is a carpenter, i'm a year out of vo-tech working for an electrical shop near asbury. we want to start an LLC on the side, register as a home improvement contractor with the state, and do bathroom refreshes, decks, and the "small electrical" like fixtures, outlets, fans. he says the HIC registration covers all of it as long as it's under the LLC. is that right? and what insurance would we even need for something like that? we're not trying to do panels or anything crazy

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: as I understand NJ's rules, home improvement contractor registration is not an electrical license and doesn't cover electrical work. If you're paid for it, a licensed electrical contractor has to be the one running it. "Small" isn't a category in the code.

Call the Division of Consumer Affairs and ask them directly before you form anything.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Same in my trade. As I understand it:
- HIC registration covers general home improvement work
- Licensed trades (electrical, plumbing, HVACR) need the license, or a licensed contractor running the work
- An LLC is a business structure, not a license
Your buddy's carpentry side may be fine under HIC. Check with Consumer Affairs for your exact case.

threads.title: No kids in the trade. Who buys a 2-truck shop when you want out?
threads.body:
Business side question, for the owners and for any Juniors thinking long-term.

My father ran this shop for three decades and handed it to me. None of my kids want it. My nephew in Hamilton is in IT. So in ten years or so, who buys a 2-truck residential shop on the Hudson/Bergen line? The trucks and tools aren't worth much. The customer list and the phone number are the whole business.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
We've started thinking about this too. What I've learned so far:
- The license is personal; a buyer needs their own, or a licensed person running the work
- Your books need to be clean for years before anyone pays real money for goodwill
- The most likely buyer is someone already working for you
That last one means you start grooming someone now. Ten years goes fast.

replies.author: threeway_02
replies.body: Not an owner, I haven't even started yet, but I spent 11 years in insurance claims and saw a lot of small businesses get valued. Clean records and repeat customers were always what moved the number. Kash is right about the books.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: The someone-already-working-for-you part is what I keep coming back to. I hired a vo-tech kid last year who might be that guy, if he doesn't go union first. My father would laugh at me for worrying about any of this.

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: My teacher says public school jobs pay way more. What is prevailing wage?
threads.body: Before school let out my shop teacher was going on about how the summer school renovation jobs pay "prevailing wage" and that's why everyone fights to get on them. I nodded. I have no idea what it means. Is it a union thing? Would I make more as a helper on one of those jobs? And why would a school pay more than a house? Explain it like I'm a vo-tech kid in Hamilton whose whole resume is one summer carrying wire, because that's what I am.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
Short version: on covered public jobs in NJ (schools, municipal buildings, a lot of publicly funded work), contractors have to pay at least the rates the state sets for each trade and county. Those rates are published by the state labor department.

It isn't only a union thing. Non-union shops like mine do prevailing-wage work and pay the rates. The paperwork is certified payroll: every week, every worker, every hour. That's part of why not every shop bids them.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
To add the helper part:
- Apprentice rates on those jobs generally depend on being in a registered apprenticeship program
- If you're not in one, a shop may not be able to use you as an apprentice there at all
- Ask your teacher about it before you graduate
Check the details with the state, not with me.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie

fact_risk: prevailing wage coverage thresholds/exceptions

threads.author: mbell_wireman
threads.title: Prevailing wage vs PLAs: why the big public jobs look the way they do
threads.body:
This keeps coming up, so here's the union-side view. I'd welcome the non-union contractors here to correct me where it's different for them.

Prevailing wage is a floor. On covered public work, everyone gets at least the published rate for their trade and county, union or not.

A project labor agreement is a different thing. It's an agreement for a specific project, usually a big one, about labor terms: hiring through the trades, how disputes get handled, no strikes. You'll hear about them on large public construction.

If you're an apprentice and you land on one of these jobs, a few things will be new: sign-in sheets, long safety orientations, and someone checking that your classification matches your paperwork. Bring your ID, bring your card, wear your glasses. Stay safe.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Mostly right, and thanks for asking for the other side. One thing I'd adjust: it isn't every public job. There are thresholds and exceptions, and the state's site spells them out. From the non-union side, the certified payroll is the real cost of public work, not the wages. On PLAs, I'll just say not every contractor thinks they're good for competition, and leave it there.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Fair correction on the thresholds, and I appreciate you keeping it civil. Plenty of people on my side would say the same thing about PLAs from the other direction.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: From the inspection side: whatever the labor terms are, the code doesn't change. I've seen people on public jobs assume the rules are different because the paperwork is. Check which code edition is in effect for the project, and read the project specs, which sometimes ask for more than code.

threads.author: Kash_sing
threads.title: Where the money from a $189 service call actually goes
threads.body:
Every year a new tech sees an invoice and asks why he makes $22 an hour when we charged $189 for forty minutes. Fair question. Here's roughly how I explain it at my shop. Numbers differ everywhere; this is the shape, not a formula.
- The tech's wage, plus payroll taxes and workers' comp on top of it
- The truck: payment, fuel, insurance, repairs, the stock on the shelves
- The office: the person who answered the phone and scheduled you
- Drive time between calls that the customer never sees on the bill
- Callbacks, which we fix for free
- Slow weeks in October when the phones are quiet and everyone still gets paid
After all that, a healthy shop keeps a margin, and plenty of shops don't. I'd rather you understand this before you go out on your own and price yourself out of business.

> a healthy shop keeps a margin

replies.body:
Because some of them are. Two things:
- A lot of owners pay themselves last
- Equipment margins and service margins are very different animals
I'm not saying every owner is honest about it. I'm saying the $189 isn't profit.

replies.body: Same on the mechanical side. The number new guys never see is unbilled time. Here's what I look for in a tech who's earned a raise: the one whose calls don't come back. A callback is the most expensive hour we have.

- If it isn't, that's a conversation with your boss, and the state labor department has the details

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it: NJ is strict about who counts as an independent contractor. As far as I know, the state uses a test where, among other things, you have to be free of their control and actually running your own independent business. Their schedule, their shirt and their calls sounds like an employee to me. Read the NJ Department of Labor's material on misclassification, or talk to an accountant, before you sign anything.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
From the owner's side, here's what a 1099 usually means you pay for yourself:
- Both halves of payroll taxes
- Your own insurance, and no workers' comp if you get hurt
- Van, fuel, tools, phone
- No overtime
Subtract all of that from the higher rate before you compare. It's often less money, not more.

threads.author: dreb_jman
threads.title: For the Jersey apprentices on my crew: the commute, honestly
threads.body:
Half my apprentices live in Jersey, so I've heard every version of this. Here's what I tell them.

Don't drive in unless the job pays for parking or you have a spot. Between the crossing, the tolls and a garage in Midtown, you're working the first hour of the day for free. Train or PATH, then walk.

Leave earlier than you think. A 7am start means on the floor at 7 with your glasses on, not walking in the door.

Don't move to the city in year one. You don't know where your jobs will be in two years, and rent will eat you alive.

And I'm not one to talk. My sister lives in Bayonne, and every Sunday after dinner I sit in tunnel traffic going home and swear never again. So I get it, brother.

threads.author: ms_almonte
threads.title: First week of the fall semester: 22 new faces, three have held a torch
threads.body:
Every September I swear I'll stop being surprised, and every September I'm surprised. New class started this week. Twenty-two of them. Three have held a torch, and one of those set his sleeve on fire in the first hour. Nobody hurt, everybody learned something.

First thing I teach, before anything technical: where the extinguisher is and how to use it. Second: how to sweep a floor properly. They laugh at that one. They stop laughing when they find out how much of the job it is.

For anyone who trains helpers: what's the first thing you make a new person learn? Ask me how I know it matters.

replies.body: Proud of you, brother. You left the right way. Nobody in this trade remembers why you left. They remember how.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Two weeks and a thank-you. You'd be surprised how many guys can't manage that. The owner will remember it when somebody calls him for a reference, and somebody always does.

replies.author: wchen_controls
replies.body: fwiw 'unsafe' is reason enough, you don't owe anybody details. good luck at the new place. fit-outs means you'll see some low voltage, pay attention to it, it's a real trade

threads.author: Dev.R
threads.title: first week running calls solo. no callbacks yet
threads.body: 3 years riding with a lead and this week they gave me my own van and my own calls. pemberton, browns mills, mount holly. 14 calls in 5 days, mostly no-cools on the last hot days and two furnace checks. no callbacks yet. called my lead twice, once for weird thermostat wiring and once because i couldn't find the attic access in a split level. he answered both times and didn't make me feel stupid. anyway. that's it. just wanted to tell people who get it

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Nice!! A first solo week with no callbacks is a good week... my first solo week I called my lead eleven times. Twice is nothing lol. Keep calling when you need to

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's what I look for in a new service tech: calls the lead when he isn't sure instead of guessing. You're doing it right. Callbacks will come eventually; how you handle the first one is what matters.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Congratulations. One habit for the first year:
- Photo of the nameplate, the thermostat wiring and your readings on every call
When a callback does happen, you'll know exactly what you left.

threads.author: rui_t_kearny
threads.title: My best helper got the call from the Local. Happy for him. Mostly.
threads.body:
The vo-tech kid I hired last year, best helper I've had in a long time. Shows up early, listens, asks the right questions. He applied to the plumbers' local in the spring without telling me. Got the call this week. Starts in January.

I'm happy for him, and I mean that. I was in the union myself for a few years. I know exactly what he's getting: real schooling, real benefits. My father used to say you can't keep a good kid in a small shop, you can only be the shop he's glad he started in.

Still. I'd started thinking he might be the one to take this place over someday. Back to the hiring pile. Anyone else lose their best guy this year?

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Every spring I lose students to the locals and every spring I'm proud and a little sad. You did your part. He'll remember who taught him to carry a water heater properly.

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: the guy from deptford is still reading, just saying lol. appreciate the advice from the other thread either way

replies.author: benplumb79

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Some do. I did, didn't I? Took me a few years. The door's open for him, and I told him so.

threads.author: sweatjoint200amp
threads.title: Since the pork roll thread settled nothing... Wawa or QuickChek?
threads.body: Sorry, I know there was already a whole pork roll war on here... but nobody settled the other one. I'm in Little Falls, I just started riding with a crew that does commercial bathrooms all over, and this week we were in Hamilton and the guys from down there acted like I insulted their mother when I said QuickChek coffee is better. So... Wawa or QuickChek? And is it a north/south thing or an actual coffee thing? Defend your answer, I'm buying coffee for the crew Friday and I need to pick a side...

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Wawa. Not even a question... I've been going to the same Wawa in Cherry Hill for 15 years and they know my order lol. QuickChek is a nice gas station. Wawa is a lifestyle

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: QuickChek. I said it in the other thread and I'll say it again. Up here it isn't even a choice, it's geography.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: I'm from Hamilton. I wasn't there, but I would have been one of the guys acting insulted. Wawa. The hoagie line at 6am is a sacred place and you walked in and disrespected it.

replies.author: QuickChekCrew
replies.body: In my defense the handle was a joke... I live in Cherry Hill. I'm Wawa. I'm sorry to everyone who expected otherwise.

replies.author: WawaRunWired
replies.body: fair lawn. my handle is also a lie, the closest wawa is a real drive. quickchek every morning. sorry

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Kid, I've been drinking deli coffee in Lodi for 28 years. You're all wrong. Buy the crew coffee at the deli by the supply house and nobody fights.

replies.author: sweatjoint200amp
replies.body: ziggy that is the most boss answer possible... but which one would you pick if you HAD to?

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: QuickChek, because it's on my way. That's the whole reason. Don't tell anybody down south.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig

replies.author: TaylorHamHVAC

replies.author: Bergen_Ducts
replies.body: hackensack, but my mom's from toms river so we drive past six wawas to see my grandma... honestly wawa coffee is better and the quickchek sandwiches are better, fight me

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Ok Bergen_Ducts gets a pass because his mom raised him right... the rest of you up north are still lost

replies.author: ms_almonte

replies.author: peteplumb80

replies.author: dahvacnj

replies.author: mbell_wireman

replies.author: Kearny_Pipefitter

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: cherry hill... wawa. i didn't know quickchek was a real place until i was 19 lol

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: the coffee on route 1 jobsites comes off a truck. drink it and go to work.

replies.author: big_ben_tools
replies.body: glassboro. wawa. didn't know this was even a question until this thread. edit: my teacher just said quickchek has better coffee and i don't know what to believe anymore

replies.author: sweatjoint200amp

threads.author: EssexPipes
threads.title: Boss threw a pipe wrench across the basement. Quit on the spot.
threads.body: Two years out of the county vo-tech, 14 months at this shop in Essex. All demo, all carrying, and a boss who throws tools when he's in a mood. Today it was a pipe wrench across a basement. Didn't hit anybody. I put my stuff in my car, told him I was done, and drove home. Already have an interview Thursday with a shop in Montclair that does service. Did I mess up by not giving notice? Should I call him and smooth it over or just let it go?

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body:
What's your actual question? Because "did I mess up" and "should I call him" have different answers.

Did you mess up: no. Someone throwing a pipe wrench in a basement is a safety problem, not a mood. Should you call: a short text saying you won't be back and where to send your last check is enough.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Don't trash him around the supply houses, though, even if he deserves it. People will hear about the wrench without your help. You just be the guy who shows up Thursday.

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: montclair has a few decent service shops. good luck thursday. wear the clean boots

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Agree with both. Thrown tools are how people get hurt, and you don't owe notice to someone who makes the site unsafe. Write down the date and what happened, in case it ever matters for anything.

replies.author: EssexPipes
replies.body: Sent the text. He replied with a thumbs up. That's the most communication I've gotten from him in a year. Interview's Thursday, boots are clean.

threads.author: CentralJersey_Coils
threads.title: Got the 608 Universal on the first try (core was the hard part)
threads.body: Took the EPA 608 at a supply house testing session Saturday and passed Universal. Core was the hardest section, like everyone says. Big thanks to ms_almonte, who told me to drill Core until I could recite the dates in my sleep. Still a vo-tech student, but now I'm allowed to actually hook up gauges with my lead watching. The shop I'm doing Saturdays at said they'd bump me a dollar once I had it, so we'll see if they remember.

threads.author: kofihvac87
threads.title: First heating call of the season and the thermostat was set to COOL
threads.body: First cold morning this week and the phones at the shop went off. My first heating call of the season, in Roselle: "furnace blowing cold air." I pulled the panel, checked the flame sensor, checked the inducer, checked the filter. Twenty minutes in, the homeowner's daughter asked if the thermostat was supposed to say COOL. It was. Switched it to HEAT and the furnace fired right up. We still charged the service fee because the office said so, and I felt terrible. Lol. Two years in and I still fell for it.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Lol everybody has one of these... thermostat first is the oldest lesson in the book and we all learn it the hard way anyway. Welcome to heating season

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Don't feel terrible about the fee. You drove there, diagnosed it, and checked the flame sensor and filter while you were in there, which is real work. Two things I'd do:
- Tell the customer what you checked, so they know they got something
- Write "tstat in cool" on the ticket so the office starts asking that question on the phone
The first cold week is full of these.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First thing I tell students on a no-heat: talk to the thermostat before you talk to the furnace. Second: ask the homeowner what changed since the last time it worked. Ask me how I know you'll still forget once a year.

replies.author: big_zach_hvac
replies.body: did the exact same thing last week in elizabeth. except it was the fan set to ON not AUTO. homeowner thought it was broken because it blew cold between cycles

threads.author: OpenNeutralBlues
threads.title: Got the call. Interview for the IBEW apprenticeship is next month
threads.body: Applied over the summer because my shop teacher would not stop bringing it up. Took the aptitude test. Got a call today with an interview date. I was at the Wawa when my phone rang and almost dropped my coffee. Not in yet, I know. But I didn't think I'd get this far. What do I wear and what do they ask?

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Brother, congrats. That's a big step. I can only speak for how mine went years ago: clean simple clothes, on time means early, and be honest. They want to know you'll show up and listen. Don't pretend you know more than you do.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Congratulations. Bring proof of any work or school you have, even weekend helper hours. Know why you want this trade in one or two sentences. And when they ask about safety, mean it. Stay safe.

replies.author: mselecnj
replies.body: 1st year 164. i wore a button down and was the most overdressed guy in the room lol. still got in. just be on time

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Practice saying your answers out loud before the day. My students who do mock interviews with me always do better than the ones who wing it. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: epa60812_2
replies.body: congrats brother. hvac guy here but rooting for you, update us after the interview

threads.author: blowerwheel_91
threads.title: Accepted into the steamfitters' apprenticeship. I start in January.
threads.body: Sorry if this isn't the right place for it. I'm two years out of the Morris County vo-tech HVAC program. I applied to the steamfitters' apprenticeship last spring, did the test and the interview, and got the acceptance call today. I start in January. My parents didn't really understand why I was so excited until I explained the benefits part. Anyway, I wanted to tell people who would understand. If anyone has advice for the first year, thanks in advance.

threads.author: DinerCoffeeHVAC
threads.title: GC's super ripped into me on a JC jobsite. This time I deserved it
threads.body: Doing a ductless install in an apartment renovation in Jersey City. I left a ceiling access open and a bag of insulation in the hallway overnight. Fire inspector walked through first thing in the morning. The GC's super found me at 7am and let me have it in front of the drywall guys. He was right. I was embarrassed. Apologized, cleaned it up. Sorry if this is a dumb post, I'm just stewing on it. How do you get over getting yelled at when it actually was your fault?

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body:
First: you owned it and fixed it. That's most of it.

Second: tomorrow, be the first one cleaning up at the end of the day, without being asked, where he can see it.

Third: let it go by the weekend. Every one of us has a story like this. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Open ceilings and material in an egress path are a real problem on a multifamily job, so he wasn't wrong to be upset. Take the lesson, ignore the tone. Do an end-of-day walk every day: access panels closed, path clear. Stay safe.

replies.author: Passaic_Sparky
replies.body: idk, getting yelled at when you were wrong is alot easier than when you weren't. at least you know what to fix

replies.author: DinerCoffeeHVAC
replies.body: fair. did the end of day walk today. super nodded at me on the way out. that's probably as good as it gets

threads.author: plumbnj77
threads.title: Rain rant: nine days of mud on an underground job in Jackson
threads.body: Not a question, I just need to yell. New construction in Jackson, we're supposed to be setting underground for six houses. It has rained nine of the last eleven days. The trench is soup. The GC wants it done by Friday anyway. My boots weigh ten pounds each and I've lost a glove in the mud every single day. How do you guys keep your stuff dry? Does anyone own boots that actually survive this, brother?

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: rotate two pairs of boots. one dries by the heater overnight while you destroy the other one. thats the whole secret

replies.author: RainDayRestock
replies.body: My handle is literally about this. On rain days my boss sends us to restock the van. Underground guys don't get that luxury I guess.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Kid, mud's part of it. Rubber boots over your work boots on trench days, and a bucket with a lid for your tools. And don't let the GC rush you into a bad joint because of a deadline. The inspector won't care that it rained. That's the job.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: Electrical vo-tech kid here. I thought the attic in July was the worst thing in the trades. This sounds worse.

replies.author: plumbnj77
replies.body: attic in july is worse for like 2 months. mud is worse the rest of the year. both suck brother

replies.author: ThreeWayConfusion
replies.body: I'm in Jackson too and it's been miserable. Our new-construction job got pushed a week because nobody could get trucks down the access road.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Lol we once did a rooftop changeout in a nor'easter because the crane was already paid for... nobody should do that. Stay dry out there

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: It was 97 outside and I swear 140 in that attic
threads.body: Summer job, helping an electrical contractor while school's out. Today we ran a new circuit for a bathroom fan in a Cape in Hamilton, which meant the attic. In the heat wave. My shirt was soaked through in four minutes. I drank three bottles of water and my boss made me come down every 20 minutes, which I was mad about until I got dizzy on the ladder coming down the last time. I'm fine. Sat in the truck with the AC on for a while. Is this just what summers are? How do you all do this for 20 years?

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Your boss made the right call, and I'm glad he did. Heat illness sneaks up on people, and dizziness on a ladder is exactly how someone gets hurt. Do attic work early in the morning, take breaks before you need them, water plus something with electrolytes. If you feel off, you come down. Stay safe.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: try a walk-in compressor on a boardwalk roof in july. at least your attic had shade lol

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly the shore attics are the worst. Raised houses, dark shingles, no ventilation. I schedule attic work before 10am in July and August now, period. Took me way too long to learn that.

replies.author: big_paulie_plumb
replies.body: 20 years? i'm 4 years in and i already bought a cooling towel and a little fan that clips on my hard hat. no shame

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: hvac helper in clifton, we did 3 attic air handlers this week. my handle was a joke when i made it. it's not a joke anymore

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: Ordering the cooling towel. My boss also said nobody gets a medal for staying up there. Writing that on my tool bag.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Lol that's a good boss... So this one time in AC, a guy on my crew didn't come down when he should have and we had to help him out of the attic. He was ok. Come down when your boss says come down

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: One thing from my side, since I inspect a lot of summer attic work: when you're miserable, you rush, and rushed connections are what fail later. Take the break, then make the connection right. Heat makes people skip steps.

threads.author: leadfree98
threads.title: Homeowner tried to hand me a $20 tip. Do you take it?
threads.body: First month as a helper at a shop near Long Branch. We fixed a leak under an older lady's kitchen sink today, and while we were packing up she tried to hand me a $20 and a bottle of water. I took the water and said no to the money because idk what the rule is. My lead laughed at me in the truck. Is it ok to take tips? Does the shop care? Do you split it with your lead?

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly, at my shop the rule is simple: if a customer insists, say thank you and take it, and never ask or hint. Some shops have a no-tip policy, so ask your boss once and then you know. Splitting with your lead is a nice move when he did most of the work, which in month one, he probably did.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Take the water every time, kid. Take the money if she insists twice. Never take it from someone who looks like they can't afford it. That's the job.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: my foreman says a tip means the customer liked you, it's not a payment. he gives it to whoever did the cleanup. no idea if that's a thing everywhere

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Down here in summer it's cold Gatorade and leftover hoagies... I've been tipped in tomatoes from a guy's garden. Took the tomatoes lol

replies.author: leadfree98
replies.body: ok asked my boss. he said keep it if they insist, nothing over $20, and buy the lead a coffee. so now i owe my lead a coffee for a tip i didn't even take lol

threads.author: big_hector_plumb
threads.title: Customer called the office and asked for me by name
threads.body: 4 years in, running service on my own in Hudson. I'm not a talker. Customers usually ask for my boss or the other guy, the one who can talk to anybody. Today the office said a lady in Weehawken called back for a second job and asked for "the quiet one who explained the water heater." Small thing. Made my week. The explanation was me drawing on a piece of cardboard because I'm better at that than talking lol.

threads.author: JerseyTomatoWires
threads.title: A first-year asked ME how to bend an offset today...
threads.body: 4th year in 164... today a brand new first-year on our job asked me how to bend an offset and I just showed him without thinking about it. Then I realized I was him three years ago, asking the same thing and wasting half a stick of EMT. My foreman saw it and said "see, you're useful now." Weird feeling... anyway, I top out next year. Just wanted to say it somewhere

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: That's the moment. Teaching someone is how you find out you actually know it. Keep doing it, and teach him the safety part along with the bend. Stay safe.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Good. The apprentices who teach well usually make the best journeymen. Teach him why, not just how. 'Because that's how we do it' is how bad habits travel from crew to crew.

replies.author: TwistAndTape
replies.body: 2nd year 164 here, still the one asking lol. i hope somebody on my job is this nice

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: appreciate it... and yeah, the safety part, I made him put his glasses on first. learned that one from my foreman too

threads.author: jess2093
threads.title: Week one done. Everything hurts and I'm weirdly happy
threads.body: Left insurance claims last month, I'm 28, and I started as a plumbing helper at a shop out of Glassboro on Monday. Five days of carrying cast iron out of a basement in Pitman and hauling a water heater up some stairs. My hands are wrecked, my back is wrecked, I fell asleep at 8:30 every night. And I haven't checked a work email in a week. Don't know if I'll last. Anyway. Week one, done.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Week one is the worst one, physically. Your body catches up in about a month. I switched over from restaurant management at 26 and I remember falling asleep in my boots. It gets better. Keep going.

replies.author: FluxOnMyBoots
replies.body: career switcher too. week 1 i couldn't close my hands in the morning lol. by week 6 i was fine

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: pitman basements are no joke... welcome. it gets easier, or you just stop noticing

threads.author: ThirdYearTinknocker
threads.title: worked all of labor day weekend on strip mall rooftops. rant incoming
threads.body: everybody i know was at the beach labor day weekend. me? three days straight of rooftop units on strip malls around neptune and ocean township, 90+ and humid, and every RTU in monmouth county decided to die the same weekend. one roof had no hatch so it was an extension ladder in the heat with a bag of tools. made good OT. hate everything. appreciate you guys reading this far

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Labor Day weekend in HVAC is a tradition... nobody in this trade is at a barbecue lol. Congrats on surviving it

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: same weekend every year down here, ice machines and walk-ins on the boardwalk nonstop. the tuesday after labor day everything goes quiet and you sleep for a week

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Holiday weekends are where the money gets made and where techs burn out. If you work a lot of them:
- Ask how holiday pay works before the weekend, not after
- Bank some of that OT
- Take a day when it slows down, and ask for it in writing

replies.author: matt_the_hvac

threads.author: oldsteam_zig
threads.title: Torch work in old houses: stick around after you put the torch down
threads.body:
Had a helper sweat a couple of fittings on a boiler near a joist bay in Lodi last week. Nice joints. We packed up, I went back down for a tool I forgot, and I smelled it before I saw it. The old wood and the dust up in that bay had been smoldering the whole time.

Nobody got hurt and the house is fine. But here's what everybody on my trucks does now, and what I should have made him do:

Fire cloth behind the joint before you light the torch, not after. Wet down old framing if it's dry as paper. Spray bottle and an extinguisher on the floor next to you, not out on the truck. And when you're done, stay and watch it for half an hour. Put your hand near the wood. Look up into the bay with a light.

Old balloon-frame houses in Bergen have bays that run open floor to floor. A spark goes up there and you won't see it until it's a real problem.

Thirty minutes of watching is cheap. That's the job.

replies.author: EssexPipes
replies.body: Good one. What kind of fire cloth do you guys actually use, the cheap felt ones from the supply house or the pricier ones? And do you wet the wood every single time or only when it's old?

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: The felt ones are fine for half inch and three quarter copper if you keep them in good shape. I spray old wood every time, it costs nothing. And check the other side of the wall. Hoboken brownstones share party walls, and the smoke shows up in the neighbor's place first.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First thing I teach before anyone touches a torch: know where the extinguisher is and what's on the other side of the wall. Second: you're not done when the joint is done. Students hate the waiting part. Ask me how I know it matters.

threads.author: joe.plumb
threads.title: Press coupling spit water under test... boss says I never pressed it
fact_risk: press fittings designed to leak when left unpressed (manufacturer feature)
threads.body:
So we did a small repipe in a ranch in Cherry Hill, all press, and when the boss put it under test one of my 3/4 couplings was spitting... he took one look and said I never pressed it. I swear I did. Then he showed me the pipe and there was no depth mark, because I skipped marking on couplings since "I could feel it seat"...

Couple questions. Is it normal for an unpressed fitting to leak like that or did I just get lucky? And if I DID press it and it still leaked, what else causes that? Trying to not do this twice

edit: boss redid it, passed. buying a marker for every pouch I own

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
You got lucky in the right way. A lot of the press fittings on the market now are designed to leak when they haven't been pressed, so you find them under test instead of months later behind drywall. It did its job.

If a fitting is pressed and still leaks, the usual causes on our jobs: the pipe wasn't fully inserted, a burr or a rough cut nicked the O-ring, dirt on the pipe, a dented or out-of-round end, or the wrong jaw for the size. Cut square, deburr, wipe, mark, insert to the mark, press. Every time.

Here's what I look for when I hire, by the way: somebody who marks depth on couplings too.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: my uncle makes me mark depth and then he checks the mark after the press before he lets me move on. annoying but it works

threads.author: DinerCoffeeHVAC
threads.title: Why does my lead flow nitrogen when we braze linesets?
fact_risk: flowing nitrogen while brazing to prevent internal oxide scale
threads.body: Sorry if this is a dumb one. Doing a lot of AC changeouts in Bayonne and JC this summer. Every time we braze the lineset my lead hooks up the nitrogen bottle with a regulator and has a little flow going through the pipe while I braze. He told me "so you don't make crud" and walked off. What crud? In school we just brazed. Is this actually a big deal or is it one of those things one guy does?

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Not a one-guy thing... it's a big deal lol. Copper heated with air inside it grows black oxide scale on the inside wall. Later that scale flakes off and goes where you don't want it: the metering device, the screens, the compressor oil. A low flow of nitrogen pushes the oxygen out so the inside stays clean. So this one time in AC I cut open a line on a casino job where nobody flowed nitrogen and it looked like the inside of a chimney. Low flow, through a regulator, just enough to feel on your hand.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Plumber's side of it, kid: on water we sweat with soft solder and nobody cares about a little oxide inside. Refrigerant is brazed and the system is sealed, so whatever's inside stays inside forever. Different animal. Listen to your lead on this one.

threads.author: middlesex_coils
threads.title: mini-split flare connection leaking on a brand new install
fact_risk: flare nut torque per manufacturer spec
no thread sealant on flare faces
nitrogen pressure test and micron-gauge vacuum decay test
threads.body: apologies if this is basic. we installed a single zone mini-split in a split-level in woodbridge last week. pulled a vacuum, it held for a few minutes, released the refrigerant, and two days later the customer says it's blowing warm. my lead found the liquid line flare at the indoor head leaking. i made that flare. what usually causes a flare to leak, and how do you know a flare is good before you tighten it? i would like to stop guessing on these.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Flare leaks are almost always one of these:
- Cut not square, or not deburred (or deburred so hard the wall got thin)
- Flare nut not on the pipe before you flared it (everyone does it once)
- Wrong flare size, or an off-center flare from a worn tool
- Not torqued to the manufacturer's spec. Too loose leaks, too tight cracks the flare
- Dirt or a scratch on the flare face

Before you tighten it, look at it: smooth, even, no cracks, sits flat on the cone. Torque wrench and the number from the install manual. Then a nitrogen pressure test and a vacuum on a micron gauge, held long enough to mean something. A few minutes isn't a decay test.

A callback like this eats the margin on the whole install, so it's worth getting right.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Plumber here, so take it for what it's worth. My father used to say a flare is a sealing face, not a thread joint. Don't put pipe dope or tape anywhere near it. I watched a guy do that on a gas flare once and I'm still mad about it.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: torque wrench. every time. the guys who do flares by feel in july are the ones i see again in august. if you have to redo one, cut it off and flare it fresh, don't just crank it tighter and hope

threads.author: plumbguy917
threads.title: Brownstone gas job: why are we still threading black iron?
fact_risk: NYC gas work must be done under a Licensed Master Plumber
NYC DOB gas work qualification for workers
press systems listed for gas and NYC acceptance
NYC periodic gas piping inspections (Local Law 152)
threads.body:
1st year. On a brownstone gut reno in Park Slope with my journeyman, running new gas from the meter in the cellar up to the kitchen on the parlor floor. All black iron, threaded, and I'm the one cutting and threading all day lol. The water side of the same job is all press and it goes like 5x faster.

So why not press the gas too? Journeyman just says "not on this job" and "the inspection is the inspection." Is it a code thing in the city, a cost thing, or is he just old school? Not trying to do anything myself, just want to understand what I'm doing.

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body:
In the city it's different, and gas is where it's most different. Gas work here has to be done under a licensed master plumber, the workers need their own DOB gas qualification, and the work gets inspected and tested before the utility will turn anything on. A lot of buildings also have periodic gas piping inspections now, so old brownstone lines get looked at much more than they used to.

On press for gas: some press systems are made and listed for gas, and I've seen them used. Whether a given job can use one is something I check against the current code and DOB requirements every time. I won't tell you yes from memory, and your journeyman made that call for this job.

Ask him to show you how he checks a thread. That's the part worth learning.

replies.author: ginaj75
replies.body: jersey side, 2 years in and my boss still won't let me near gas. i carry the pipe and clean up

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question: why black iron, or why him and not you? Black iron because that's what he's confident will pass on that job. Him because you're a 1st year and it's gas. Learn to cut a clean thread. Same deal in Jersey City brownstones.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Jersey side we still thread most gas too, kid. Press is fine when it's the right listed system and the inspector's good with it. Your journeyman's being careful with somebody else's house on a gas job. That's the job.

replies.author: plumbguy917
replies.body: update: asked him. he said every press system for gas he's seen needs its own fittings and jaws and the company doesn't own them yet lol. so it's both. he let me stand with him on the pressure test though

threads.author: elecny85
threads.title: Plumber says the water pipe bond is pointless now that it's PEX
fact_risk: metal water service as grounding electrode, connection near entry, jumper around the meter (NEC 250.52/250.53/250.68)
bonding of interior metal water piping (NEC 250.104(A))
NYC Electrical Code amendments to the NEC
CSST bonding requirements
threads.body:
non union apprentice in brooklyn... we're on a 3-family townhouse new build in east flatbush. copper water service comes in from the street to the meter, then the plumber ran everything after the meter in PEX. my foreman wants the water bond done a certain way and the plumber is laughing at him, says "it's all plastic brother, there's nothing to bond, that's from the 80s."

my foreman just said "do it anyway." I'd like to actually understand who's right because they're both going to ask me to do stuff on this job... is the plumber right that PEX means no water bond? and why does the meter matter at all? thanks in advance

replies.author: HelperForNow
replies.body: following. our shop just clamps to whatever copper is near the panel and calls it a day, now im wondering

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Two separate questions, and the plumber and your foreman are each answering a different one.

One: is the water service an electrode? If the pipe coming in from the street is metal and in the earth long enough, it counts as a grounding electrode, it gets connected close to where it enters, and the connection can't depend on the meter, so there's a jumper around it. If the service is plastic, it isn't an electrode and you need others.

Two: is there metal water piping inside that has to be bonded? If the inside is all PEX, there may be very little. But a copper service up to the meter is metal piping either way.

You're in the city, so it's the NYC Electrical Code with its own amendments, and I inspect in Jersey. Check which code edition applies to your permit, and ask your foreman.

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body: In the city it's different on paper, but the physics is the same. On my townhouse jobs the service comes in copper to the meter, the electrician bonds it near the entry with a jumper around the meter, and after that we go PEX. Nobody argues about it on my jobs.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: My father used to say never cut a water pipe without a jumper on it first. If there's an open neutral on the street, the current goes looking for a path, and the plumber holding both ends of a cut pipe becomes the path. I keep a jumper cable with two clamps on my truck for exactly this.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: wait so if it's all pex then there's nothing to bond and the plumber is right? our shop teacher said pex basically killed the water pipe ground. so the plumber kind of has a point

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
> pex basically killed the water pipe ground

Partly. It changed what's there to bond. If there's no metal water piping, there's nothing to bond on that system. But on his job the service is copper up to the meter, so that copper is still in play. The answer is always what's actually in the building, not what someone says is in it.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Whatever the answer on paper, treat that pipe as possibly energized until you've proven otherwise. I've watched a meter get swapped in an occupied building with no jumper on and the plumber got bit. A jumper and gloves cost nothing. Stay safe.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question: who's right, or who has to do it? On my jobs the bond is the electrician's. My part is not removing it, and putting a jumper on before I cut anything.

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Brother, in the high-rises it's the same story, just bigger. Bonding on the water risers, the gas, the steel. Nobody on my job touches a bond without the foreman knowing.

replies.author: elecny85
replies.body: ok this is making more sense... so the plumber is half right? the pex isn't anything to bond but the copper service before the meter still is. thanks for the patience lol

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Half right is how most job-site arguments end up, kid. Tell the plumber to put a jumper across before he swaps that meter, and tell your foreman where the bond is so nobody "cleans it up" later. That's the job.

replies.author: groundrod_05
replies.body: Apex grad here. We were taught the clamp goes on the street side, within the first few feet of where the pipe enters the building, not on some random pipe near the panel. Appreciate everyone explaining the jumper part, that one we didn't really cover.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I see the flip side of this down the shore. After Sandy a lot of houses got repiped in PEX and the old water bond got left clamped to a stub of copper going nowhere. Looks official, does nothing.

replies.author: HelperForNow
replies.body: edit to my earlier post: asked my boss. he said we clamp the service copper near where it comes in, and he just bought the plumbers a jumper lol. so "whatever copper is near the panel" was me not paying attention

replies.author: auelecny
replies.body: Career switcher in Ozone Park here. idk if this is a dumb question but what about the gas pipe, brother? Does that get bonded too or is that a different thing?

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body: Gas is its own question. Metal gas piping gets bonded too, and the yellow flexible gas tubing has its own bonding requirements from the manufacturer and the code. In the city I let the electrician and the inspector settle exactly how. Gas bonding is not a place to get creative.

threads.author: emt_bender_200amp
threads.title: Set screw or compression EMT fittings? Our instructor won't just say
fact_risk: set-screw EMT fittings for dry locations; raintight compression for wet; concrete-tight in concrete (NEC 358.42)
threads.body:
Ok so context, I'm in a trade program in Queens, senior year, we're doing conduit right now and I'm the kid who actually likes bending (hence the name). We've been using set screw connectors and couplings on everything in the shop. Today the instructor handed out compression fittings for the "outdoor" mockup, and when I asked when you use which, he said "when the job tells you." Which is not an answer.

Is it just wet vs dry? Is compression better everywhere and set screw is just cheaper? And what do you use in concrete? Thanks in advance, I just want to understand it before I'm on a real job looking stupid.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Your instructor is right, but here's the longer version. Set screw fittings are generally for dry locations. Wet and damp locations, outdoors, anywhere water can get in, you want fittings listed for that use, which usually means raintight compression. Embedded in concrete, you need fittings listed as concrete-tight. The listing on the box tells you where it's allowed, so read it.

Field side: compression costs more and takes longer, and a nut that wasn't tightened will pull apart. Set screws strip if you lean on them. On our data center jobs it's set screw inside the building and compression for anything outdoors or on the roof. Stay safe, and enjoy the bending. It's a skill people pay for.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Plumber here. Compression fittings are my whole world and they leak if you don't tighten them. Apparently it's the same idea for you guys.

replies.author: LiveFrontLessons
replies.body: 1st year out of vo-tech in jersey. we did a whole porch in set screw and the inspector made us redo it in raintight. so yeah wet vs dry is real. does anybody actually use concrete tight on residential?

replies.author: OpenNeutralBlues
replies.body: Our shop teacher at the vo-tech says the same thing as yours. Read the box. We literally got quizzed on box labels.

replies.author: LateStartPlumber
replies.body: sorry, plumbing guy on staten island, but why emt outdoors at all and not pvc? is that a cost thing or a code thing

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly down the shore I run a lot of PVC outdoors because salt air eats steel. EMT outside works with the right fittings, it just rusts near the ocean. Depends on the job and the spec. And to the other question, yes, concrete-tight on residential when there's conduit in a slab, garages mostly.

replies.author: emt_bender_200amp
replies.body: This is the answer I wanted. Read the listing, wet vs dry, concrete tight in concrete, and the beach eats everything. Bringing box labels to class tomorrow lol

threads.author: leadfree98
threads.title: swapped one hallway switch and now the light only works from one end
threads.body:
plumbing guy here so go easy. my mom's hallway in long branch has a light switch at both ends. one switch was cracked so I bought a new one at the hardware store, breaker off, swapped it wire for wire (I thought). now the light only works from the new switch when the other one is in one position, and sometimes not at all. did I buy the wrong switch or wire it wrong? idk why it would care which screw. also is this a call-an-electrician thing at this point

edit: it was the dark screw thing. thanks

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly this is the most common 3-way mistake there is, don't feel bad. A 3-way has one darker screw (the common) and two lighter ones (the travelers). Your new switch probably has the common in a different spot than the old one, so the wire that was on the old common ended up on a traveler screw. Breaker off, verify dead with a tester, then find that wire. If you didn't mark it, that's where it gets harder. If the wiring is cloth or crumbly, stop and call someone. Long Branch has plenty of hallways like that.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: To your second question: if you can't sort it out with the power off and a tester, that's the point to call an electrician. Next time, put a piece of tape on the wire from the dark screw before anything comes off.

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: same thing happened to me in my apartment in deptford. it was the common. took me an hour. appreciate it, learned something too

threads.author: peteplumb80
threads.title: what does a 4-way switch actually do in the middle?
threads.body: UA 1st year, plumbing, so this is pure curiosity. The electrician on our job (commercial bathrooms in a building in Montclair, long corridor outside them) was explaining the corridor lights at lunch. 3-way at each end, I followed that from the other thread on here. Then he said there's a 4-way in the middle and it "flips the travelers" and he lost me. Flips them how? Why can't you just put a third 3-way in the middle?

replies.author: JughandleJourneyman
replies.body: IBEW 2nd year here... the way my foreman explained it: both travelers come into the 4-way, and the 4-way either passes them straight through or crosses them over, so traveler A goes out on B and B goes out on A. Flipping it swaps which traveler is live at the far end... so any switch can change the light. A 3-way only has one common and two travelers, it can't do the swap, which is why the middle one has to be a 4-way. You can put as many 4-ways in a row as you want between the two 3-ways.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly that's one of the better explanations I've seen. Draw it: two 3-ways on the ends, the 4-way in the middle, and trace it with your finger in every position.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: One thing to add for when you see these in the field: check the 4-way's instructions for which screws are the pair in and which are the pair out. They aren't always laid out the same, and mixing them up gives you exactly the "works sometimes" complaint.

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: ok the crossing over thing finally clicked. kind of like a diverter on a manifold, sort of. thanks guys, back to toilets

threads.author: HelperForNow
threads.title: re-identifying the white wire on a switch loop, is tape enough
fact_risk: re-identifying the white conductor in a switch loop, white as the supply (NEC 200.7(C))
neutral at switch locations (NEC 404.2(C)) and when it applies
threads.body: residential remodel in manahawkin. old part of the house has a ceiling light fed at the fixture, with a 2-wire cable down to the switch. my boss wraps black tape on the white at both ends and moves on. in school they mentioned something about needing a neutral at switches now. is the tape enough on an existing loop, and does the newer code mean we have to rewire it when we touch it?

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Re-identifying the white with tape or another permanent marking, wherever it's visible and accessible, is the long-standing way to use it as a hot in a switch loop. In a loop the white is supposed to be the supply going to the switch, not the return to the light.

The neutral-at-the-switch requirement applies to switch locations in the code editions that have it, with exceptions. Whether touching an existing loop pulls you into it depends on the edition and the scope of the permit, so check which code edition is in effect and ask your inspector before you assume.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly on remodels, if the wall's already open we pull a new 14/3. Costs you ten minutes and the next guy who wants a smart switch there will thank you.

threads.author: groundrod_05
threads.title: Prewar Bronx building: fixture is hot with both 3-ways off
fact_risk: Carter system wiring prohibited for new work (edition/year not stated)
NYC Electrical Code vs NEC
threads.body:
Working non-union in the Bronx, mostly apartment renovations in prewar buildings. Today we were replacing a hallway fixture in a unit in Kingsbridge. Both 3-way switches off, and I checked the fixture with my non-contact tester anyway and it lit up on both wires. My mechanic checked with a meter, said there was voltage to ground on both conductors, then said "it's a Carter, leave it and call the office."

I have never heard of a Carter system. We did 3-ways at Apex and none of this matched. What is it, and why would both wires be hot with the light off? Appreciate any explanation.

edit: nobody touched anything live. He made us stop and the office is sending someone to look at it.

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body:
Brother, your mechanic did exactly right. A Carter system is an old way of wiring 3-ways where the travelers carry the hot and the neutral, and each switch picks which one goes to its side of the light. Light's on when one side gets hot and the other gets neutral. Light's off when both sides get the same thing, and that can be both hot. So "off" doesn't mean dead.

It's been prohibited for new work for a long time, I couldn't tell you the year. You still run into it in old buildings up here. You don't fix it by swapping a switch. It gets rewired properly, under a permit, by whoever the office sends.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Good catch testing a fixture you'd been told was off. That's the whole lesson. I inspect in Jersey, not the city, so I won't speak to the NYC code, but I've seen a couple of these in very old houses at the shore. Same answer: rewire it, don't patch it.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: This is why we test before we touch on every job, even when somebody swears it's off. Verify with a meter you've just checked on a known live source. Stay safe.

replies.author: threeway_02
replies.body: I'm just starting out as a career switcher and I would have assumed off meant off. Glad I read this before my first really old house.

replies.author: groundrod_05
replies.body: Appreciate it, all of you. Going to look up the diagram tonight so I recognize it next time.

threads.author: BackflowBlues
threads.title: smart switch needs a neutral, can i just use the bare ground?
fact_risk: equipment grounding conductor may not carry normal current / be used as a neutral
listed no-neutral smart switches
threads.body: plumbing guy, mostly demo right now lol. my mom wants a smart switch for the porch light at her house in lawrence. got it out of the box and it wants a neutral. switch box has a black, a white taped black, and a bare copper. guy at the store said "some people use the ground as the neutral, it's fine, it only draws like nothing." is that ok or no. not doing anything till somebody tells me

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
No. Don't. The equipment ground is not a current-carrying conductor. It's there to carry fault current long enough to trip the breaker. Put normal current on it and every grounded thing on that circuit, metal boxes, fixture housings, appliance frames, carries a little current all the time, and if that ground path ever opens, those parts can sit at line voltage with nobody knowing. Small current doesn't make it fine.

What you described, a black and a white taped black, sounds like a switch loop: no neutral in that box. Your options are a smart switch listed to work without a neutral, a smart bulb in the fixture, or a new cable with a neutral to that box. Breaker off and tested dead before anything comes apart.

replies.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
replies.body: honestly people do it all the time, my cousin did it in his whole house. a smart switch pulls a few milliamps, nothing is going to happen. no inspector is ever coming back to look at a porch switch

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I've been on service calls where the "few milliamps" guy did his whole house, and we found it because the GFCIs and AFCIs kept tripping. It's not about the inspector coming back. It's about whoever touches that fixture someday when the ground's loose. Don't.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Agree with both of them. And whatever you end up doing, kill the breaker and verify dead with a tester you've checked. Porch lights sometimes share an outdoor circuit with things you wouldn't expect. Stay safe.

replies.author: wchen_controls
replies.body: fwiw the no-neutral smart switches are a real product, listed, and they work by trickling a tiny bit of current through the bulb instead of through the ground. downside is some leds flicker or glow with them. low voltage guy here, we run into this all the time on retrofits

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Sorry if this is a dumb question, but how would you even tell the white is taped because it's a switch loop and not just somebody's random tape?

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Not dumb. Breaker off, open the fixture box and look. In a switch loop the white from the switch cable is spliced to a hot, not to the other whites. If you can't tell, assume it isn't a neutral.

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: UA here, and this is the same conversation we have about tying a vent into a drain because "it works." works until it doesn't

replies.author: plumbnj88
replies.body: smart bulb is the easy answer. we had them at the bar i used to work at, zero wiring, never had a problem

replies.author: BackflowBlues
replies.body: update: got the no neutral one that says it's listed for that. my foreman's brother is an electrician, he came by and put it in. porch light works from the phone. mom happy. thanks

threads.author: Exit117Plumber
threads.title: LED bulbs on the basement stairs glow when the switches are off
threads.body: Helping my uncle again this weekend. His basement stairs have a light with a switch at the top and the bottom. He swapped the old bulbs for LEDs and now with both switches off they glow really faint, like a nightlight. He says it's cheap bulbs and to ignore it.
