I'm a plumbing kid so I don't really know electrical, but it bugs me. Is that a bulb thing or is something wired wrong? Should I be worried about it

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: had this in my apartment, swapped brands and it went away. so cheap bulbs, or was something else going on with mine too?

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body:
Could be the bulbs, could be the wiring, and it's worth knowing which. The common harmless cause: on a 3-way the two travelers run side by side in the same cable, and on a long run a little voltage couples from one to the other. An incandescent never shows it. An LED needs so little that it glows. Lighted switches do the same thing.

The cause you want to rule out is the switches breaking the neutral instead of the hot. Then the fixture is still hot when it's off, and somebody changing a bulb gets a surprise. Have someone qualified check it with a meter. If it's coupling, a different bulb or a small device made for this usually fixes it. Stay safe.

replies.author: peteplumb80
replies.body: my parents had this in Montclair, turned out to be the lighted switch at the bottom of the stairs. took it out, glow gone

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question? "Should I be worried" is the real one, and the answer is: not until somebody checks it. Have your uncle get an electrician to look. It's a short visit.

threads.author: RainDayRestock
threads.title: Bedroom AFCI at my dad's place trips every couple nights. Just swap it?
fact_risk: breaker size limited by conductor (14 AWG / 15 A)
combination AFCIs with ground-fault sensing trip on shared neutrals
AFCI trip indicators vary by manufacturer
threads.body:
Sorry if this is a dumb question, I'm about a month in as a helper in Brick. My dad had his panel replaced in the spring by an electrician (not my boss) and now the breaker for the back bedroom trips every two or three nights. Always at night, sometimes with nothing on but a fan and a phone charger. It's one of the breakers with the test button.

My dad's answer is "you work for an electrician now, put a regular breaker in." I said I'd ask first. The house is a 60s ranch, some of the wiring is original. Is the breaker just bad? Is it the fan? What would you even check?

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: Not an expert, I'm in vo-tech, but in our class we learned breakers trip when the load is too high. If it's a 15 amp, maybe it just needs to be a 20 amp so it stops tripping. That seems like the simplest thing to try first.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Please don't. The breaker size is set by the wire, not by what you want to plug in. If that bedroom is wired in 14 gauge, a 20 amp breaker lets the wire overheat before it trips, and that's how fires start. And a breaker that trips with a fan and a phone charger on isn't tripping on load anyway.

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: Understood, thank you for the correction. I didn't realize the wire was what set it.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly the first generation of these nuisance tripped like crazy and I cursed them on every Sandy rebuild. The newer ones are a lot better, but I still see the odd one that just doesn't like a certain fan motor or treadmill.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Thiago's right that the early ones had problems. What I see now, most trips are telling you something real. Field version of what I'd check, in order:

Is it a combination type that also senses ground faults? Many are. Then a neutral from that bedroom shared with another circuit somewhere, or a neutral touching ground in a box, will trip it, and a 60s ranch that's been added onto is exactly where that hides. Next, a loose connection or a backstabbed receptacle on the run. Then damaged cable: a nail, a staple driven too tight. Then the loads. Unplug the fan for a week and see.

And don't put a regular breaker in. That panel was just replaced under a permit, so call the electrician who did it back. It's very likely theirs to solve.

replies.author: dahvacnj
replies.body: hvac not electrical, but my house in toms river did this and it turned out to be the window ac. new ac, no more trips. thanks in advance for not laughing

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: plumbing guy in deptford. question for the electricians: how would he even find a shared neutral, is it just opening every box? appreciate it

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Pretty much, plus some tricks. Circuit off, look at how the neutrals land in the panel, open the boxes on that run and the ones next to it. In an old ranch you're also in the attic looking for junction boxes nobody remembers. It's a couple of hours, not a couple of minutes.

replies.author: Passaic_Sparky
replies.body: service guy here. most of these i find a neutral tied together in a box in the attic or the basement. idk why people did that, saved a wire nut i guess

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... hotel room kept tripping and it was the guest running a hair dryer and a space heater on the same outlet lol. Not saying that's your dad, but ask what's plugged in back there.

replies.author: WawaRunWired
replies.body: sorry if dumb but does the breaker tell you anything about why it tripped? some of ours have lights that blink after

replies.author: Passaic_Sparky
replies.body: yeah some of them do, depends on the brand. there's a code on the label or the manufacturer sheet, like arc vs ground fault. look it up for whatever's in his panel before you start opening boxes

replies.author: RainDayRestock
replies.body: update: unplugged the fan all week and it still tripped, so dad gave in and called the electrician back. He found the bedroom neutral tied in with the hallway circuit's neutral in a junction box in the attic, from some old add-on. Separated them, no trips since. Mom says thanks too, she was tired of resetting it.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: There it is. Shared neutral in the attic. Good on you for asking before swapping the breaker.

replies.author: JerseyTomatoWires
replies.body: saving this one... my foreman always says the breaker is just the messenger. appreciate it

threads.author: ExRetail_NowHVAC
threads.title: Vacuum pump keeps tripping a bedroom AFCI on install day
threads.body:
End of my first week at the new job, sorry if this is obvious to everyone. We were doing a ductless head in a back bedroom in Washington Township and I plugged the vacuum pump into the bedroom outlet. Tripped the breaker within a minute. Reset it, tripped again. Lead told me to run a cord from the garage instead and it was fine.

Homeowner was annoyed and asked me if something's wrong with her house, and I definately had no idea what to say. Is it the pump, the breaker, or her wiring? And what do you tell the customer in that moment without sounding like an idiot?

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: how does an AFCI actually tell a bad arc from a light switch?
fact_risk: how combination AFCIs detect series and parallel arcing
threads.body: ok so last year in class we covered AFCIs and the teacher said they detect "dangerous arcing." but every time you flip a switch or plug something in there's a little arc, and a brushed motor like a drill arcs constantly. so how does the breaker know which arc is the bad one? is it just guessing off some pattern? because from what I hear on here they trip on random stuff and miss other stuff, so I'm skeptical. also the teacher couldn't really answer it so here I am

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Good question, and the skepticism is reasonable. In plain terms: the breaker has electronics that watch the current waveform for the signature of a dangerous arc, the erratic high-frequency noise and the pattern a loose or damaged conductor makes over time, as opposed to the brief, predictable arc of a switch or the steady noise of a motor. Combination types look for arcing in series, like a loose connection, and from line to neutral or ground, like damaged insulation. Many also sense ground faults.

It is pattern recognition, so it isn't perfect. Some motors and electronics look suspicious to some models. That's part of why the designs keep getting updated.

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Plumbing guy, but that was a better explanation than I've gotten from two years of listening to electricians complain about them. Thanks for asking it.

threads.author: big_paulie_plumb
threads.title: new lower element in an electric water heater and the breaker trips instantly
fact_risk: typical residential element resistance range
fill and purge the tank before energizing (dry-fire)
threads.body: sorry if this is a dumb one, 4 years in and i mostly do gas tanks. condo in north bergen, electric 40 gallon, no hot water. tested and the lower element was bad so i swapped it. drained it, new element in, filled it up, turned the breaker back on and it tripped right away. reset, tripped again. didn't touch anything else. is the new element bad out of the box or did i do something

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
First question, kid: did you open a hot faucet and let it run until the water came out solid, no spitting, before the breaker went on? If the top of that tank had air in it, the upper element runs dry and dies, and sometimes takes the breaker with it.

Second: an instant trip usually means a short, not a weak element. Breaker off, verify dead at the heater, pull the wires off the element and check it with your meter. Across the two terminals you should read some ohms, roughly 10 to 17 depending on the wattage. From either terminal to the tank should read open. While you're in there, look hard at the wires you pushed back under that cover. That's the job.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Agree with all of that. From the electrical side, a straight short to ground trips any breaker instantly, and the usual spot after an element swap is a conductor pinched by the cover or nicked on the bracket. Check the insulation on both leads before you close it up.

replies.author: Elizabeth.traps
replies.body: burned up my first element that way, breaker went on before the tank was full. seconds and done. my foreman makes me bleed every tank now

replies.author: big_paulie_plumb
replies.body: update: it was the wire. the lower lead got jammed against the edge of the bracket when i stuffed the insulation back in, cut right through. new piece of wire, works fine. element was ok the whole time

threads.author: plumbguy917
threads.title: New dishwasher trips the GFCI on the dry cycle. On us or the electrician?
fact_risk: GFCI protection for dishwasher outlets (varies by code edition and NYC code)
threads.body:
1st year, Local 1. Last week my journeyman had me do the water and drain on a dishwasher in a Bay Ridge apartment, the electrician did the circuit. Customer called back: it runs through wash and rinse fine, then the GFCI trips on the heated dry. Electrician says it's the appliance. Customer's blaming us because we were the last ones under there lol.

Is there any way a water connection trips a GFCI, or is this not our problem?

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: It can absolutely be your problem without being your circuit. A GFCI trips when current leaks to ground. Two common causes on a new dishwasher: the heating element leaking current once it gets hot, which is the appliance, and water getting into the junction box under the front, which can be a weeping supply fitting right above it.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: had a callback like this in cherry hill... the elbow on the supply was weeping onto everything, you couldn't see it unless the kick plate was off and it was running

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly the dry-cycle detail is the clue. Heat makes a failing element leak, and heat plus a little water in a box makes a GFCI unhappy. Look at your fitting first because it's free: dry the whole area, run a cycle with the kick plate off, flashlight on the connection. If it's bone dry and it still trips on heat, it's the appliance and the customer calls the manufacturer. Either way, nobody bypasses the GFCI.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: My uncle tapes the threaded side of the dishwasher elbow (never the compression side) and checks it with a paper towel after the first fill. The paper towel shows drips you can't see.

replies.author: plumbguy917
replies.body: update: went back with my journeyman. elbow was weeping right onto the j-box. redid it, ran two full cycles, no trip. so yeah it was us lol. paper towel trick is going in my bag

threads.author: codebook_dale
threads.title: Sump pumps on GFCI: what I tell homeowners after every big storm
fact_risk: GFCI required for basement receptacles in current NEC editions
removal of the dedicated single-receptacle (sump) exception several code cycles ago
hardwired sump pumps and GFCI rules / local acceptance
threads.body:
Every big rain, I hear the same complaint: "the GFCI tripped and my basement flooded, why does code make me do this?" Here's how I explain it.

Current code editions want GFCI protection on basement receptacles, and the old exception that let a single dedicated sump receptacle skip it went away several cycles back. Check which code edition is in effect for your permit, because an older install may have been legal when it went in.

A GFCI that trips on a sump pump is usually telling you something. Pumps sit in water, and as they age the windings and cords leak current. That leak is exactly the thing that kills people in wet basements.

So the answer I give isn't "remove the GFCI." It's: put a high-water alarm in the pit, think hard about a battery backup pump, test the GFCI and the pump before storm season, and replace a pump that keeps tripping it. Not legal advice, just how I'd look at it after too many flooded basements.

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly I'm torn on this one and I'll say it. After Ida I had three customers with flooded basements, and every one was a tripped GFCI on the sump. I install it the way the code says, but I push the alarm and the backup pump hard, because a GFCI by itself is a bad plan in a basement that floods.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Fair, and we're not that far apart. The GFCI isn't the plan, it's the protection. The alarm and the backup pump are the plan.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Plumber's side: half the pumps I pull that were tripping GFCIs have a cord that's been sitting in water or a motor on its way out. Replace the pump, check the check valve while you're there, and the trips go away. A good pump tripping a good GFCI is rare.

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: As a student, may I ask why not put the sump on its own hardwired circuit with no receptacle at all? Wouldn't that avoid the GFCI question entirely?

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Good question. Depending on the pump, the code edition and what your local office accepts, hardwiring can change the analysis, but most pumps are cord-and-plug so they can be swapped fast at 2am. Ask the inspector before you plan around it. I wouldn't treat it as a loophole.

threads.author: ms_almonte
threads.title: Target superheat needs indoor wet bulb. Students, buy the probe.
fact_risk: target superheat charts use indoor (return) wet bulb and outdoor dry bulb
threads.body:
Every summer a few of my former students come back from their first jobs saying they "checked the superheat" on a piston system and it was fine. Then I ask what their target was and they look at me.

First, superheat by itself is just a number. On a fixed orifice system you compare it to a target, and the target comes from the manufacturer's chart or a target superheat chart, using indoor wet bulb and outdoor dry bulb.

Second, wet bulb, not dry bulb. Wet bulb tells you how much moisture the coil is dealing with, and that moves the target a lot. A sticky July afternoon in Paterson and a dry day in September want different numbers.

Third, measure the return air at the unit, not in the hallway.

Buy a decent wet bulb probe before you buy the fancy gauges. Ask me how I know which one matters more.

threads.author: QuickChekCrew
threads.title: Should gauges go on every system at a maintenance visit?
fact_risk: refrigerant loss from hoses on connection
low-loss fittings
threads.body:
Night program student here... I've been doing a ride-along with a tech this summer through a friend. At every maintenance visit he puts gauges on. My instructor says don't hook up gauges on a system that's working unless you have a reason, because you lose refrigerant every time... The tech says you can't know it's working without them.

Who's right? Or is it one of those "depends" answers... I'd like to understand the reasoning so I don't pick up a bad habit early. Thanks in advance.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Your instructor is closer, in my opinion:
- Every connection is a chance for a leak, a contaminated port, or a valve core that doesn't reseat
- On a small system, what's left in the hoses is a real share of the charge if you don't handle it properly
- You can learn a lot without them: temperature split, line temperatures, amp draw, airflow, a clean coil
- When those tell you something's off, then connect, with low-loss fittings

Plenty of good techs disagree with me on this, and that's fine. Just have a reason for every connection.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: I'm one of the ones who disagrees lol... I don't put hoses on every visit, but I do put clamp-on temp probes and wireless pressure probes on most systems. Low loss, and I'd rather see real numbers than guess from a temperature split. So this one time in AC the split looked fine on a rooftop unit and the superheat said it was way short on charge. The split doesn't tell you everything.

replies.author: joe.plumb
replies.body: we put a gauge on every water heater and boiler job, static pressure on the house, takes a minute... is hvac different?

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: he's asking about refrigerant gauges, not water pressure lol. different thing. on walk-ins i only connect when the box tells me something's wrong. every connection is a leak waiting for july

replies.author: WhichTradeTho
replies.body: Taking a night class too and we got told the same thing as your instructor. Interesting that the field guys split on it.

threads.author: HeatwaveOnCall
threads.title: where can a condensate pump actually drain in a finished basement
fact_risk: acceptable condensate disposal points (local plumbing code / inspector)
air gap or air break for indirect waste
condensate pump safety switch wiring
threads.body: ok so long story, we're doing a furnace and coil swap in a split-level in clifton and the basement is getting finished. right now the condensate pump just dumps into the laundry sink with the tube clipped on the edge. homeowner wants it "hidden," so the contractor finishing the basement asked if we can run it into the washer standpipe or tie it into the sump pit. my lead said "depends" (of course) and that it's the inspector's call. what are the normal options and which ones get people in trouble? also does the pump need anything wired to it besides the plug

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: First thing my students forget: condensate is waste, and where it goes is a plumbing code question in your town, so the inspector really is the answer. Second: whatever it drains into, don't make a direct connection to a drain without an air gap or air break. You don't want sewer gas coming back up the tube, or a backup pushing into the pump.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Field version, around here:
- Laundry tub, or a standpipe with an air gap, is the common option and usually accepted. Check locally
- The sump pit gets used a lot and some towns don't allow it. Ask before you do it
- Never glue it straight into a drain or a vent with no trap and no air gap
- Wire the pump's safety switch so the AC shuts off if the pump fails. Most pumps have the switch; plenty of installers never connect it
- Leave access. Finished basements bury pumps behind drywall and then it's a callback

The safety switch is the one that saves the new floor.

replies.author: epa60812_2
replies.body: brother we had one in paterson where the pump was buried inside a soffit, took my lead an hour just to find it. leave it where you can get to it

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: update: inspector was fine with the standpipe with an air gap. we wired the safety switch into the furnace control so the ac stops if the pump dies. contractor is building a little access door. thanks everyone

threads.author: OpenNeutralBlues
threads.title: Electrical student: why does the HVAC float switch cut the thermostat wire?
fact_risk: float switch wired in series with R or Y per instructions
threads.body: Electrical student at the county vo-tech, Nutley. I've been shadowing an HVAC tech friend of my dad's on Saturdays. He put a float switch on an AC drain pan and wired it into the thin thermostat wire, not the power. In class everything we do is 120 or 240, so I asked why not just cut power to the unit. He said "it's the control side." Can someone explain why it's done that way, and which wire it goes on?

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
"Control side" is the right answer. Here's why:
- The thermostat wiring is 24 volts and tells the system when to run. Open one wire and the call for cooling stops
- Most of those float switches are made for low-voltage control wiring, not for the line voltage the equipment runs on
- It usually goes in series with the R or the Y, depending on what you want shut down and what the instructions say
- Killing line power can also shut off things you might want running, like the blower

Follow the switch instructions and the equipment's wiring diagram, not a rule of thumb.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: And low voltage still deserves respect. First thing my students do on 24 volt wiring is short R to C and blow the little fuse on the control board. Second thing they do is swear it wasn't them. Ask me how I know.

replies.author: wchen_controls
replies.body: fwiw controls is a whole trade built on exactly this. a small signal decides what the big equipment does. if that part interests you, look at low voltage and controls. the work is mostly indoors in august too

threads.author: ExRetail_NowHVAC
threads.title: First fall startups: high-efficiency furnace drain lines, what size and how much pitch?
fact_risk: condensate drain not smaller than 3/4 in and not reduced from the equipment connection (mechanical code)
minimum slope 1/8 in per foot
manufacturer guidance against double-trapping condensing furnaces
freeze protection per manufacturer
threads.body:
Haven't started yet, but my new shop let me ride along on fall startups this week, sorry for the basic question. We're doing fall startups and maintenance, and two furnaces this week had condensate problems. One in a garage in Sicklerville where the line ran dead flat and was half full of slime, one in Blackwood where somebody necked the drain down to 1/2 inch tubing because "it's just a furnace." That one was shutting off on the pressure switch.

My lead fixed both, but I want the rules in my head. What size should the line be, how much pitch, and does it need a trap if the furnace has one built in? And what about the garage one freezing this winter? Damn, I thought heating was going to be the easy season.

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body:
First: don't neck it down. The mechanical code I learned on wants condensate drains no smaller than 3/4 inch and no smaller than the equipment's connection, all the way to where they end. Check which edition your town enforces and the furnace manual, because the manual can ask for more.

Second: pitch. At least an eighth of an inch per foot, more if you can get it. Flat lines grow exactly the slime you saw.

Third: traps. Most condensing furnaces have their own trap, and the manual will usually tell you not to add a second one in series, because a double trap can air-lock. Read it for that model.

Fourth: the garage. Protect it from freezing the way the manual says, or reroute it inside. Ask me how I know what a frozen line does in January.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Two more from the business side:
- Condensate from a condensing furnace is acidic. If it's going into a cast iron drain or onto a floor, talk about a neutralizer. Customers like hearing why
- Fall startups are where you clean the trap and the line and pour test it. That prevents the January no-heat call, which costs you more than the visit pays

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: plumbing side, we see these tied into floor drains and laundry tubs. is there a rule on where it can go, or is it the same as an AC drain? appreciate it

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Same idea as the AC drain, where it lands is the inspector's call, and an air gap if it's going to a drain... So this one time in Gloucester a whole basement smelled like sewer every fall. Somebody glued the furnace drain straight into the stack, and the furnace's trap dried out every summer. Fix took ten minutes, finding it took two hours lol.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: drain lines freeze down here too, not just up north. had a walk-in freezer in somers point go down on the coldest night because the drain line ran through an unheated hallway with no heat tape. winter is when you learn

replies.author: ExRetail_NowHVAC
replies.body: This is gold, thank you. Writing "3/4, eighth inch per foot, read the trap section" on the inside of my van door. Lead says that's how he learned too.

threads.author: dreb_jman
threads.title: Midtown tower going all heat pump. How do these do 40 floors up in January?
fact_risk: NYC Local Law 97 driving building electrification
cold-climate heat pump capacity at low ambient
supplemental heat in electrical load calculations
threads.body:
Question for the mechanical guys. The office tower in Midtown I'm on is ripping out the old steam and going all electric heat pumps, because of the city's emissions law from what the owners say. My side is new feeders up the risers, a lot more amps on every floor than the building was ever built for. Fine. That's our work.

What I want to know from the mechanical side: rooftop and setback units up there get wind like you wouldn't believe. On a 10 degree January night, 40 floors up, with wind, do these things actually keep up? Or are we going to be back in two winters adding electric heat and more feeders? Asking because I'm the one who'll be up there.

Also the 7 train is down again, so I have time to read.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Not a high-rise guy, but these are the questions I'd ask the engineer:
- What's the rated capacity at the design low temperature, not at 47 degrees? Cold-climate equipment publishes it
- Is there backup or supplemental heat in the design, and is that load already in your feeder calc?
- Defrost: where does the water go, and does it freeze on the roof?
- Who services them, and can they get to them in February?

If the engineer has answers to all of those, you're probably fine.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Data center side, we see the same thing: every mechanical change ends up being an electrical change. Get the supplemental heat into the load calc now, not as a change order later.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... the casino I worked at had rooftop heat pump units on the garage that iced up every time the wind came off the ocean in February lol. Wind matters. The engineers who've done tall buildings use screens or put the units on mechanical floors instead of out in the open.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: From the inspection side, and I don't inspect in the city: the load calculation and the equipment nameplates will tell the story. Whatever the mechanical engineer says about supplemental heat should show up on the electrical drawings. If it doesn't, ask.

replies.author: threeway_91
replies.body: staten island apprentice here, brother. our shop wired a bunch of heat pumps in houses out here last winter and they kept up fine. in houses though. no idea about 40 floors up

replies.author: neutral_bar_99
replies.body: Student question, possibly off topic: why not geothermal for a building like that? We read about it in class and it seemed like it avoids the cold air problem entirely.

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Not off topic, brother. You need somewhere to drill, and in Midtown there's a subway and a lot of foundation under you. Some buildings in the city do it. Not ours.

replies.author: HelperForNow
replies.body: following this one. our shop in manahawkin does more heat pumps every month and nobody talks about the electrical side until the panel is full

replies.author: dreb_jman
replies.body: Appreciate it. Sent the engineer Kash's list. Answer on defrost was "we'll look into it." So that's going great.

threads.author: peteq75
threads.title: Galloway colonial on propane: cold-climate heat pump or keep the furnace?
fact_risk: cold-climate heat pump ratings at 5°F
NJ Clean Energy and utility rebates (change often)
whole-house load calculation for panel capacity
nameplate MCA/MOCP
threads.body:
Sorry if this belongs somewhere else. I'm brand new on the electrical side, career switcher, but this one is my own house. 90s colonial in Galloway, no gas on our street, propane furnace and a central AC that's on its last legs. The propane bill last winter was ugly. My wife wants to go heat pump since we have to replace the AC anyway.

Everybody I talk to says something different. One guy says heat pumps don't work when it's cold. One says get rid of the furnace. One says keep the furnace as backup. And since I'm "the electrical guy" now, everyone asks me if our 150 amp panel can handle it, and I don't know.

What would you actually do here? Appreciate it.

replies.author: HelperForNow
replies.body: my old boss said heat pumps quit working under like 30 degrees and then you're on strip heat and the electric bill kills you. so keep the furnace

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
That was true of a lot of older units. It isn't true of current cold-climate equipment:
- Cold-climate heat pumps are rated to put out real heat at 5°F. Look at the published capacity at your design temperature, not the brochure
- Size it from a heat load calculation on your house, not from the old furnace's number
- Ductwork that was fine for AC can be marginal for heating airflow, so have someone check it
- NJ Clean Energy and utility rebates change often. Look up what's current before you sign anything

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body:
I'd do it a little differently from Kash, with respect. In your situation, with a furnace that still works, I'd look hard at dual fuel: a heat pump for most of the season and the propane furnace for the coldest nights. You give up a little efficiency on those nights, you keep a backup if the heat pump goes down in January, and you don't need electric strips loading your panel.

If the furnace were old too, a properly sized cold-climate heat pump with strips can absolutely carry a house in Atlantic County. Either way, step one is the load calculation. Anybody quoting you without one is guessing.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body: Fair point. With a furnace that has life left, dual fuel is a good answer and I quote it all the time. I was answering the "they don't work when it's cold" part.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: On the panel: 150 amps might be fine. You find out with a load calculation for the whole house, done by an electrician, not by adding up breaker handles. The heat pump nameplate gives you the minimum circuit ampacity and the max breaker size. Strip heat is usually what pushes a panel over.

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: egg harbor twp here, same story on half my street, propane and no gas line. the ones who went heat pump with the furnace as backup are happy. and our design temp down here isn't north jersey's

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: So this one time in AC... I did a heat pump in Absecon for a guy who swore it would never keep up, and he called me in February just to ask why the house felt so even lol. It runs longer and lower than a furnace. Tell your wife to expect that.

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body: Permits for both the mechanical and the electrical side. And if strips are part of it, make sure that circuit is in the load calculation, not added later.

replies.author: ThirdYearTinknocker
replies.body: 3rd year hvac in monmouth, we put in alot of these now. warn her the air at the register feels cooler than a furnace, like 90 something instead of way hotter. totally normal, but people call about it

replies.author: peteq75
replies.body: This is way more than I expected, appreciate it. So: load calc first, look at dual fuel since the furnace is only 8 years old, panel calc by an actual electrician. Not by me lol.

replies.author: HelperForNow
replies.body: ok i stand corrected on the 30 degree thing. old boss was going off old units i guess

replies.author: peteq75
replies.body: update: had two companies do load calcs. both came back with a cold-climate unit and keeping the furnace as backup. electrician's calc says the 150 is ok without strips. signing next week

threads.author: hec_does_ac
threads.title: Cape Cods: ductless heads upstairs or a ducted unit in the kneewall?
fact_risk: multi-zone outdoor units powering heads through the interconnect
threads.body:
Settle a fight at my shop... we're doing a lot of Capes in Gloucester and Camden County this summer, upstairs is 85 by 3pm and there's no ductwork up there. Half our guys sell a head in every bedroom. The other half want a small ducted air handler in the kneewall or the attic with short runs to each room.

So this one time in AC I put three heads in a Cape and the customer called the next summer saying the kid's room was freezing and clammy and the other two were fine lol. Oversized head in a tiny room.

What do you guys do and how do you decide? Not looking for a brand war.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
How I decide:
- Small bedrooms: the smallest wall head is often too big for them, so it short-cycles and doesn't pull moisture out. That favors ducted
- Kneewall space: if there's room for an air handler with short, sealed runs and a real return, ducted is quieter and cleaner looking
- If the kneewall is cramped, or the customer wants room-by-room control, heads
- Either way, the insulation in those kneewalls is usually terrible, so price the air sealing in

Margins are better on the ducted job if you price the labor honestly.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Here's how it plays out for us: the ducted kneewall unit is the better system when there's room, but it takes a tech who can actually design duct. Heads are more forgiving for a crew that's still learning. I sell the system my people can install well.

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: we did a cape in clifton with one ducted unit in the attic over the dormer and it was so quiet the customer thought it was off. getting up there in july was brutal though

replies.author: tnguyen_refrig
replies.body: attic air handler in a cape in july, enjoy. whatever you pick, put a pan and a float switch under it. i've seen what a kneewall full of water does to a ceiling

replies.author: thiago_sparks
replies.body: Honestly on the raised houses at the shore after Sandy we did a lot of heads, because there was nowhere to put anything. Not Capes, but the same problem: no space, no ducts.

replies.author: peteq75
replies.body: Electrical side question, sorry if dumb: does one ducted unit mean one circuit instead of three? That's a lot less work on our end.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body: Depends on the setup. A multi-zone outdoor unit usually powers its heads through the interconnect, so that's one circuit to the outdoor unit. Three separate single-zone systems are three circuits. Follow the install manual either way.

replies.author: TaylorHamHVAC
replies.body: customer question i get a lot in secaucus: do the heads look bad? and can you hide the linesets on the outside of a cape without it looking like spaghetti?

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Lol the spaghetti question... lineset covers, run them on the back of the house, and talk about it before the install, not after. Some people hate the look of a head no matter what. Those are your ducted customers.

replies.author: big_zach_hvac
replies.body: first summer in hvac, we did 6 capes in union county, all heads. didn't know ducted in a kneewall was even an option. learning

replies.author: ms_almonte
replies.body: Good thread, I'm stealing it for class. What students should take away is that you decide from the house: the room sizes, the space, the insulation, the customer. Not from whatever your shop usually sells.

threads.author: JunctionBoxJunkie
threads.title: Parents' Cape is getting mini-splits. What's the electrician's part?
fact_risk: circuit sizing from nameplate MCA and MOCP
HVAC disconnect within sight of the unit (NEC 440.14)
GFCI for outdoor HVAC equipment (2020 NEC 210.8(F)) and later changes/local amendments
threads.body: my parents' cape in hamilton is getting a 3-zone mini-split next month and the hvac company said "you'll need an electrician for the power." my dad looked at me because I'm in the electrical program at vo-tech, which, no, I'm a student. but I want to understand what the electrician is actually going to do so I can watch and not be useless. like how do they know what size breaker, what's the box on the wall outside for, and does it need a GFCI? our book says something about outdoor GFCI but my teacher said it's complicated

replies.author: codebook_dale
replies.body:
Your teacher's right that it's complicated. Here's the outline. Wire and breaker size come from the outdoor unit's nameplate: the minimum circuit ampacity sets the wire, the maximum overcurrent protection sets the largest breaker allowed. The box outside is the disconnect, which the code wants within sight of the unit so a tech can kill it while working on it.

The GFCI part: a recent code edition expanded GFCI requirements for outdoor outlets in a way that caught HVAC equipment, a lot of inverter units nuisance tripped, and there were changes and local amendments afterward. Check which code edition is in effect for your parents' permit. That's a question for the inspector, not the internet.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body: From the HVAC side, also watch the interconnect between the outdoor unit and the heads. Most multi-zone units power the heads from the outdoor unit through that cable, and the manual specifies the wire. Nobody should be using leftover thermostat wire for it.

replies.author: Exit117Plumber
replies.body: Watch where the condensate from each head goes too. Not electrical, but my uncle got called to a Cape where a head was draining into the wall cavity lol

replies.author: big_zach_hvac
replies.body: we just did 3 of these in elizabeth. electrician was there like 2 hours total, disconnect, whip, breaker, done. we ran the interconnect ourselves

threads.author: MonmouthPlumber
threads.title: One multi-zone outdoor unit or separate single-zone systems for my Cape?
fact_risk: single-zone vs multi-zone part-load efficiency and low-temperature ratings
threads.body:
This is for my own house, not a job. Cape in Middletown, upstairs has two bedrooms and a small bath, downstairs has the original oil-fired baseboard and window units. We're finally doing mini-splits before next summer.

I have two quotes. One is a single multi-zone outdoor unit with three heads. The other is three separate single-zone systems, one for each bedroom plus one for the living room, so three outdoor units. The second is more money and more equipment on the side of the house.

The salesman on the first one says multi-zone is "the same thing, just one box." I'm a plumber, so I get suspicious when someone says that. What are the actual tradeoffs? Thanks in advance.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
It's not the same thing:
- One multi-zone outdoor unit fails, every room is down. Separate systems fail one at a time
- Multi-zone units often run less efficiently when only one small head is calling, which in a bedroom is most of the night
- Single-zone units usually have better low-temperature heating ratings, if you care about heat
- Multi-zone is fewer boxes outside and one circuit, which some houses need

For three rooms I lean singles if the budget and the wall space allow. For five rooms in a small house, multi-zone starts making more sense.

replies.author: hec_does_ac
replies.body: Agree with Kash mostly... the one thing I'd add is ask both companies for the head sizes, room by room. Small bedroom with a big head is the callback I see the most lol

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Sorry if this is off topic, but since the downstairs is oil baseboard, would they replace that too, or do people keep the boiler for heat?

replies.author: MonmouthPlumber
replies.body: We're keeping the boiler for now. Getting the upstairs comfortable is the goal this year, heat can be the next project.

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: plumbing in deptford. my parents went multi-zone and the outdoor unit died last july, whole house hot for a week waiting on a part. appreciate the singles point

replies.author: PullingWireAgain
replies.body: Electrical side... three singles is three circuits and three disconnects... ask who's doing the electric and whether it's in the price

replies.author: NorthJerseyCopper
replies.body: UA 24 1st year. Asking for the same reason, my parents have a Cape in Fair Lawn. Following.

replies.author: MonmouthPlumber
replies.body: update: asked both for head sizes. The multi-zone quote had a head in the small bedroom about twice what the other company sized. Going with the singles.

threads.author: FluxOnMyBoots
threads.title: what actually happens in an oil to gas conversion, start to finish
fact_risk: utility gas service and meter process
oil tank removal/abandonment rules vary by town
permits and inspection before utility turn-on
threads.body: career switcher, night class, ewing. my neighbor is converting from oil and asked me what's involved since i'm "in plumbing now" lol. i have no idea and ziggy's on a job all week so asking here. who does what, how long does it take, and what happens to the tank in the basement? just want the big picture so i don't say something dumb to him

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
Big picture, roughly in order:
- Utility first: is gas available on the street, and how long for a service and a meter. That timeline drives everything
- Equipment: a new gas boiler or furnace is the usual answer. Converting the old oil boiler with a gas burner is possible but less common
- Venting: a liner for the chimney, or a direct-vent unit out the side wall
- Gas piping sized from the meter to everything that will burn gas
- Permits and inspections before the utility turns it on
- The oil tank: removed or properly abandoned, depending on the town and where it is

A licensed contractor for all of it. Your neighbor's job is to pick someone good, not to figure it out.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Kash covered it. One thing for you, kid: next time the neighbor asks, the right answer is "call two licensed shops and ask them about the chimney and the tank." Knowing what to ask is half of it. That's the job.

replies.author: NorthJerseyCopper
replies.body: UA 24 here, 1st year. We did two of these in Fair Lawn this summer. The tank part took longer than the boiler both times. Idk why but every time.

threads.author: TryingAllThree
threads.title: Three conversion quotes, three different answers on the chimney
fact_risk: orphaned water heater draft problems / chimney liner sizing
sidewall vent materials per manufacturer
threads.body:
Different kind of question from me. We're finally converting our own house in Piscataway from oil to gas: split-level, oil boiler with baseboard, hot water off a tankless coil in the boiler. Got three quotes and they disagree on the chimney.

Quote 1: new gas boiler and a new gas water heater, both into the chimney with a new liner.
Quote 2: high-efficiency boiler vented out the side wall in plastic, new water heater into the existing chimney, no liner.
Quote 3: high-efficiency boiler out the side wall, a separate sidewall-vented water heater, chimney not used at all.

Quote 2 is cheapest. Quote 1's guy says Quote 2 is going to cause problems. Who's right, and why does the chimney matter so much? Appreciate it. Joy told me to get more than one quote, so here we are. Still doing ride-alongs too, so this is half for the house and half for me.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body:
Quote 1's guy is pointing at a real problem, kid. That old chimney was sized for an oil boiler sending a lot of hot exhaust up it. Take the boiler out, and a gas water heater alone in that big flue is what we call an orphaned water heater. Not enough heat to draft right, so the flue gas cools and condenses, and you get weak draft, moisture eating the masonry, and possibly exhaust spilling into the basement.

That's why conversions get a liner sized for whatever's left in the chimney, or take the chimney out of the picture like Quote 3. Quote 2 could be fine if they actually checked that chimney, so ask them exactly how. If the answer is "it'll be fine," that's a no.

And CO detectors on every floor, whoever you pick.

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
What I'd ask all three:
- Did you do a heat loss, or are you matching the old boiler's size? Old oil boilers are usually oversized
- Who removes or abandons the oil tank, and is it in the price?
- Who handles the gas service with the utility?
- What's the warranty on the installation, not just the equipment?

replies.author: BackflowBlues
replies.body: my foreman did one of these in lawrence where the water heater got left orphaned in the chimney. went back in november because the co alarm kept going off lol. relined it

replies.author: benplumb79
replies.body: Sorry, newer guy question. Is the side wall vent the white plastic pipe sticking out of the side of houses? I always wondered what those were.

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body:
Thanks Ziggy, this is exactly what I needed. Going to ask Quote 2 how they checked the chimney.

edit: Quote 2 said they'd "see when they get there." Going with Quote 3.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: Good call. "We'll see when we get there" on venting is the answer that gets people hurt. And benplumb, yes, usually PVC or a similar plastic on high-efficiency equipment, whatever the manufacturer specifies.

threads.author: big_hector_plumb
threads.title: Customer wants the old oil tank left in the basement after the gas conversion
fact_risk: NJ DEP involvement and certified contractors when a heating oil tank leaks
municipal permits for tank removal or abandonment in place
homeowners insurance coverage of tank leaks
NYC rules for cellar/vault oil tanks
threads.body:
Service tech, Union City. Finishing a conversion next week in a two-family in Weehawken. Customer wants the 275 gallon oil tank in the basement just left there, empty, "for later." Then he tells me the home inspector on another house he's buying found a buried tank in the yard during the tank sweep, and the seller says "it was abandoned years ago."

Boss is out till Monday and I'm bad at talking to customers lol. What do I tell him on both? I know we don't do tank work, I just don't want to sound like an idiot.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Basement tank first. Empty is never empty, kid. There's always sludge and some oil in the bottom. Leave it and it leaks someday, or the next buyer's inspector flags it. On most of our conversions the tank comes out: pumped, cleaned, cut up, hauled. Your town may want a permit for the removal. Tell him your boss will price it, and don't let him keep it "for later."

replies.author: SumpPumpSeason
replies.body: our boss in woodbridge puts the tank removal right in the conversion quote so the customer can't skip it. saves you this exact conversation. appreciate the thread

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body:
On the buried tank, from my experience in NJ:
- Ask the seller for paperwork. "Abandoned" without a permit and closure paperwork from the town means very little
- If there's any sign of a leak, it becomes a cleanup, and in NJ that brings in DEP rules and certified contractors
- His attorney and insurance company should hear about it before closing, not after
- None of this is yours to sort out. Send him to his attorney and a tank company

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: And on the buried one, I'd want it pulled and the soil tested before I bought that house.

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: Respectfully, Ziggy, pulling isn't always the answer on buried tanks. Some are under a porch, an addition or a driveway, and abandonment in place, done properly with a permit and soil sampling, is what gets done. The paperwork is the thing. Depends on the town.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: Fair, Rui. If it can't come out, it's done on paper. My point is "abandoned years ago" with no paper isn't abandoned.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body: What's your actual question? You asked two. Basement: it should come out, your boss prices it. Yard: not your job, send him to a lawyer and a tank outfit. Two sentences, then stop talking.

replies.author: big_hector_plumb
replies.body:
> Two sentences, then stop talking.

lol that's the part i need

replies.author: bklyn_arkady
replies.body: In the city it's different in the details. Some older buildings still have oil tanks in the cellar or a vault, and the rules and who you call are city ones. Same principle though. Nobody believes "empty" and nobody believes "abandoned" without paperwork.

replies.author: HeatwaveOnCall
replies.body: dumb question, why is a buried tank such a big deal if it's just sitting there? like if it's not leaking what's the problem? and who even checks

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body: Because old steel in wet soil eventually leaks, and nobody knows when. When it does, the cleanup can get very expensive, and it can land on the homeowner. That's why buyers here do tank sweeps, and why sellers get nervous about them.

replies.author: Dev_H
replies.body: had one in deptford where the customer's homeowners insurance didn't cover the leak. paid out of pocket. appreciate this thread

replies.author: blowerwheel_91
replies.body: Apologies if this is basic. In Morris County a lot of houses still have oil. Is tank removal something HVAC companies do, or is it always a separate company? Thanks in advance.

replies.author: haddad_mech
replies.body: Mostly separate. On our commercial jobs it's always a sub with its own insurance for that work. Here's what I look for in that sub: their permits and paperwork, every time.

replies.author: mbell_wireman
replies.body: Electrical side note: the oil burner circuit and its emergency switch should be removed or properly reused during the conversion. I've seen dead burner switches left at the top of the stairs for decades confusing everybody. Label it or remove it.

replies.author: plumbnj77
replies.body: brother we pulled an "empty" one out of a basement in brick last month, bottom had a few inches of sludge. smelled for days. who even takes that stuff?

replies.author: big_hector_plumb
replies.body: talked to him today. basement tank is coming out, boss is pricing it. told him the yard one is a lawyer question. he actually listened lol. thier inspector already told them the same thing so that helped

replies.author: rui_t_kearny
replies.body: That's how you do it. My father used to say the customer remembers how you said it more than what you said.

replies.author: TryingAllThree
replies.body: We're in the middle of our own conversion and tank removal was in all three quotes. Reading this, I'm glad it was.

threads.author: EssexPipes
threads.title: Sizing gas pipe for a conversion: why does everyone talk about the longest run?
fact_risk: longest-length method for gas pipe sizing (fuel gas code tables)
CSST bonding requirements
pressure test and inspection before utility turn-on
threads.body:
2 years in, Bloomfield. We're doing a bunch of oil to gas conversions this fall and I'm finally being let near the gas piping, carrying and cutting at least. My journeyman sized the pipe for a house with a boiler, a water heater and a range and kept saying "the longest run" and "total BTU." Why the longest run and not each run on its own? And why does it matter if the pipe's a little small, the gas still gets there right?

Not planning on doing any of this myself. I just want to understand it before somebody quizzes me on the job.

replies.author: joyd_plumbing
replies.body:
What's your actual question? Two, I count.

Why it matters: undersized pipe means not enough gas reaches the appliance when everything runs at once. The burner runs starved, burns badly, and can make carbon monoxide. "Gets there" isn't enough. It has to get there at the right pressure.

Why the longest run: the common method in the code tables sizes every section using the total length from the meter to the farthest appliance, and the BTU load that section carries. It's conservative on purpose. Your journeyman reads the table for that gas pressure and pipe material.

He does the sizing, the master signs for it, the inspector checks it, and it gets tested before the utility turns anything on.

replies.author: oldsteam_zig
replies.body: And the load is the input rating off each appliance's nameplate, not a guess. Add them up and think about what they might add later, a dryer, a generator. Cheaper to run it right once, kid.

replies.author: dhollis61
replies.body: use the table for your pressure and material. test it. get it inspected. don't light anything that wasn't tested.

replies.author: epa60812_2
replies.body: brother hvac helper in paterson here. we see undersized gas on furnace calls all the time, burner looks lazy and yellow. now i know why

replies.author: hudson_conduit
replies.body: electrical guy here but the yellow flexible gas pipe needs to get bonded right? our shop got called about that on a conversion lol

replies.author: Kash_sing
replies.body: Yes. CSST comes with its own bonding instructions, the code has a say too, and it matters mostly because of lightning. It gets bonded the way the manufacturer and your local code say. Nobody should be making that one up on site.

replies.author: OpenNeutralBlues
replies.body: Our shop teacher mentioned bonding that yellow gas tubing last week. Didn't understand why until this thread.

threads.author: neutral_bar_99
threads.title: What is the red switch plate at the top of my basement stairs for?
threads.body:
Vo-tech student, electrical, Passaic County class of '27. This is about my grandparents' house in Wayne, which I've been looking at much more carefully since I started the program. At the top of the basement stairs there's a switch with a red plate that says something like "burner emergency." My grandfather says it's for the oil burner. They converted to gas a few years ago and the boiler is new.

Does that switch still do anything now? Is it supposed to stay with a gas boiler, and if so, why is it at the top of the stairs and not next to the boiler? I'm only asking out of curiosity, I'm not planning to touch it.
